A COUNTRY LIFE FOR ME. A country life for me, mi lads, A country life for me! O'er breezy hills an' eawry dales Aw's ramble till aw dee. Aw fost si leet wheer t' sky wer breet, An' throstles sung so gay, An' awlus loved th' owd country side When aw wer miles away. Eawr Bill, 'at lives V yonder teawn, Thinks th' country varra grand . When t' summer sun shines gaily deawn, An' breetens o the land; But when there's snow, or cowd winds.blow, I' th' bracin' winter time, He's no moor taste for th' country lanes Than angels hey for crime! He says it's ankle-deep i' slutch So wheer yo set yer feet, An' t' looans are awful after dark • For want o' gradely lest. Beawt music-halls, theatres, balls, Or owt to pass time on, He thinks he'd be a gradely foo Afoor a month wer gone. Well, well! aw comd expect as fooak Will o think like misel ; But why they dornd, o'er sich a thing, Is moor nor aw con tell. • When t' rain comes deawn so dree teavrn, A fella's spirit drops To ceawr th' heawse wi' nowt to see But slates an' chimbley tops. I' th' daytime th' factory chimblies belch Their smook mony a street; There's drunken fooak an' railway trains As rowl abeawt o neet ! There's childer thin, 'ate never sin The bonny brids and trees, Their faces look so white for want 0' th' healthy country breeze!

Aye, give to m; the country lanes, Where peace an' quateness dwell, For theer.a sweetness floods mi heart As words can never tell I O'er breezy hills an' fleawry dales Aw'm fain to ramble still, An' fo asleep i' th'.owd churchyard A, th' foot o' yonder bill! Higher Walton, March, 1888.
GEORGE BULL.

Each man is a hero and an oracle to somebody. Our words and actions to be fair must be timely. A drop of water has the properties of the sea, but can- not exhibit a storm. Joy does not mean levity, witty sayings, or repartee; it is habitual serenity. A political orator, noted for his quickness of repartee, gave an opportunity, after speaking one evening, for any, in the audience to ask questions. A member of the opposite party proposed a question which he tried to answer, but did not succeed the first time. Alter trying again, he said to the questioner, "There, are you satis- fied now ?" "No, there is a little woo over my eyes still." "Well, I guess it naturally grew there," was the sharp rejoinder. AN ENLARGEMENT OF THE LIVER...—They were house- keeping in a summer cottage near New York, a young mrrried couple and their several college friends. One afternoon on the piazza, before a game of tennis. the Wesleyan man discovered a joke in a city paper which he thought the young housekeeper would relish. He handed her the paper, with the remark, "That's pretty good." The Queen read the following :--- Scxxx—Brrektrae9 SHOP.

Young Married Lady "What have you to-day?" Butcher : "Not much to-day, mum—a hind quarter of veal and liver." Young Married Lady (after a moment's deliberation): "Well. I will take a hind quarter of liver." Having read, although evidently a little puzzled, she im- mediately said, with that ever ready and ever-to-be- remembered smile, "Why, any one would know better than that." And when the Wesleyan man asked, "How is that?" she responded, "A hind quarter of liver would be too much." Emu AND Low.—A few years ago the Episcopal dio- cese of Kentucky appeared to be torn up with dissen- sions about High and Low Church views. The Bishop unfortunately allowed his sympathies to be drawn out to one of these parties as against the other, and there- after, becoming disheartened and discouraged, resigned the bishopric. The present Bishop, when called to the diocese, was determined to ignore these dissensions, and if possible to harmonise his people and bring them into the broad, liberal views of the Church. For some time neither of these parties was able to discover whether his sympathies were with one or the other party, until, an occasion presenting itself in a social circle, a lady (with the curiosity of the sexi said: "Bishop, what are your views? We cannot find out. Are you High Church or Low Church ?" Instantly the Bishop replied: "Madam, lam High, Low, Jack, and the Game." It is needless to add there are no dissensions now. The Game has been won; Jack is forgotten; High and Low, rich and poor, are in harmony under his ministry.—Harper's Magazine. ASLEEP IN THE PuLprr.—Those old days of deliberate shooting with a muzzle-loader and dogs were very pleas- ant, though perhaps we were rather drowsy. But "repose" is the virtue to be preached and practised now. I remember, however, one parson of my youth who somewhat overdid this combination of performance and doctrine, since, one Sunday, he went to sleep while he was preaching. Fact. A friend of ours was present, and saw him do it. He was always slow, and on this occasion got slower and slower till he stopped altogether. This woke UP those who nodded,and on looking towards the pulpit they saw him sleeping while he stood; like a horse. I forget the end of the story. But he passed from a sermon into a snore. So did another man. That was in Rutlandshite. A parson there told me of it. This second sleeper had gone kindly to take the duty for a neighbour a few miles off; in August. He walked to the church, and being well in time looked into the vicar- age. The kindly servant said, 'You seemed tired, sir; won't you have a glass of ale after your walk?" Yes, he would; and did—and felt refreshed. The day how- ever was very hot, the afternoon was its hottest part, and the freshly dined rustic congregation (who had been reaping and binding all the week) mostly fell asleep. There was a (nasal) murmuring among the people. The doors, too, were wide open, and bumble bees sailed slow- ly down the aisle adding to the hum. Thus when the preacher went into the pulpit he caught the sentiment of the congregation, and after putting his face reverently between his hands for a few seconds remained in the same attitude, fast asleep. There was no record (at least I remember none) on this occasion either of the awakening of anybody. My friend learnt of the incident from the rustic Clerk.—Cornhill Magazine. NOVEL TOAST Lisrs.—The March part of C'lambers' Journal contains a chatty chapter on "The Poetry of Toast Lists and Menu Cards." The writer says that toast lists and menu cards are often very interesting; they are frequently artistic in design, and enriched with quotations from the poets, which render them of more than passing interest. A few quotations from some of the best of these which have come under our notice are surely worth reproducing. The authors represented cover a wide field, ranging from Shakspere to 'Tenny- son. The former is the most quotable poet, and he is most frequently drawn upon. Burns, however, runs hira very closely. In turning over a pile of toast lists, the first to attract our attention is the one prepared for the Hull Shaksperean Festival. On the front page is a portrait of the bard and the familiar line of " rare" Ben Jonson He was not for an age, but for all time. Under the first toast—that of the Queen—are two lines from "Henry V.":— God and his angels guard your sacred throne. And make you long become it The toast of the evening follows: "The Immortal Memory of Shakspere "—Dr. Johnson's well-known verse beneath it:— Each change of many-coloured life he drew; Exhausted worlds, and then imagined new; Existence saw him spurn her bounded reign, And panting Time tolled after him in vain. The third speaker had for his topic "Shakspere's Univer- sality, with a motto from "Romeo and Juliet:"— Monarch of the universal earth.

Actors and actresses were next toasted under the head- ing of "Shaksperean Exponents," with a quotation from " Othello :" Speak of me as I am; nothing extenuate. Nor set down aught in malice. The next theme was " Shakspere and Tragedy, with a line from " Richard !IL lixe to look upon their tragedy. Then followed " Shakspere and Comedy." with two lines from the "Taming of the Shrew :" Frame your mind for mirth and merryment, Which bars a thousand harms. Under the sentiment of " Shakspere and History," is a line from "Henry IV." (Fart II.) : There is a history in all men's lives. Lastly, "Shaksnerean Women" were remembered, and under the toast are three lines as follow from the third part of "Henry VI. :" 'Tis beauty that doth oft make women proud • 'Tis virtue that doth make them most admired; 'Tis modesty that makes them seem divine. The programme of music is headed with a couple of lines from "Twelfth Night:"— It music be the food of love, play on; Give me excess of it. At the foot of the card is printed "Good Night," and a quotation from "Macbeth," as follows At once good night; Stand not upon the order of your going, But go st once. div.p: THE SINGULAR FATALITY AT WARRINGTON. A DOCTOR'S CERTIFICATE QUESTIONED. On Saturday Mr. S. Brighouse, coroner for South- west Lancashire, held an inquest at the General Wolte Inn, Church-s'..reet, Warrington, respecting the death of Thomas Blackburn, (62) of 129, How- ley Quay, which occurred on the previous Tuesday, under circumstances that were explained in the evidence. Before witnesses were examined, the Coroner informed the jury that on the previqus Sunday night deceased, who was then in good health, was out walking with a Mr. Knight, his nephew. They wervon an errand to the Work- house. Deceased looked at a sign, and as he tnrned to continue in the direction the two were going, he caught his head against a lamp post He- % com- plained that he had hurt himself, became uncon- scious when he got home, and died on the Tuesday following. He was attended by Dr. Fox, who certi- fied that his death was due to apoplexy. Deceased, when he came home on Sunday. had complained that he had nearly killed himself, but, notwithitand- ing that, the doctor had certified the death as one attributable to natural causes. The police had re- ported the case to him, and he had come to •ask them to hear evidence, and to say whether they did not think that death was due to the injuries which thp deceased had accidentally received. Evidence was then taken and Martha Blackburn, the widow, deposed that deceased had always enjoyed good health, and that he had never, to her recollection, had fits of dizziness. When he returned home on Sunday evening he put his hand to his head, and said—" I have very nearly killed myself; I caught my head against a lamp post." He then became unconscious, and remained so up to the time of his death, which occurred at five o'clock on Tuesday evening. Witness's nephew told Dr. Fox about deceased having knocked his head against a lamp post.—William Knight, of 15, Bl'a.ckley-street, the nephew spoken of, said that on Sunday he was walking in Guardian-street, with the deceased, who was taking a letter to the Workhouse. Deceased was looking at a sign of a public-house' and, in turning, knocked his head against a lamp post. Witness, having also spoken of the subsequent events, said that when deceased became unconscious he went for Dr. Fox, and told him what had happened.—Dr. Fox said that on Sunday he was called in to see the deceased, and was told the history of the case, —how. Blackburn had knocked his head against a post in Guardian-street. When he got to the house deceased was unconscious and he remained so up to the time of his death.—The Coroner: Do you think the injury he re- ceived in Guardian-street had anything to do with his death P—Witness I should not liketosay.---The Coroner: Did the symptoms correspond with such an event ? Witness: It may have been due to the accident or to natural causes.—The Coroner: As I understand, you say "primary cause, apoplexy ? "—Witness: Yes; that is, rupture of a blood vessel on the brain.—The Coroner: There is nothing on the certificate to guide the registrar as to whether it was caused from natural causes orother- wise.—Witness :I could not certify without a post-mortem examination whether it was due to accident or not.— The Coroner: It was as reasonable to think that death was due to the accident.—Witness: I had some doubt as to whether I should have reported it or not at the time.— The Coroner: You are called in to see a case; you are

told --a-,;;-„, has knocked his head against a lamp post, and has injured himself. When you get there the man is unconscious. Suppose the same thing were to occur again would you still certify apoplexy P—Witness: He was perfectly conscious for three hours afterwards, walked about apparently as though he might have had no accident at all, and it is just possible that the blood vessel may have been ruptured independent of that.— The Foreman of the Jury: Were there any marks ? Witness: The slightest bruise on the right cheek; no- thing of any consequence. In fact, it had to be pointed out to me that he had one. The Coroner, addressing the jury, said that, as it seemed to him, the whole thing was consistent. The deceased was in good health; there was nothing to lead to the supposition that he was a likely subject for apoplexy. If they believed the nephew' who was evidently the witness of truth, the deceased knocked his head against the lamp-post, and the deceased himself, evidently referring to that fact, told his wife that he had nearly killed himself. He did not think that it was right on the part of Dr. Fox, having had this history/ related to him, to certify the death as being due to natural causes. He admitted that, under the Births and Detiths Registra- tion Acts of 1874, it was laid down that When a medical man attended a person in his last illness, he was entitled to certify the cause of death, whether such death was due to natural causes or -Otherwise. Not only was the medical man entitled to give a certificate, but the rela- tives were entitled to ask him for one. But there should _ _ _ .

...... be pointed out circumstances that would lead the regis- trar of deaths to judge whether he should register the death or refer it to the coroner. The onus rested with the registrar. He was not saying that the doctor should not have given a certificate, for, unfortunately, under the present state of the law, the relatives were entitled to demand it. He thought that, the history of the case having been repeated to Dr. Fox in the way that the witne.!ses had related, which was admitted by the doctor, the least be could have done would have been to say that the primary cause of death was injuries to the head' and that the secondary cause was apoplexy. In that case the registrar would have referred the case to the coroner. —Dr. Fox took exception to the coroner saying that he had certified death to be due to natural causes. It was a rupture of a blood vessel on the brain, but whether from natural causes or accident he did not know.—The Coroner Your certificate says " primary cause, apoplexy," and there is nothing on that certificate to lead the registrar of deaths to find out anything about it. I say advisedly that the police and the registrars have grave duties imposed upon them, and are not in the same position in life that medical men are, and who yet have greater duties imposed upon them, cannot carry out the law satisfactorily unless they are helped by others.—Dr. Fox: We should have to write a letter to every certifi- cate if we had to write all the circumstances. I say now that my certificate does not certify whether death is due to natural causes or to an accident.—The Coroner; If I had been a medical man I should have said to the rela- tives—" lam not certain that it is a death' from natural causes; there is a doubt about it. The registrar will register the death, and, to save time, it will be better for you to relate the circumstances to the police at once." The jury then unanimously expressed the opinion that deceased had died from injuries accidentally re- ceived, and returned a verdict to that effect.—After a little conversation, the jury added to their verdict the fol- lowing rider :—" The jurors present that they agree with the remarks of the coroner, and that in their opinion Dr. Fox ought to have set out in his certificate the fact that deceased had received injuries in the man- ner described to him by the nephew of the deceased."

TRADES CONFERENCE.—A conference of delegates repre- senting the organised trades of the United Kingdom was held on Thursday at the Westminster Palace ifotel. Mr. Burt, M.P., presided, and there were also present Messrs. W. Crawford, M.P., and C. Fenwick. M.P., and dele- gates from all parts of the kingdom. The object, of the conference was to obtain from representatives of the great industries:some definite declaration with respect to fiscal policy. Resolutions were passed declaring unshaken belief in the policy of Free Trade, denouncing State bounties, and calling upon the Government to adopt measures with a view to the abolition of foreign State bounties. div.head: TAT EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH 24., 1888.
div.p: TAT EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH 24., 1888.
PUBLICANS AT THE POLICE COUIIT.

At the Borough Court. at Warrington, on Mon- day, before the Mayor (Alderman Sutton) and Councillor Greening, Minnie Dolan, a married woman, was summoned for having been drunk on licensed premises on the 13th instant. Evidence was given by P.C. Monoghan to the effect that on the afternoon oi the day in question he. in company with Inspector Spinks, visited the Higher Angel Inn, Buttermarket-street, kept by Thomas Higgm- sori. They then saw defendant, Who was intoxica- ted, with a glass of beer in her hand. Higginson, he landlord, •on having his attention called to her, remarked that "she was not bad." The officers took defendant to the house where she was lodg- ing. Corroborative evidence was then given by Inspector Spinks, who said that defendant was drinking" fourpenny " beer, which, he admitted, was not very strong. The Bench decided not to give an opinion in Dolan's case, until a charge against the landlord, who was summoned for hav- ing permitted drunkenness on his premises, had been heard. The evidence was the same as in the first case, but Mr. Jenkins, who appeared to defend Rigg,inson, put several questions to Inspector Spinks, who said that he was satisfied that the glass of beer he and Constable Monoghan saw was the only one with which Dolan had been served. The landlord said that it was a "penny jill." In de- fence Mr. Jenkins said that he believed Minnie Dolan had been in another house, where the police found her asleep, and that she afterwards went to the Higher Angel. The landlord and another person were, at the time she went to the house, engaged in repairing the electric bells of the establishment. Dolan called for a" penny jill," and Mrs. Higginson' not observing that she was under the influence of drink, supplied it. AlmOst before Dolan had time to drink any of it the Inspector and Constable came in. He did not wish to blame the police for the action that they had taken, but he con- tended that drink had been supplied inadvertantly, the landlady not perceiving that Dolan was any the wotse for drink. For the defence, Frederick Kirkham, a wire drawer, who was in the house working at the time in question, gave it as his opinion that Dolan was Dot drunk, Mrs. Higginson said that she did not notice any- thing to lead her to suppose that the woman was tipsy, and the defendant Higginson said positively that she was sober,—After the Bench had heard this evidence the Mayor said that in defence to the opinion of his brother magistrate on the Bench, he would hear another case before the present one , was decided.—Mr. Jenkins claimed that he was entitled to have a verdict before any other case was gone into.—The Mayor intimated that as far as he was concerned he was ,ready to give a decision at once.—Councillor Greening: I think it is only right that we should hear the evidence as touching the state of the4woman when she was in the Gun Inn. We have the evidence of the two police 'officers who swear that the woman was drunk, and we have the evi- dence of Higginson and his wife, who swear that she was not drunk. What are we to make of it ?—Mr. Jenkins

said that it was illogical and unreasonable that the minds of the magistrates should be influenced by the facts of a second case, before they gave a dedsion in the present one.—Mr. Greening: Do not impute 'motives of that kind to me, if you please. Mr. Jenkins : I am ,bound to do so.

_ Councillor Greening: You must not.—The Mayor: I am prepared to'give a decision on this case at once. I do not think anything that follows will influence me at all. My mind is made up as to what the decision will be. So far as lam concerned Ido not think it willmake the slightest difference.—Mr. Jenkins said that, without any disrespect, he must claim that he was entitled to ask fora decision. What he had said was a logical deduction to be drawn .—Councillor Greening : If yen think I have come here to be partial to one thing or another, it is quite time I was removed.—Mr. Jenkins: I do not think it, sir.—Councillor Greening: In my opinion the evid- ence shows that the woman was drunk.—Mr. White (magistrates' clerk) : The question is whether there was anything to lead Mrs. Higgmson to know that she was drunk.—Councillor Greening remarked that he did not say that Mrs. Higginson had supplied chink with a guilty knowledge.—. The Mayor: In this case we will give a decision. I think we both perfectly agree upon it. We believe that, according to the evidence of the police officers, the womom had had too much drink, and ,that they were perfectly justified in interfering in the manner that they did. But according to the evidence that , has been given by the various witnesses on behalf of the defendant Higginson we are of opinion that there is a doubt as to whether Mrs. Higginson knew that she was drunk. We believe, rather, that Mrs. Hig- ginson could not see that she had had too much drink, and that she had no intention of supplying drink te one who wag not entitled to it. We think that under the cir- cumstances, we should give the benefit of the doubt to Higginson, and, as far as he is concerned, we dismiss the case. Regarding the female defendant we will reserve our decision until we have heard the other case against her. Minnie Dolan was then charged with having been drunk on the licensed premises of Joseph Proctor, the Gun Inn, Scotland-road, on the same date, and Proctor was charged with having permitted drunkenness. The evidence in this case was to the effect that the police found Dolan on a form at the Gun, and that she was most certainly drunk. After being turned out of that house she went to the Higher Angel. The case for the defence was that she was perfectly sober, but that, having been turned out of the house during the night by, her husband, she was very sleepy.—The Mayor said that it was just possible that having been up all night caused her to appear to be in a drunken condition. He thought that the police had acted perfectly right, but both he and Councillor Greening thought that the evi- dence was quite insufficient to justify them in saying that Dolan was drunk. Under the circumstances they felt justified in dismissing all the cases. He thought, however, that if landlords were more careful, the magis- trates would not have so many drunken cases before them.

_ EAWR MOLLY'S I' LUV. A gret change hes cum o'er yon lass, Hoo's getten so natty lan quare ; Her temper's turned wrang side abeawt— To plague her is mooar than aw dare. Hoo's fidgetin' up un deawn th' heawse, Ne'er sattled, but allus on t' move; Aw've watched her, un, judgin' bi th' way Hoo's shapin'—eawr Molly's i' luv ! Sumtimes hoo's so gaumless tin dull— Avv korn'd help bud nooatis her ways— Hooll ged up i' higs abeawt nowt, Un try iv a row boo con raise. Boo's sulky and cram'd wi' us o, Nod th' odd un con do owt ut's reight ; Ho* mon be upset in her thowts— Aw dorn'd keer heaw soon they ged streyt. • Hoes like a gret mopus th' nook, Sweet tempered un mild as a bear; Un iv hoo's disturbed just the leeast Hool hanch ut o them as is near. Hoo's like as hoo's muddled a bit, But thinks as ther's nobry con tell, Hoo's cooartin' !—awm certain o thad, ' Aw once wur th' same way misel. 800 tries bits o' oddments on t' quate, Un fancies hersel afooar t' glass ; Her hair's twisted up i' th' new style, Un hoo's started o' grippin' ut brass. When wimmin ged on i' that rooad, Yet seem as they keer'd nod a rap, It's a sign as is never far wrong, Ther' lookin' weel after a chap. A while sin hoo sung like a lark, Wur hooamly un gentle beside, Till hoo went to thad kess'nin' " do " 0' Flobby-foot Jemmy's ut th' Guide. Hoo's done no good sin hoo wur theer, Her payshunce is scattered to th' winds; Un th' way as boo snaps eawt "Go look!" Wod flay nervous fooak off ther minds. Aw laft hard on Valentine Day, Eawr Molly looked gawpy un green; Bud when hoo'd a big letter browt, 800 fair turned up th' whites ov her een ; Then oppen'd id, ditherin' wi' joy. Eawr Seth th' pictufd doves chanced to spy, Then sheawted, "Hey, sitho ! heaw nice! That's th' brid as won th' twenty-peaw.nd fly !" . He few, fain to ged eawt o' th' gate, Un Molly's sulked at him sin' then; Hoo's eawt a conceit wi' hersel, Un just like an owd cluckin' hen. Hoo's awtered thad bonnet ov hers, Hey ! isn'd id nobby un grand! Hool swagger abeawt wi't as wed As onny fine lady o' th' land. 800 scrapes her tongue neiw when hoo tawks, Bud Grimshaw Park logic creeps in! Yo' shad watch her waddle her "cage," Her ways 'ud mek onny one grin. 800 wur sin abeawt wi' a chap I' th' Park nobbut last Sunda' neet ; Un ther's summat aw've heeard as tells me West soon hey a. weddin' th' street. JACK O'ANN'EI.

div.head: OUR LONDON LErTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LErTER.
LONDON. THURSDAY NIGHT.

Mr. Ritchie's Local Government Bill has now been before the public for three days, and the marvel it has created rather increases than dinkinishes. The qnestion at issue is not one that appeals to popular passion. Park palings are safe as far as the Local Government question is concerned, and the right of public meeting is not likely to be raised in connec- tion with County Boards. This is the naorAs remark- able as it is impossible to name any question more far-reaching or closer in its personal interest. Rate- payers bear the existing system of county govern- ment, and have borne it for generations. simply because they do not understand its intricacies. One of the men who are supposed to know something of the question is Mr. Goschen. He is familiar with it as a financier and a statesman. But it is his everyday experience of the working of the sys- tem that brings him in closer sympathy with or- dinary people. Speaking on this subject long be- fore he had any prospect pf assisting to legislate upon it as a Conservative' Cabinet Minister, Mr. Goschen said: "Everyone knows that the first re- form needed is to consolidate all rates, and to have one demand note for all rates, and a single author- ity for levying the rate and distributing the pro- ceedst among such other authorities as have power to call for contributions. It is astonishing that this should not have been done already. Let me give you my personal experience. I myself received in one year 87 demand notes on an aggregate -valua- tion of about £l,lOO. One parish alone sent me eight rate-papers for an aggregate amount of 12s 4d. Thejntrieacies of imperial finance are simplicity itself compared with this local financial chaos. I will waste no words on 'a reform so universally de- manded; only it pught to be carried out." The reform, it should ,be frankly admitted, has been placed in the shape of a Billhy a Conservative Government, and there is reasonable hope that it will be carried out. certainly this year or next it will be done. The only lion in the path, as far as the present session is concerned, is the collosal character of the measure. The government have shirked nothing, not even the question of the re- foim of the government of London. No one sup- posed that they would deal with that. There was, indeed, some doubt whether they would grapple with the licensing question. But that, too, they mean to deal with, and there is no doubt that if the Bill 'noes upon its present lines a very thor- ough reform will have been worked in the system which for generations has baffled succlissive groups of statesmen. Certainly the government have a chance of the kind which rarely falls to the lot of ministers. They are providentially cornered, and for dear life's sake must take the only path where- in lies safety. I do not suppose that Lord Harting- ton cares much about reform of local government. But Mr. Chamberlain does. It is one of his pet hob- bies, and his final ambition whilst yet a colleague of Mr. Gladstone was to pass a Bill dealing with the subject. He has undonbtedly made action on this matter the price of his continued support of the government. With him in opposition the end of things could not be far delayed. Either a thorough Local Government Bill or discordant disaster. The government have chosen the better path, and the Liberals, seeing their own work done by unaccus- tomed hands, are the very last people in the world to throw obstacles in the way of the Bill passing. Mr:Ritchie's measure may shed some of its limbs as the great bulk moves slowly through the session. But in some modified and not unsatisfactory form we shall certainly have a Local Government Bill passed this session. The immense' advantages under which a Con- servative Govei nment works as compared with Liberals in office is 'strikingly illustrated just now. There is not, as far as I can remember, any pre- cedent during the last fourteen years of Mr. Glad- stone bringing in a bill on any subject and receiv- ing from the Opposition that loyal assistance with which a Government it would be very easy to hamper are now assisted in the House of Commons. The only approach to such common action is to be found in thd passing of what were called the Urgency Rules in the session of 1881. That was a kind of coercion of the Irish members which ap- pealed to the finer sympathies of the Conservatives, and for once they joined hands with Mr. Gladstone and carried the Rules through in a single sitting. But that is a solitary exception to the rule of frac- tious, unwearying, and unprincipled obstruction with which the steps of Mr. Gladstone's Government were dogged. The Liberals, being in Opposition, adept as a matter of course a line of courteous for- bearance towards the Government. The best and most powerful friend of the Treasury Bench just now is, not Lord Hartington, who is seldom there. not Mr. Chamberlain, who has only just ' returned from his American trip, but Mr. Gladstone, who is in constant attendance on the Front ORposition Bench, and ever ready to extend a helping hand to the Government so long as he finds them struggling along in the right path. To do Mr. Smith, Mr, Goschen' and Mr. Ritchie justice, they are effusively grateful for the benevolent attitude adopted by the Leader of the Opposition. It is to be hoped that the example may hereafter bear fruit. In the mean- time things are going on swimmingly: Conserva- tive gentlemen sit on the Treasury Bench and wear the dignities and draw the salaries of Ministers of the Crown. But Liberal principles predominate, and it is only by the adoption Of Liberal policy thatl the Tory Government can live. To-night the Queen will be speeding across France on her way to spend the early spring at Florence. Early this morning the royal (and costlsf) yacht, Victoria and Albert, steamed across to Cherbourg, escorted by the yachts Alberta and Galatea. All last night, whilst the Victoria and Albert lay snugly moored in Portsmouth Harbour, a guard boat, re- lieved every watch, rowed silently round the yacht; a solemn duty, but in the circumstances rather a , chilly one, and significant of the curious nervous- ness with which the Queen faces any occasional emergence from her accustomed privity. Amongst • European Sovereigns, it is only the Emperor of Russia whose movements through the public thoroughfares are watched with greater precau- tion. The present Emperor of Germany, like his father, moves about in friendliest confidence among his people, and so do the other Continental Sovereigns, always Saving the hapless Czar. I re- member, being in Rome two winters ago, seeing a lady pass in an open carriage and pair unattended save by the ordinanf driver and footman. The only thing that attracted a stranger's attention to the oc- cupant-of the carriage was that as she passed every hat was raised, and friendly smiles were turnedl upon the carriage, meeting with pleasant response.l The cabman who was driving me bared his head, and looked supremely happy when the handsome lady smiled upon him. I asked him who it was, and, wondering at my ignorance, he said "The Queen." I could not help thinking of' another queen driving rapidly through the streets of Lon- don in a closed carriage, with the police on the qui vice all along the line, or incommoding thousands of her subjects going about their daily business, and finding railway stations closed because "the Queen is expected." This unfounded apprehension of the unknown public which is of late years growing in the Queen's mind till it threatens to become a mania, is not very complimentary to a peaceful and *ell disposed people. The only persons who, save for the guard boats, might be expected to angrily board the Royal yacht are to be found in the ranks of high society, which the Queen by way of gracious leave taking has profoundly stirred. On Tuesday, the day before leaving Windsor for her continental trip, thd Queen, breaking through her own arrangements earlier ordered, commanded a drawing room to be held by the Princess of Wales on Saturday. At the same time a levee was ordered for to-day. These announcements have convulsed the social world to an extent not easily understood by the vulgar mind

The Rev. George Frederick Wilfrid Ellis, rector of Wetheringsett, Suffolk, has been arrested, charged with having feloniously solemnised certain marringes accor- ding to the rites of the Church of England. In the Scotch Court of Session on Wednesday, David Bain, merchant, of 62, Commercial-road, Dundee. was ordered to pay £2,500 for slandering in a most scanda- lous manner a lady who is now the wife of a merchant in Calcutta.

FIRM IX ESSEX: THREE LIVES LOST.—A fire in which three lives were lost, occurred at Maldon, Essex, on Tuesday merning. Early on Monday night two gar- deners, named Charles Hitchen and Jonathan, Rayner, and their families, the occupants of two cottages on Wykome Hill, retired to rest. Shortly after midnight a smell of fire awoke Hitchen, who, going downstairs, found on fire a beam in the chimney serving both cot- tages. He immediately aroused the Rayner family, and returning got his wife and mother and tWo children out of the house. Its son William, aged 18, also escaped ; but Another son, James, aged 15, who was following hiln, appears to have returned to the rescue of two other chil- dren—Millicent, aged six ; and Charles, aged four. Mean- while the flames had rapidly pread, and the cottages were soon enveloped. The room in which the children slept was entirely destroyed, and the charred remains of James, Millicent, and *Charles were subsequently found amidst the debris. The members of the Rayner family escaped. . . Tim PRINCESS CHRISTIAN, whose interest in nursing Is so well known, will contribute an article on " Nursing as a Profession for Women," to the April number of the Woman's World. LORD HARTINGTON AT CARLISLE.—Lord Hartington, addressing a meeting at Carlisle, on Wednesday night, said the Liberal Unionists exercised their own judg- ment; and did not believe.in passive obedience or in un- convinced conversions. " By-elections would not influence them. The decision of the constituencies as a whole was the only thing to which they would listen. They had maintained in power a Government which had conduc- ted with dignity and ability the foreign affairs of the country, defeated Parliamentary obstruction, asserted the authority of the law, and proposed long-promised measures for the benefit of the people. He commended the Local Government Bill as a comprehensive, liberal measure, which in the best sense of the words was a Home Rule measure. It would satisfy the aspirations of the English people, and ought to satisfy the aspirations of the Scotch and Irish. His position as to its extension to Ireland was simply this. He had not the smallest ob- jection to a wide extension of local self-government in Ireland. It seemed to him simply a question of expedi- ency, of time, and of circumstances. They had a right to inquire, before extending local self-governing insti- tutions in Ireland, in what spirit they were asked for, in what temper they would be received, and what would be the probable results. His lordship concluded by de- claring emphatically: that there was no danger of a break- ing up of the Unionist party. " Skso-LtNi," or Linseed, Soap, cherishes the cuticle. W. post free. The annOyance, which, according to current report, the Prince of Wales freely expresses is, more 'easily comprehended: His Royal Highness was in Berlin when the edict was suddenly flashed forth, and had made arrangements to stay at Brussels till Saturday. But his arrangements, like everybody elses con- cerned, were ruthlessly upset, and he had to hasten home. Everybody having quite unnecessarily and unexpectedly been made as uncomfortable as possi- ble. the Queen has set out on her journey, and looks for a pleasant time at Florence. The Rev. Isaac Nelson, whose quiet funeral at Bel- fast finds record in an obscure paragraph, was another of the .eceentrics of the Parliament of 1880 who has passed away, and leaves beltind no sucees- sot. Mr. Nelson was, up to the year 1880; a Presby- terian clergyman at Belfast. In that year he gave up the pulpit, took to politics, and was returned for Mayo in the train of Mr. Parnell. He was rather a favourite with the House of Commons, where his curious appearance and eccentric demeanour occa- sionally varied the severities of debate. Mr. Nelson would make the most common-place remarks in a voice of thrilling force. His gestures were violent and peculiar. He wrestled with hiniself, in desperate fashion, and it used to be said that he had a special allowance from the maintenance fund since a coat, however strongly made, would . never last him through more than 'three speeches. His final ap- pearance was on the famous night when 37 Irish members were suspended. .When it came to Mr. Nelson's turn to be put out ha firmly grasped the post of the Cross Benches, and all the reserve forces ' , of the Sergeant-at-Arms were brought up in andel- ' pation of a terrific struggle. When they were mar- ' ' shelled the member for Mayo let go the Cross Bench and walked quietly out, =id roars of 'laughter. Shortly , afterwards lie resigned his 'seat, and has since disappeared from the public gaze, till his, name is recalled by the announcement of his funeral. Whilst the Queen of England has gone to Italy to make holiday in the spring time; the Empress of Austria has come to England. Her Majesty has put up at a well known private hotel in London, , where her name is written in the visitors' book as Frau GrAfin von'Hohenerabs. .Every year English people rush to try the German waters. There are many famous springs within the bounds of the . empire of Austro.-Hungary, but tlie Empress han- kers after Bath. and the Erglisb coast watering- places from Brighton to Torquay. The earlier . visits of the Empress of Austria to this Country were for hunting purposes. But increasing rheu- matism has dismounted her Majesty, and her hunt- • ing days are over. The Empress has come to Eng- land for a quiet time, and happily is not likely to be embarrassed by proffers of hospitality from our 1 Conn.
TOWNSHIP MEETING AT A.PPLETON.

On Thursday evening a meeting of the inhabitants of the township of Appleton, in the Runcorn Union was held at the" Thorn Inn, Appleton, for the pur- pose of transacting the yearly township business. The chair was occupied by Mr. B. Davies, and there ,was a good attendance, including the overseers, Messrs. T. Hall and H. Derbyshire. At the commencement' of the meeting Mx. Hall complained that the assistant over- seer (Mr. Calvert) had not been sufficiently active in get- ting in the rates, and that he was nearly £lOO in ar- rear. Mr. Calvert, he said, was well qualified for his duties, but seemed to leave everything to the last ' minute. The first call was paid punctually.—Mr. Cal- vert said that there was £lO3 18s 10d out at the end of last year, whioh \had been the cause of the -whole thing. He had done all that he could to get the money in.—Mr. Hall: You promised that this year there should be a clean sheet on the 29th of March, and here we have practically £lOO in arrear. Correspondence that had passed between the overseers and the Guardians on the subject was then read, and a discussion followed in which Mr. Hall alleged that the assistant-overseer had failed to keep his appointments with the overseers.— Mr. Knowles: You have been very kind to Mr. Calvert. —Mr. Hall: It has been a source of great anxiety to us. —The Qiairman : It must be taken into account that Mr. Calvert is new to the business, and perhaps that is some excuse.—Mr. Calvert: There is more work than anyone has any idea of.—Mr. S. Woods: I think he has made a mug of the job. - (Laughter.)—Mr. Halt said he hoped that next year there would be no cause for com- plaint. The overseers intended to have meetings monthly, at which they would go through the accounts with the assistant overseer.—Mr. Calvert: I am quite agreeable to thb,t.—The subject then dropped.—Messrs. Joseph Knowles, William Hewitt, and William Rostock were proposed for nomination as Guardians for the year next ensuing, and Mr. James Knowles was re-elected waywarden for the following year. Messrs. Thomas Hall, Hugh Derbyshire, J. Pimblett, William Darlington, junr., John Whitlow, and James Briteh were nominated for the position of overseers; Messrs. W. Darlington, junr., and Calvert were elected assessors of taxes; Messrs. John Weir and John Marsh were selected as burleymen ; and Mr. W. Bostock was asked to act as constable of the parish.—This was the principal bush , ness.

A IfROICEN PROMISE.

Prince Sergins had taken up his quarters In an hotel in Albemarle-street, and there he and his confidential valet asef are installed in rooms be- fitting the high rank Of 'their occupant; rooms which have nothing of the. petit maitre about them. Prince Sergius, luxury-loving though he-is, is not the sort of man to indulge to any -degree in the effeminacy which dwells in some of the abodes of the golden youth of the nineteenth. century.. He does not expend capital on flowers exce2t to give to women; even a .button-hole is never to be seen gracing his manly breast, unless it is placed there by seine fair fingers. Altogether there is the same amount of sternness about Serghis LenSkofrs quarters, as there is about the general eternal appearance of the man. It is the day after his meeting With Irene Stan- hope at Lady Bertha Cnintning's garden- party, and n gravity which surnasSes even his usual severity of nianner has -settled itself frowningly upon his brow. 'Vet it is rather care than anger that has produced the lines: There are evidently annoyances in life that even his princely omnipotence cannot overcome, and he is compelled at times to recognise the fact that worry and anxiety, though from different causes, Come alike to prince and peasant. He lias been .writing letters ; several missives are sealed and stamped, mostly. with foreign stamps, on the table before him. He' has trashed his correspondence, and thrown himself back in his chair in a thoughtful attitude, when the door opens, and Josef walks in. He is a little man, so small that there is something' almost comic when you think of him as valet to this big powerful Sergins. The prince, however,- knows his unequalled . merits too well to allow any sense of the ridiculous to Step between him and Josef's devo- tion. Josef is not a Russian. He is .a Southener, half Greek, half Italian ; it were difficult to name his actual birthplace. -Of himself, he always says he is, cosmopolitan: As far as languages go :he., knows almost as Many as his master; but for. die most part they converse in French. • • , ?" asks the prince, rousing himself and looking straight into Josef's eyes as he entefs the room. " I have found the man, monsieur, but not without some little difficulty." - "Never mind the difficulty, so long as you have found him. Where, does he live?"

• "At Wandsworth, monsieur; he is a builder, keeps also a timber yard, and prides himself on the suc- cess of his funerals." "He is well off; then ? " • "According to his own telling, no; according to his ncighbmws', yes."' •, • -" And you are sure he is the right-man ?" "'Simon Knight married Hannah Brown,the miller's daughter at Warleigh. • Has one daughter, ;Phyllis.' "Phyllis Knight—why that is the girl ..who is always with the Stanhopes.-" "Yes, a great devotion exists between these Knights• and the Stanhopes ; a greater perhaps than some people think for," and Josef laughed a little spasmodic sardonic laugh, thus shewing that he knew or . guessed more than perhaps he altogether chose to relate, at all m'ent;s to his master. • "I know, I know," said :the prince hurriedly; "you mean that Geoffrey Stanhope loves this Phyllis. Of Course he will not marry her ; such a thing Would be absurd." "Certainly it would bc., if Monseigneur has any intention of taking the beautiful Mademoiselle Irene to Russia."

"Who said I lisA any stull intention? Yon Presume too much, Josef.". And the prince looked verylierce. His wrath, however, did not seem to affect Josef, who only shrugged his shoulders and spread out his bands demonstratively, . . .

"If MonF.e.kine ir does not love the daughter why this looking into the affairs of the father ?" " That is my business." "And it is sometimes mine to discover nothing," answered Josef, psintedly. • "Bah, Josef; good Josef ! do not be disagreeable. Well, since you will know, I do love Irene Stanhope, but her father knows too muoli about me to give her to me if I do not bring pressure to bear. This Simon Knight, if he is the man I take him to be, will be a powerful coadjutor." Pr'nse Sergius humbling himself and explaining his reasons to his valet ! There ws..carcely one of his acquaintances wha -would have bell :ved such a thing possible. The few words served to restore Josef's good humour, and he said, • "Bien! Monseigneur, but I do not understand how this Knight can he:p you. He is a rough coarse man, thoroughly English, speaks not one word of any foreign tongue. Ido not believe he has ever been out of this country in his life." "You have had an interview with then ? " "Yes, Monseigneur, yes; and what is more I have bidden him come here by six. Your highness will -then see him and judge for yourself. I told him you wanted some work done abroad by English workmen and you had been recommended to him," "You have acted with your usual acumen, Josef. I give you great credit. As it is just six, go and watch for this man at the door and bring him in yourself." Josef, with a bow, did as he was bid, and for a brief space Prince Sergius was left to his meditations. Very soon, hoSiever, they were interrupted by the arrikal of Simon Knight, who, considerably over- awdlr at being sent for by a prince, came shambling into the room in a 'most ungainly fashion, looking very red and excited. It was obvious that he had been calling up his courage by a tolerably free use of alcohol. Prince Sergius scanned Simon Knight's bloated features very closely; but wl ether he recognised him or not didnot transpire, and certainly it did not seem that Simon had any recollection of the prince. But then perhaps alcohol had saniewhat dimmed his memory. No words were spoken of any transactions of the past. Prince Sergius told the builder that lie understood he was a workman of no small renown, ; and that he was anxioas to send someone bearing such a character to Russia to repair some work that had been done in years gone by by an Englishman. SiMon Knight muttered somth eing about a journey to Russia being expensive business, but he had no doubt he could- find some one who would go. "Some one who will go—and yourself ?" " Myself ; no thank your highness, I will never go to Russia again if I knows it. "Again ! You have then been there already ? " " The man coloured up as though sorry he had com- mitted himself. "As a mere boy," he said, " I re- member very little about it. I went with my master who was engaged on a Russian railway." -" Did you dislike the country so much that you decline to go again?" "The country? No s but there, I don't want to go. I'm an oldish man, and I've got enough for my humble wants." " lam sorry. I believed you to be exactly the in- dividual I require. The work I wish to have done is to pull down a wall and restore a chapel that I know is behind it, in an old house which I 'lave lately bought in one of the outlyisg portions of St. Peters- burg. " \\ldle the prince was speaking, every tinge of colour forsook Simon Knight's usually scarlet face, and he shook all over as with uncontrollable fear.

" Bless me I " -‘;.•ent igp-rinc-e7a7i-h-o-u-g-1;--s.ud- denly noting the effect of his words, "what is the matter? It surely cannot be anything I have said that has upset you." " It's•nowt at all, don't you mind me," answered, Knight roughly, "hem as lets me bide at home and mind my business, and look after my wife and child are the folks as I like, I don't want no junketing off to Roosia, and no tomfoolery." "I thought, perhaps, if Mr. Stanhope Iwished it you would go. "I ain't obliged to go at Mr. Stanhope's bidding. I don't owe him nothing; and for the matter of that, he don't owe me nothing ; we're quits." "Since you are content with your lot, and do not wish to add to the fortune you have already made, Mr. Knight, I am sorry, but I suppose we have no- thing further to say. I wish you good afternoon." " Good afternoon, your highness. Anything; in this yere country as I can do for you, especially funerals —I prides myself on funerals—l'll be happy, but don't you go askin',me to go to Roosia ; t'aint the kind country as I over wants to set foot in again.o, "Exactly, exactly, Mr. Knight. I quite under- stand, and if I should want you to do anything for me in the way of a funeral, I'll let you know." And there was a sagacious smile playing on the prince's features while- he spoke, which by no means pleased Simon Knight, who could not help fancying that there was something more in this interview than his stupified senses could altogether take in. He shambled out of the room as he had entered it, muttering to himself as he went downstairs- a sort of ray from the past falling on him the while and seeming to light up on his slowly awakening memory the features of this Russian magnate. Josef, however, stopped him at the bottom of th?, staircase before his recollection had become fully de • veloped, and writing his weakness''. suggested that h 3

should come and have a drink. kluriosity more Os* his master's interests prompted him to this step. would learn, if possible, what were the actual facts(); this old story that Prince Sergius was anxious unearth. He little knew how wary Simon Knight even in his cups. Meantime Prince Sergius gathi up his correspondence and locked away the papers lay littering about the table. A smile playing at. his lips • he looked more like the Prince Charming I' Irene's dreams than he was wont to look except when in the presence of some woman he loved. To all outward seeming the interview with Simod Knight had proved abortive; yet, although Knight himself knew it not, it had completely fulfilled the prince's expectations. The man he wanted was r hand, could be found at any moment, and as his being able, if necessity urged, to make this do what he required of him he did not doubt it-tos second. It wasseven o'clock by the time he had col' lected his ideas and his papers. He would stroll out for an hour before dining at a club of which he wag an honorary member, and then he had a projed in hand which would take up his evening. Into t' park, then, he sauntered. It was already beginn: to thin ; carriages were rapidly conveying their ft freight home to dress for their numerous evenit engagements. Prince Sergius's lucky star seemed on; more to be in the ascendant, for scarcely had he crossed over from Ap>ley House than, standing in the thick( of the throng, he saw a carriage.in which was - Irene Stanhope by her mother's side, Lady Fedora had been not a little (IT.appointed, the garden party,whele she hoped matters would', ha' been brought to a climax ; but her spirits rose col siderably when she saw the prince, almost at the nt of his life, come between several carriages so as I stand by theirs and talk to them, his large eyes fixi so rapturously on Irene's face that even Lady redo could not 'doubt that he loved her. Her spirits, ho' ever, fell again to zero when on her asking him come and dine that evening, he ref used, as thought, somewhat cohliy. How she upbraided he for the false step she believed she had taken! Prot bly she would have done so with even greater veer, had she known that Prince Sergins had no positie engagement for that evening,thet is to say,no fashion' ble one which he inten, eel to keep. Nor was Irene exactly pleased when she h( Prince Sergius decline her mother's invitation ; least, there was a shadow on her brow. How col

• she know that this wealthy prince, whom Lend worshipped, was afraid of meeting his old frii Henry Stanhope in the intimacy of a family party, cause he loved his daughter? How could she kno' that after he left her, Prince Sergius strolled alom Piccadilly, his hat well set on his brows, ad ev

more sorrow in his heart at ,being compelled to nay to Lady Fedora's invitation, than there was ill Irene's own breast when she listened to his refusal?. The prince ate his dinner in so morose a allelic though the room was full of dincrs,that some of thi who saw him predicted an attack of indigestion; a' then, for more than an hour, he sm,ked i simil
silence which no one ventured to break, At laat, as night wore on, he sallied 'forth, walking' about streets in a desultory,purposeloas fashion as it seem(

yet Prince Sergius' ac7s were seldom without an obje A little after eleven he found himself in the seigk bourhood of Covent Garden, elose to the street IA which Ferdinand Stanhope's club, the Bandits,- went situated. He paused on the threshold and asked fat Mr. Ferdinand Stanhope. Ths poreer was not sv whether he was there, bat, after a second or two, d. jag which inquiry was made, Ferdinand came oat looking white add wan,snd invitcd the prince to coral In.
"I have accepted your invi,tition, you see," L Sergius smiling, "and have come to see you and be i tiated, as a foreigner should be, in the doings of Bandits."
Ferdinand tried to smile back, but it was 'only feeble effort ; and the Prince went on: "I saw your mother and sister in the park evening." "My mother—ah !" muttered Ferdinand in a 10' voice.
• • "Good gradons ! • Why, what do you mean? anything ham :plied since I saw them ?

Notking,- nothing, at least not to them," and Far dinand led the way into the interior of the building —a spot into which strangers, as a rife, were 1191 allowed to penetrate; but this Russian had prine' rights. Accustomed to even madder, wilder play-haunt, then those In which the Bandits dwelt, ho took in etc entire situation at a glance. Baccarat was holding ir mighty sway, and Ferdinand Stanhope had punished more severely than his modest repo could meet. Prince &Tins had heard it :lanolin , that the boy was more or less attaohed to th. pleasures of the green table,and he had come in a g measure to investigate the troth for I cruse!. He scarcely a man to reprobate gamb lag with mucx, severity, but he was considerably disappointed witness the almost craven express,on of Ferdirteu` face. He knew nothing of the young man's absolu.a remorse at having been weak enough to break el Soon every promime he had made to Lady F.:dors, an° he attributed his agonised appearance entirely to the losses he had sustained. That they, were heavy—vl heavy for Ferdinand as a younger son—be soon dili" covered, but Prince Sergius bedeved Henry Stanbolle to be rich, so that there would be no difficalty obtaining the money, he presumed. He said as mu° as this to Ferdinand. Four hundred pounds was melt: tioned to him, which sum, adeed to a hundred aiP fifty, which he had lost twice within the last weli made seven hundred in all. Bills bad been back and given for three hundred, bills which neither II: nor the backer ever expected would bo met, and no" unless help came from some unknown quarter what till/ to be done? ;het

"Bleed the prince," suggested one of Ferdinam friends, but Ferdinand Was under the influence of tl broken promise to his mother, and be had no eneri to break fresh ground, lie would go on playill Superstitious, like all gamblers, he thought, Wit* this Russian in the room, the luck would change. Alas, luck, at all events from cards, was not CO u° his that night. Another three hundred was voce before the neighbouring clocks had struck midnigbl and Ferdinand, whose excitable temperament cot stand no more disappointment, was lying in ade faint on the floor, Sargius Leuskoff himself unt7i?! his cravat, and raising his hea I, while sums a companions sprinkled water on his face.

div.head: FOREIGN NEWS.
div.p: FOREIGN NEWS.

GENERAL BOULANGER AND THE FRENCH GOVERNMENT. SEVERE MEASURES PROPOSED. PAWS, MOND/A.—ln the Chamber, to-day, hi. Paul de Oaatagnse, the Bonapartiet leader, laked permission to lateresellate the Government respecting their reasons for teaming General Boulanger from his command. M. 2.lrard, the Premier, saM the Government would prefer to discuss the interpeliation teemoirow, as they had de- cided to take fresh measures against the General. This samouncement caused some sensation, and was the sub- iect of excited comment in the lobbies. It is understood that the fresh naeasnres referred to include the placing af Generalßoulanger en retraite, i.e., on the retired list. Buch a course would seriously reduce the General's in- come, but at would have the effect of rendering him eligible for election to the Chamber, and it would not deprive him of the chance of being replaced on the active Est in the event of a war or-the accession to office of his friends. Pains, MONDAY.—Several Communistic meetings were held yesterday in celebration of the 18th of March. At bloat of them-the speakers denounced General Boulanger. The Radical Congess of the Ande has rejected the candi- dature of General Boulanger. TERRIBLE RAILWAY DISASTERS IN AMERICA.—MANY LIVES LOST. Naw YORK, FRIDAY.—A serious accident occurred to-day on the Delaware and Lackawana Railway. A - train fell over an embankment a height of 30ft., and the stoves became ignited. Twenty-seven persons were hurt, and it is feared that in two cases the injuries will Prove fatal. A telegram from Mexico states that six Persons have been killed and 20 injured owing to a con- struction car running off the line on the Mexican Na- tional Railway. Nisw YORK. Stranay.—The strike of enginemen on the Atchison, Topeka, and Sante Fe Railway has ended. New YORK, SUNDAY.—As a train, which was proceed- ing from Now York to Jacksonville., Florida, was crossing a trestle bridge near Savannah, the structure gave way. and several of the CRIS were precipitated through the gap and smashed to pieces. Nineteen persons were killed outright, six have since died from the injuries which they sustained, and others are expected to suc- cumb. A large number of passengers were injured. Mr. Wilber, president of the Lehigh Valley Railroad, was in the train, With three of his sons, one of whom was killed, although the two others and their father escaped se/Wi- les& The train consisted of a combination car, a smoking car, one ordinary coach, two sleeping saloons, Mr. Wilbar's private car, and a luggage van. The whole of the train was wrecked and. immehately caught fire, but the flames were quickly extinguished. The total number of injured is now stated at 35. Among the killed and injured are a number of negroes. SUNDAY NIGIIT.—Every carriage was filled with pas- , 'eager°. Scarcely one escaped unhurt. The shrieks and of the wounded, mingled with the wild cries ot groans women, was heartrending. The continued blowing of whistles soon brought help, and then the work of getting the wounded out began. The sight was horrible, and stout men turned pale as they listened to • the groans of those imprisoned under the wreck. Car- riages and ox and mule carts were all pressed into the service, and the wounded carefully conveyed to Meek- shear. The people there threw open their houses, and were indefatigable in their efforts to render every assist- ance possible. Among the slightly injured was a son of Mr. Jay Gould, who was going south with his wife. Accounts differ as to the cause of the accident. The Company say the axle on the forward waggon broke; others say the trestle was weak. STORMS ABROAD.—APPALLING SCENES AND LOSS OF LIFE IN AMERICA.-- FLOODS IN HUNGARY.-30 VI.T.LAGES DESTROYED.—INUNDATIONS. PHILADELPIDA, SATURDAY.—As the country emerges from the snowdrifts, reports of disasters and loss of life increase. Over 200 persons have perished. The fiercest effects of the gale were in and around New York. As the workmen dig out snowpits, corpses are found in them frozen to death, standing upright in the streets where the snow overcame them. Twenty-one lives are already reported to have been lost in New York, 24 deaths in and near New Jersey, four near Raritan, seven at New- haven, and 26 in and near Fairhaven, Cor.necti- cut. Terrible reports come from Long Island Sound, where the towns are just getting into communication with the outside world. Besides the lives already re- ported lost in the Chesapeake Bay, twelve additional are reported drowned. The most painful tale is sent from Crisfield, Maryland, where a vessel was seen flying a sig- nal of distress. After great exertion aid was sent to her from the shore, when the entire .crew of five men were found frozen dead. Two more New York pilot boats are reported safe, and another is disabled at Delaware break- water. Out of the whole fleet eleven are missing, twelve are known to have been wrecked, and six have been saved. Three thousand men and 1,000 horses, carts, and trucks have worked throughout the night in New York clearing a passage through the centre of Broadway, where the snow lay 61 t. to 10ft. deep, also to the ferries. So business, therefore, is moving again. Amapa the troubles of New York is the inability to reach.the cemeteries with funerals, and 500 corpses have accumulated unburied throughout the city. Attempts were made to break a passage into Greenwood Cemetery, Brooklyn, where 100 bodies await burial. After hours , of work a passage was made of 3001 t. to the receiviiie vault, but it was impossible to reach the graves. In many eases funeral services have been conducted, bte, the corpses remain at home. Petern, SUNDAY noirr.—From all parts of the country news is coming in of fresh disasters cause by the floods. An enormous extent of territory is now inundated. More than 39 villages have already been totally ru;ned. and the town of Szathmar partly destroyed. The 38.000 inhabitents of Bekescsaba have since Friday been literally struggling for their lives against the floods arising from the overflow of the Koros river. Fait of the town has been inundated, and numerous houses have fallen in. It is very doubtful whether the town out escape total ruin. PARIS, MoNnsT.—The north and north-western parts of France have been visited by snowstorms unprece- dented at this time of the year. In Normandy, between the stations of Les Ifs and Granville, well known to all visitors to Etretat, the snowdrifts have been such as to Stop the railway traffic. In Paris there has been a con- stant downpour of pulverised spew, with a temperature below freezing point. The London mails of this mornine have not been delivered, the train being delayed by snowdrifts. On the branch line from Beuzeville to Fes:amp there are from five to seven feet of snow on the railway, and traffic is consequently at a standstill. MADRID, MONDAY.—We have been visited once more by severe snowsterms. The northern provinces have suffercd immensely. In the province of Orviedo the trains can scarcely run. On the other hand the floods are causing enormous damage in the south. The com- munications between Madrid and Seville are interrupt ed, and the valleys in the provinces of Murcia and Guada- laxara are inundated. A MAIL TRAIN MISSING Six DAYS.— Denmark is suf- fering from the effects of a very heavy snowfall. Rail- way and other communication is interrupted, and in some places the snow is ten feet deep. The mail from London of the 10th inst. had not arrived at Copenhagen up to yesterday.
THE LATE EMPEROR WILLIAM.

STUMM, SATURDAT.—The late Emperor's apartments are to be turned into a museum for the public. They are to be preserved exactly as they are; not the smallest article will be moved or altered. The late Emperor's Will is to be-opened to-morrow. It la stated that the personalty is estimated at 54,000,000 marks (£2,700,000). The Empress Augusta, who is much shaken by her bereavement, intends to leave for Baden-Baden as soon as possible. The Royal theatres in Berlin, se., those subsidised by the State, are to remain shut until Easter. The managers of the other theatres had intended holding a meeting with the object of arriving at a unanimous decision as to a suitable term for the cessation of all dramatic performances. The meeting, however, did not take place owing to an order issued by the President of Police for the obligatory closing of all theatres. Thisi order, coming as It does immediately on the top of the proclamation of the Emperor Frederick, in which he gave notice than no period or conditions of mourning would be imposed on the people, who were to act in the matter entirely according to their own feelings, has given rise to great dissatisfaction. The Municipality of San Remo have conferred the right of honary citizenship upon Sir Morell Mackenzie, and requested him to represent the town at the obsequies of the late Emperor.

THE EMPEROR FREDERICK. ERWIN, SWNDAY.—The Emperor Frederick received, on Saturday, the princely personages now in Berlin, and to-day the other Envoys of foreign States. Everyone who has seen his Majesty testifies to his erect bearing and genial manner, which in no way. suggest a man struck by a mortal disease. This morning the Emperor, with the rest of the Royal family, was present at Divine ser- vice in the Schloss of Cltarlottenburg. The first law to which the signature of Frederick HI. has been attached is one relating to German protectorates abroad. The • Prince of Wales and Prince Albert Victor at.. ' ' tended service at St. George's English Church ' this morning. The preacher made a telling allusion 'to the great qualities of the late Emperor. The church I was still draped with black. Even in the streets funeral . flags are still flying. The decorations erected for Friday's 'ceremony are left untouched, and 'great numbers of people still patrol the Linden. At the sittings on Monday of the Prussian Diet and German Reichstag, Messages were read from the King- moeror formally announcing his succession to the i.Royal and Imperial Thrones on the death of his august ; father. The Messages explained the circumstances twhich at present prevented his Majesty appearing per- Lsonaliy to take the necessary oaths, but announcing that he hoped to do so at a future time, and in the mean- * wille declaring his a.dhesion to the Constitution, and fhis determination to carry out the law faithfully and lo pally. In the Reichstag, after some remarks by the President, Prince Bisinarck addressed the House, and having, in the name of the Emperor referred to .'the universal marks of sympathy received from all parts of the world on the death of the late Ern- paror. asked for authority to convey to European •

Powers the thanks of Germany for this unprecedented testimony to the memory of their revered Sovereign. A proclamation was also published on Tuesday at Stras- burg, in which the Emperor declares his determination to preserve the rights of the Empire over theterritories of Alsace-Lorraine. The Emperor declares that the union between these territories and the Fatherland has again become as close as it was before the separation of the provinces. INDISPOSITION OF THE CROWN PRINCE

WILLIAI2 BF.ELIN, MONDAY MORNING.—The town Prince William is somewhat indisposed, owinz to the anxiety and ex- citement of the past week. His Royal Highnesaisiinder the treatment of Professor Von Bergmann.
BLOWING UP OF AN EXCURSION STEAMER: TERRIBLE SCENES.

-------- - Particulars which have noise to hand of an ex- plosion on board an excursion steamer in South America show that some terrible scenes were witnessed, and Vic loss of life was between 20 and 30, the exact number not being known. The disaster happened a few miles from Cartagena, on the river Dique. The excursionists num- l'ered 40, and had been up the river at a fair. It was nearly dark when they were returning, and the steamer got fast in the Mud. She could not be refloated, and Dr. Pareja., of Cartagena. who along with his wife, was a passenger on the Rlfaele Reyes, took a small boat and made for Cartagena to get assistance. The steamer remained ashore all night, and the captain, gatting impatient, ordered the engineer to get up steam next morning. This was done, and the engineer had hardly touched the lever to move the engines when a ,arrific explosion took place. In an instant the vessel , was a wreck, and the fragments of the steamer and the dismembered bodies of dozens of her passengers were hurled in all directions, some descending in the river, others in the mud, and others again on the now shat- tered hull of the boat. It was not known who were killed or who were saved, but it was surmised that the former would number between twenty and thirty. Those who could, made their way to Car- tagena for assistance, and when the despatch was sent off the assistance was just leaving Cartagena. Dr. Pareja had left in a tug before the news reached Cartagena, and he would arrive to see the havoc caused by the explosion. The only thing that remained was part of the steamer's shattered hull. It was not kno*n,in,the confusion if the doctor's wife was killed or not. One lady who was a passenger by the steamer was uninjured, but her husband was hurled about fifty feet in the air, his dead body falling at her feet. The scene was of the most shocking nature. The fate of the captain was unknown.
A TOWN DESTROYED_ _BY FIRE.-15,000 PERSONS

HOMELESS. A Rangoon telegram published in the second editioft of the Times says the town of Myingyn, in Upper Bur- man, situate on the east bank of the Irrawady, an im- portant military post, has been almost destroyed by fire. It is believed to have been due to incendiarism. The telegram adds that 15,000 , people rendered homeless, and that grt quantities of gram, joggery, hides and other goods stored near the river atMyingyan have been destroyed. Another large fire occurred last night in Rangoon, ex- tending from Pharye-street to Sparks-street, and burn- ing seven Wicks. About 150 houses were destroyed, the majority being of little value.

div.head: OPORTO. 80 LIVES LOST. TERRIBLE SCENES IN THE BURNING'
div.p: OPORTO. 80 LIVES LOST. TERRIBLE SCENES IN THE BURNING'

BUILDING. 0 LISBON, WEDNESDAY, 11-20 A.m.—The Baguet Theatre at Oporto was destroyed by fire last night, the conflagration being 'caused by a gas accident which occurred during the last act. There was a very full house at the time. Ten bodies have been taken from the debris up to the present, and there are a large number of people injured. • 3-30 P.M.—The number of those who perished in the burning of the Baguet Theatre at Oporto last night is now calculated by the latest accounts at eighty. The greatest loss of life occurred in the third tier of boxes and in the galleries, where whole families were asphyxiated or burned to death. There was a. terrible struggle for life at ,the doors, where numbers were suffocated and others were trampled to death. Some who succeeded in reaching the street were severely injured and vomited blood. Nearly all the victims were from amorg the audi- ence. The artistes who escaped rushed out in their theatrical costumes just as they left the stage. ' Many of the audience who could not gain the exit doors jismped into the streets from the windows of the building. The gas was extinguished shortly after the fire broke out. Several bodies have been found on the stage and in the boxes. 6 P.m.--Large gangs of workmen are actively en- gaged in clearing away and exploring the ruins of the theatre. Many human remains have been dis- covered all in a charred condition. This afternoon the searchers came upon two bodies locked together in a close embrace. Forty persons are up to the present stated by the police to be missing, but it is believed that nearly all the occupants of the upper gallery lost their lives. •

div.head: M.B. CHAMBERLAIN AND MR. O'BRIEN.
div.p: M.B. CHAMBERLAIN AND MR. O'BRIEN.

Mr. Chamberlain has addressed the following letter to the Birmingham Daily Post :—"My attention has been directed to the report of a speech delivered by Mr. O'Brien, on Saturday, in which are a number of state- ments concerning myself, some of which are entirely untrue, while others are grossly inaccurate. There is , not the slightest foundation for the statement that I have at any time in any place afforded any encourage- ment whatever to any proposal for the creation of an Irish Republic or for the legislative inde- pendence of Ireland. The private letter to which Mr. O'Brien refers has, I believe, been published, and, as far as I am concerned, is, in its entirety public property. I have no copy in London, but I believe it was written in the early part of 1886, and contains the germ of a proposal which was elabo- rated and adopted by Mr. Parnell and approved by the leading members of his party. It was subsequently . known as the scheme for National Councils, and if Mr. O'Brien and his friends are now prepared to revert to it, and abandon more ambitious projects, they *ll find me still prepared to give it a favourable consideration. It is not worth my while to notice other points in Mr. O'Brien's speech, but his cause is not likely to be served by the reckless misrepresentations .of which he and his paper, United Ireland, have given so many examples." Mr. Wm. O'Brien M.P., has written to the Birmingham Daily Post of Wednesday morning, in reply to Mr. Chamberlain's letter which appeared in that journal on Tuesday. Mr. O'Brien says that Mr. Chamberlain, by ittluding his specific sf.alements, entirely confirms theni. For instance, Mr. Chamlwrllin denies that he had offered ,any encouragement for nny " proposal" to create an Irish Republic. The wrier never brought the charge against him, but reeiliv said that 'Mr. Chamberlain had privately suggested the thing himself. Prior to his meditated visit to Ireland in 1885, Mr. Chamberlain sent round a lithographed letter in which he stated that not only had Ireland a right to local government, hut that there were questions not local in any nariow sense, but which required local and exceptional treat- ment in Ireland, so that he would hand over such ques- tions as those of education, land, railway: and other communication, and taxation for strictly Irish purposes to an Irish Boa* altogether independent of English Government influence. "Mr. Chamberlain admits," continues Mr. O'Brien, "that his Irish Board was but the germ of his representative National Council, which would be an Irish Parliament in everything but official title."
MURDER BY BURGLARS: DOUBLE EXECUTION.

The execution of Jas.,Jones and Alfred Scandrett, for the murder of Mr. Philip Ballard, at Tupsley, Hereford- shire, in October last, took place yesterday at Here- ford Gaol. Berry was the executioner, and at five minutes to eight he entered the cell occupied by Jones and pinioned him, and then proceeded to Scandrett's .cell and accomplished a like operation. The gaol chap- lain (the Rev. L. spencer) had been with the men for some time previous. The condemns:A men were brought out, and placed between warders, by whom they were conducted to the scaffold, accompanied by the chaplain. Both men were ghastly pale, and much- agitated, but bore themselves with firmness, and walked without assistance to the scaffold, where they were quickly' strapped by the hangman. As the drop fell, both melt. were evidently praying, as their lips moved. Death,' appeared in each case to be.instantaneous, although the rope from which Jones was swinging appeared to quiver for a moment. The crime for Natich the men suffered, was the murder of a retired engineer, by striking him! on the head with a hatchet, they having broken into his house at night for the sake of plunder: At the inquest subsequently, a letter was read from the chaplain, stating that he received very shortly after the tria a confession from both the condemned pilsoners of the true circumstances of the crime. Scandrett struck both blows, which caused Mr. Ballard's death, with a hatchet, Jones being close to him and an eve witness. The hatchet was in Scandrett's possession the whole time. Both culprits had submitted readily to the spiritual ministrations, and the chaplain believed they died penitent. \ Miss Ballard, niece of the murdered man, and one of :hose peacefully sleeping in the house when the crime was committed, sent a bunch of violets to each pri- soner, as well as a letter, in Which she said she freely forgave them 'their wickedness, and hoped they had made their peace with God. George Parry, postman, who deposed at the trial tha.% he saw the prisoners crouching under a hedge at Tup- 41ey on the night the crime was committed, had been despondent for some time, and, on Sunday night, after returning from chapel, he drank a quantity of laudnum, trona the effect* of which he died.
