The poor- law guardians would continue to exercise their func- tions with reference to the administration' of the poor-law within the areas which exist at present Mr. J. E. Exam: Will the guardians still be elected by the poor-law vote? Mr. Hercule : We make no difference as to the election of guardians, orthe areas of the unions. Mr. Ritchie then turned to the provisions of the bill affecting the Metro- polis. It appeared that London will be made a county, with alord-lieutenant, resident magistrates, and county council of its lawn, directly elected by the rate- payers. The Metropolitari Board of Works will cease to exist, an announcement which was hailed with loud and prolonged cheering from the Oppcysition benches. The City of London will be placed in the position of a Quarter Sessions borough. Mr. Ritchie then addressed himself to the question of hemming reform. He said the bill dealt with it broadly, and that-the Government be- Nosed there well:re eraeoa eo dierke the-function of licensing welfia gieets'ttrttfe fAtiley•teerneg It would be judiciously efercised. They had a proposal to make, and if the Homo did not accept it, at alrevents they would have done their duty in making it. (Laughter.) The Government proposed to hand over the duty of licensing to the County Councils, which would divide their areas into licensing divisons, and form licensine committees for each divtsion, to consist of the members elected to the Gouncil for the division, together with ATI added proportion of other member.. In order to secure that the licensing area should be adequately large, no licensing committee will have on it less than six elected members. Towns with a population of 60,000 would form licensing divisions, and were there were not six members returned from that town the Town Council of the borough would add from their number sufficient members to make the necessary quota of elected members. The Councils would have power to refuse the renewals of licenses when they wished to re- duce the number of such licenses, and to close licensed houses on Sundays, Good Fridays, and Christmas Day. Where a complaint was made, and the justices were of opinion that a licenses ought not to be renewed, the County Council must reiuse it. compensation must be paid if a license was refused on any other ground than the justices' report.. (Ministerial cheers) The amount of compensation was to be referred to and arbitrator chosen by the parties interested, and the principle upon which it was to be calculated vras the difference in the value of a house which had a license and the value of a house without a license at the time of the passing of the bill. If the parties could not agree, the question must. go before a County Court judge, and the amount settled upon would be paid out of the County fund, but charged to the district in which the license was refused. The bill gave power to councils to increase the license by twenty per eent—(Opposition cheers)— as a set-off to the recognition of claims to compensation. With reference to the fmancial aspect of the scheme, Mr. Ritchie said that in the financial year 1889-90 the" grants In aid" of local taxation in respect to the following mat- ters will entirely disappear from the Estimates :—Turn- pike and main roads, poor law schools, poor law medical officers, medical officers of health, inspectors of nuisances, registrars of births and deaths, cost of criminal prosecutions and certain police, and grants to school boards, amounting in the total to £2,600,000. The revenue which would be handed over to the County Council amounted to £5,600,000. That was to be raised by licenses for the sale of intoxicating drink, liquor dealers' licenses, and the licenses of pawnbrokers, plate dealers, refreshment-house keepers, tobacco dealers, British wine dealers, as well as those for armorial bear- ings, carriages, dogs, game, guns, and male servants. The total thus reached was roughly £3,000,000. In ad- dition, the Chancellor of the Exchequer would propose to raise revenue from other license duties amounting to £826,000, and he would also give a contribution from personal property amounting to £1,800.000, mak- ing a total of £5,600,000. The receipts of the County Council would be subject to payments for Poor- law, schools, and medical officers, in- spectors of nuisances, pauper lunatics, criminal prose- cutions, and other grants to the amount of £2,345,000. They proposed that the election of the County Councils should be held in January next, although the new authority would not take over its functions under the bill until the 25th of March. The district councils ',Med not be elected until the November following; but after- wards all the elections for the County Councils, for the municipal boroughs, for the rural districts, and for the urban districts would take place in the same time in November. The right hon. gentleman resumed his seat at 6 55, after a.neroration in which he claimed that the Government had been actuated by a desire to settle the question on a permanent basis, and with a' full trust of the people of the country. Mr. RITCHIE replied to a number of questions on points of detail. In regard to Scotland and Ireland as affected by the bill, he said there would be every disposi- tion to deal with them in a spirit of impartial justice. Mr! Gmnszesre, rtn. /W. _.,„rettiy_ed with Opposition cheers, wished tolcaTwledgelhat the right-hon. gentle- man had discharged the arduous duty that had fallen on him in a manner that did him high honour. (Cheers on both sides.) The plans of the Government were a great deal too large to admit of the pronouncing of any conclusive judgment on 'them. He adhered to the spirit of the words he used at the commence- ment of the session; but must at present retain his whole and absolute liberty of judgment. The speech was a very frank, lucid, and able statement. In the plan proposed there were principles, the accept- ance of which as comieg from the tight hon, gentleman and his colleagues, was a very important fact in the history of Parliamentary legislation, and the fruit and profit of which he should be sorry if the Parliament and the country were to lose through the existence of a grudging or ungenerous spirit on the part of those who sit separately from the party of the right hon. gentle- man. (Cheers.) Mr. T. P. O'CoNtron (Liverpool—Scotland) complained that Ireland was promised nothing. In reply to questions put by Sir H. J. felwin-ibbetsen, Mr. Heneage, Mr. Sinclair. Mr. T. P. O'Connor, Mr. P. S. Powell, Mr. George T. Kenyon, Mr. R. Jasper Moore. Mr. Llewellyn, and Mr. Elliott Lees, Mr. RITCHIE further ex- plained some of the details of his bill. The Council in It borough would be in the position of a County Coined. The Government did not propose to interfere with the election of Town Councillors. The authority for en- forcing the Allotment Act Would be the rural sanitary authority directly elected by the ratepayers. With regard to the police, the Home Office would still continue to in• spect them, and if they found any lack of efficiency, the county authorities would be called upon to emetic, it. As to London, the bill only dealt with the question of the County Council in London, wheel would be elected from all parts of the metropolis. The Government had a plan in view in reference to the districts of London, but that plan was not before Parliament. The 'whole matter of the sale of intoxicating liquor would be in the hands of the County Council, arid not the local commit The bill would not touch the question of education at all. The bill did not make any alteration in the arrears ohdistrict. authorities. The bills were read a first time amid cheers, and the second reading was fixed for April 12th. HOUSE OF LORDS.--Mommr.

--- - THE REFORM OF TFIE HOUSE OF LORDS. Lord ItosEBERY called attention tc4he constitution of the House,,and moved for the appointment of a Com- mittee to inquire thereon. He said he brought forward a similar motion four years ago, and he renewedit now because circumstances during the interval had not been favourable. During the last seven !years 65 new peers had beea created, and the evil was a growing one. The agitation arising out of the rejection of the Franchise Bill raised the question of mending or ending the House of Lords. Speaking generally, he believed that the minority in the country, numbering about 1,100,000 electors, was only supportedCby about 30 Peers out of 556. A House which was bed alone on the hereditary principle was found-ed on the sand. 'rho conversion/15f the House into a party instrument had to a great extent weakened its powers. The arg,ureents in support of a second Chamber neve, ite his mind, irresistible. He thought in the Privy Council we had an ideal second Chamber:containing all the emi- nent politicians of the day, and of its 211 members 109 were Peers. He asserted that the ore for a reform of the House of Lords was'a real one, and it was only the ene- mies of the House who would have them be still. The Earl of Wricrss moved an amendment condemn- ing the proposal to place the constitution of the House In the power of a Committee, and asserting that if any change in its constitution were wanted they should be debateld on the motion of the responsible Ministers of the

Crown. The Marquis of SALaSBIrRY said that what was pro- posed meant nothing less than the entire reconstruction of one of the Houses of Legislature. On a question of that kind they could not settle principles first and leave the details to be considered afterwards. His lord- ship showed that the Conservative majority in the House was due to temporary circumstances—to the career and predilections of Mr. Gladstone. Whils‘ certain number of life peers would increase the efficiency of the House. that power must be restricted. No second ohamber could answer with such a Government as ours so well as one based on the hereditary principle. Earl GRANTILTR said that there was only one course left to those who desired a reform of the House, and that was to vote for the motion. Earl your.* having stated that he would support the propose; The motion was defeated by 97 votes to 50. The amendment by Earl Wemyss was got rid of by the pre- vious question, and the House adjourned.
HOUSE OP COMMONS.-MONDAY

The Speaker took the chair a few minutes after 3 p.m. A Select Committee on' Fire Inquests having been ap- pointed, and Mr. Courtney havtng been called to the table with his reports on committees, some notices of motion were given, among them being one from Mr. PicroN, to the effect that on the secoud read- ing of the Customs and inland Revenue Bill, he will move a resolution expressing disapproval of the Custom dues on tea, coffee, and cocoa. THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT BILL.

Mr. Rum& rising at 4 30, asked leave to bring in a bill to provide for the qualification and registration cf electors for the purposes of local government in England and Wales, and a bill to amend the laws relating to local government in England and Itales. The honourable gentleman was received with loud cheers. Be said his duty was one of no ordinary diffi- culty, as all those who had studied the question of local government would know. 'The desirabi-lity of reform was happily acknowledged by both parties, and there were few. Governments which had not attempted to deal with it. It was now time that it came out of the region of pro- mise, and he relied upon the co-operation of the House, and especially upon the assistance of the leader of the Opposition (who had already given them assurances on the subject of a highly gratifying character), in the task which was to be set -before the House. The right hon. gentleman went on to say that the Government of the counties by Quarter Sessions was undoubtedly an anomaly, but, on the whole, it had been well performed by these bodies, and perhaps this was one of the reasons why there was no groat and pressing demand from the country for legislation on the matter. There was however, a demand for decentralisation and a considera- tion of the composition of local bodies was, therefore, absolutely necessary. The question to be dealt with was the advisability of setting up an entirely new representa- tive body, or ex tend i ng and refor mingexisting, authorities. In order to carry out the former alternative it would be necessary to conskier the powers and duties of the local authorities within the area affected. With regard to the County; Justices, it was not intended to touch their judicial powers and functions—(" Oh, oh" from the Irish benches)—but all their existing administrative powers in Quarter Sessions would be vested in a County Council, which, in future, would deal with the county rates, and financial business of the county, with county buildings, county bridges, the provision and arrangements of lunatic asy- lums, the establishment and maintenance of reforma- tories and industrial schools, the granting of licenses for music and dancing, and for the sale of intoxicating liquors, the division of the county into polling districts for the purpose of Parliamentary elections, the regis- tration of voters, the administration of the Food and Drugs Act, and of the Weights and Measures Act The Government had also come to the conclusion that the maintenance of the high roads must in future be undertaken by the counties. They proposed that the boroughs might, if they thought right, call upon the county authority to compound with them for the main- tenance of their roads; and they also gave a new power in reference to highways. In some parts of the counties there were highways which, although they were not main roads, were very much used by the cbunties, and which are at present repairable by the highway euthorities. In regard to these roads they pro- posed to give the County Council power to contribute, if they chose, towards their maintenance and improve- ment. The police force of the counties would, under the bill, be managed by a joint committee of the County Council and of Quarter Sessions, the appointment of the chief constables remaining in the same bands as at present—(" Oh, oh," from the Opposition)—but the other powers of Quarter Sessions in relation to the police passing into the bands of the joint committee. The Council would likewise be charged with the administra- tion of the Rivers Pollution Act and the Public Health Act. There would be imposed upon the Councils further a duty with regard to the maintenance of in-door paupers by a contribution of 4d. per head per diem for every pauper in the Unions throughout the counties, and they would also have powers which would enable them to promote emigration—(Ministerial cheers)—by advanc- ing moneys for the purpose where there was a reasonable expectation of its being repaid. The County. Councils will have burrowing powers, in order that they might meet the expenses of the duties conferred upon them, and at the commencement clench year must issue a budget of income and expenditure. As to arrears, the geopraphical lines of tho various counties would be followed, except in instances where a large town is situated in two counties, in which case the county in which the larger portion of the town is situate will become the area in which it is to be included. The electoral districts would be the sanitary districts, or parts of them, and the Leval Government Board would fix the number of representatives for each county. The boroughs would fix their own divisions. Coming to the subject of the election of representatives to the Council, the right hon. gentleman intimated, amid loud cheers, that members will be elected just as members of Tarlioment are elected, aud that it is intended to extend the Municipal Corporations Act to he whole of the counties. One-fourth of the represen- tatives in the Council, however, would be elected by the local authorities, and all of them would be elected for a term of three years' service. Some of the large towns would be created counties in themselves, and the boroughs fixed upon were: Liverpool, Birmingham, Manchester, Leeds, Sheffield, Bristol, Bradford, Nottingham, Hull, and Newcastle. In ' the case of the small boroughs they would retain their municipal powers intact, but for certain purposes would he represented on the county council. The bill divided the county into urban and rural districts. The urban districts would be the existing and the future municipal boroughs and local boards. The town council would be the district council of the county. The local board dis- tricts had as their governing body a body elected by a ;aural vote. It was in-possible that they should have county councils elected by such a franchise. The Government therefore proposed that the council in the local board districts should be elected on the same prin- ciple as the municipal boroughs of the county councils. (:Hear, hear.) Sir A. Boirrnwicx : Retaining the woman franchise? Mr. RITCHIE: Yes, certainly. (Cheers.) It was proposed the rural district councils should be elected in the same way. The rural sanitary districts were at present coter- minous with unions, and were arranged entirely with a view to poor-law administration. The Government pro- posed that where the county boundary cut the union the portion on either side of the boundary should either form a separate rural sanitary district or be added to an ad- joining one. The hill imposed as one of the first duties on the county council, that of making all the necessary adjustments so that an election might be held for such district. They would also divide the rural district into wards, and fix the number of councillors for the rural district council. The county council would submit to the Local Government Board an order for the rearrange- ment of a rural district which the Board would confirm unless there was a petition against it, and in that case an inquiry would be held. In local board districtethe district commissioners would have transferred to them all existing powers ot local boards, which would then cease to exist. In the rural districts they would have the power ef the rural sanitary authorities and of the highway boards transferred to them, and those authorities and ,boards would be abolished. Every district council, whether urban or rural, would take over the existing powers as to lighting watching, the control of baths and wash-houses, widths powers under the Lodging-house Acts, and the Burial Acts. Rates would continue to be levied over the par- ticular areas in which these Acts were enforced, and committees would be formed by the district council, consisting partly of councillors and partly of•ratepayers„ to managethe districts under those Acts. The comnline

Public Health Act so as to make further provision for the prevention of infectious disease. Mr. BRUNNER brought in a bill to amend the law relating to dlerks of the peace, and it also was read a first time. THE NATIONAL DEBT BILL.—The House, after the Con- solidated Fund Bill had been read a second time, went into Committee on the National Debt Conversion Bill. —Mr. FOWLER moved an amendment to one of the clauses practically negativing the proposal that a com- mission of is 6cl per £lOO should be paid to bankers and agents in connection with the conversion; and Sir WILLIAM HARCOURT, objecting to the same proposal, said it would for the first time set a precedent of the British Government paying the Stock Exchange for its support.—Nor did Mr. GLADSTONE agree with it. Why, he asked, should this mon be paid? The Chancellor of the Exchequer had said that if the banker conveyed his own stock to the bank he would receive no commis- sion; but, added Mr. Gladstone amid cheers and laugh- ter, the banker would employ a broker to go in his stead, and the commission would be divided between them. That was not a desirable arrangement to make under an Act of Parliament. Again, why was the small holder who transacted his own business not to have the allow- ance for his trouble which would be paid if he em- ployed an agent? To that question he doubted whether an answer could be given—in fact, the payment was a mistake.—Lord RANDOLPH Cnuncnim. objected to the commission on economical grounds.—The house divided on Mr. Fowler's amendment, which was rejected by 244 votes to. 127.—1 t was decided that the 58 to be paid to holders should be treated as income.—A number of clauses were adopted without discussion, and rig. the others certain alterations were agreed to.—The bill then passed through Committee.—The sitting was suspended until nine o'clock. A COUNT OUT.—At the evening sitting Mr. PICKERS- GILL brought on his motion of censure upon Sir Charles Warren for his reflection on the West Ham Stipendiary with regard to the case of Constable Bloy, but it was afterwards withdrawn. While Colonel HUGHES was moving for a Select Committee relative to workmen at Woolwich Arsenal it was noticed that there was not a quorum present, and the House was counted out at forty minutes past ten o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNESDAY. The Ipeaker took the chair at 10 minutes past twelve o'clock.

ARREARS OF RENT HARDSHIP. Mr. PARNELL, in moving the second reading f the Arrears Bill, said he had taken section 30 of last year's Land Act as a foundation for his bill—a section provid- ing that County Courts in which proceedings were taken for arrears of rent should have the power within a limi- tation of £5O valuation to postpone or excuse the decree. But he asked the House to go a step further, and to give the courts additional power to reduce the debt in case of rent, and also to reduce the costs. The limitation, he held, ought not to be £5O but £lOO valuation, in order to meet the case of leaseholders; and he asked, like- wise, for an extention of the provision of section 30 to cases of civil bills for the recovery of rent. Failing some extension of section 30, Ireland was bound to be plunged into terrible confusion and disaster. It was said they must deal with the abatement of arrears on the same footing as other debt; but it was monstrous and absurd to attempt to set up an analogy between these two classes of debt. Urgently he asked the Government to remedy the great hardship. If the land question was the only difficulty, why did not they take it up ?—though he could not promise that even if the land question were settled on a fair basis the de- mand of Ireland for self-government would be lessened. (Cheers). Mr. PowaLL-WILLIAMS moved an amendment that no bill for a composition of arrears would be effectual for the relief of the tenants unless it dealt with their debts to other creditors besides landlords. The amendment was seconded by Lord Enangerom ; but Mr. T. W. RUSSELL expressed his intention, under the sternest sense of duty, of voting against the Government, stating that scarcely one of the evictions now pending rested on a moral basis, inasmuch as they were nearly all for arrears of rent. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN, who entered early into the debate, had soon an American expression on his tongue, for he , told the House that Irish members were only too ready to "catch on" some admitted grievance, and they developed and magnified the grievance altogether beyond what was reasonable and fair. There was undoubtedly a grievance to be remedied, but Mr. Parnell's bill went quite beyond it, and did not even put any limit to the class of arrears that were to be dealt with. The griev- ance would be metb,y a bill reducing arrears to the extent of 14 or 15 per cent. But the real difficulty was the complete insolvency and embarrassment of the large proportion of small tenants; and it was desirable to re- lieve the tenants of these embarrassments in cases where they were entirely unable to pay—in fact, the real remedy i was n a system of tenant relief. Mr. Drubs severely criticised Mr. Chamberlain's speech, and said the right hon. keit!eiriaill2cl been en; I engaged in turning political somersaults. The mover the amendment, he added, displayed gross ignorance of Irish affairs, and he warned the House lest they should unduly strain Ulster's loyalty. Mr. BALFOUR, in the course of his speech, asked whe- ther the bill, if passed into law, would settle the Irish question, and Mr. PARNELL replied "Certainly not." The Crime SECRETARY strongly denounced the bill, say- ing that it removed neither the theoretical nor the prac- tical grievance, and that it enforced the evil lesson that the worst policy of the Irish tenant was that of honesty, and that prosperity was not the fruit of industry and temperance, but of dexterous Parliamentary manipula- tion and remorseless agitation. In reply to Mr. Healy, it was stated by Mr. BALFOUR that the Government ac- cepted the amendment. Sir WILLIAM HA-Ramer, asser- ting that the only practical measure for dealing with the arrears question would be destroyed by the amend- ment, asked if that was the manner in which they ex- pected to pacify Ireland. The house divided, and there were for the bill, 243; against, 328; majority against, 85. Only slight cheers and counter-cheers were raised. Again the House divided, the figures being—for Mr. Powell Williams's amendment, 320; against, 230 : major- ity for the amendment, 90. The Consolidated Fund (No. 1) Bill was passed through Committee, and the report on the National Debt (Con- version) Bill was agreed to. The House adjourned at twenty-five minutes past six o'clock. HOUSE OF LORDS.—THIM.SDAV. • The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack shortly after four o'clock. MISCELLANEOUS.—The Mersey Railway Bills were read a second time, the Law of Distress Amendment Bill a third time, and the Merchant Shipping (Life Saving Appliances) Bill a second time. The object of the latter bill, the second reading of which was moved by the Earl 'of Onslow, was to require ships to carry an adequate amount of boat accommodation and buoys, and to pro- vide that such life-saving appliances as were carried should be kept in a proper state of efficiency. The com- mittees were named for examinino, into the present sys- tem of private bill legislation, and for inquiring into the powers of poor law guardians to cope with distress. The National Debt Conyersion Bill was broughtup and read a first time, and their lordships adjourned at 20 minutes past six o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS—THURSDAY.

The Spe.iie-r-t-o-oli-the' -Chair at three o'clock. QUESTIONS, &c.—The introduction of the Local Govern- ment Bill is likely to open up many interesting ques- tions.—One of these was put in the House of Commons by Mr. ADDISON, who 'asked whether, having regard to the proposals for diminishing, the number of licensed public-houses, the Government intended to bring in a bill dealing with clubs.—The difficulty, Mr. Itircins re- plied, was to deal with bogus clubs without interfering with bona-fide clubs; but the Government would be very glad if they were able in any way to deal withthe matter. Mr. RITCHIE was afraid he could not place on the table before Easter a paper showing the number of County Councils for each county of England and Wales under the Local Government Bill; but he promised that such a statement should be in the handl of hon. members before the House went into Committee on the Bill. The HOME SECRETARY stated, that the cost of the recent swearing-in of special constables in London was no less than £1,500, of which £1,033 is put down for truncheons and badges. Sir WILFRID LAWSON asked if the Government intended to initiate legislation for carrying out the resolution pas- sed by the House at its previous sitting in reference to arrears of rent in Ireland. Mr. SMITH'S reply that there was no intention on the part of the Government to do so was received with ironical Oppositidn cheers and great laughter. The Marquis of GRANBY took the oath and his seat for the Melton division of Leicestershire. CRIMINAL EVIDENCE BILL.—The Consolidated Fund Bill and the National Debt Conversion Bill having been read a third time, the ATTORNEY-GENERAL moved the second reading of the Criminal Evidence Bill, upon which there was an interesting debate. Sir Charles Russell and Sir Henry James argued that its provisions should no% be extended to Ireland; and Mr. T. HEALY, who moved an amendment to that effect, said in the sister country the Crown regarded a conviction as a Red Indian re- garded the taking of a scalp. Mr. SMITH, after many hon. members had spoken, moved " That the question be now put." On a division the closure motion was carried by 160 votes to 111. The SPEAKER having put the amendment, the House again divided, when there were—for the amendment, 119: agaiast, 173; majority against the amendment, 54.—The SPEAKER then put the question that the bill be read a second time, and Mr. PARNELL, submitting that he had a right to speak, argued against the bill.—The House divided, the figures being—for the second reading, 231; against, 92 ; ma- jority for, 139. After another division it was decided that the committee stage of the bill should be taken on April 12. Mr. T. W, RUSSELL moved the discharge of his Arrears of Rent Bill, leaving the responsibility on the Govern- ment, and the motion was agreed to. feSeveral bills. were introduced, and the House ad- journed at 12-15.

Tim CAP.DIFF SAVINGS BANX.—An interim report on the Cardiff Savings Bank was published on Saturday, in which Mr. Stanley advises a more complete audit of the books, but holds that the trustees and managers are per. °natty liable for all the money they paid in composi- tions to debtors. A disturbances took place, op Monday evening, in the streets of Congleton, owing to the parading of the "Sal- vation "Army, in defiance of the orders of the magis- trates. Ths_ members of the army were attacked by a mob, and their colours captured. Several of the "officers" and others were injured, and there was great disorder for a time. -

_ On Monday, several valuable bead of cattle, belonging, to a Cumberland farmer, earned Henry Cass, of Stain- burn, Workington, suddenly fell dead in a grazing field. Mr. Soulsby, veterinary surgeon, made a post-mortem examination, which showed that death resulted from poisoning, caused by cattle browsing on cuttings of yew trees. Others of the herd are not expected to recover from the effect of the poison. FATAL AFFRAY TN HUDDERSFIRLD.—A fatal affray took place in Huddersfield on Saturday night. A young man named Fisher, a painter, was walking along Manchester- road with his sweetheart and another young woman, when he was assaulted by, it is alleged, a young man named Swift. The blow knocked 15shy,,, down, and he lay unconscious, dying in the infirmary on Sunday after- noon from concussion of the brain. A verdict of "Manslaughter" has been returned against Swift. SUICIDE FROM CLIFTON SUSPENSION BRlDOS—Residents in the neighbourhood of the Clifton Suspension Bridge were startled on Saturday night by the report of another suicide from the bridge, which spans the river Avon ata height of 250 ft. The-suicide appeared to be a 'middle- aged man, respectably dressed. He was seen to mount the parapet on the Somerset side of the bridge and in- stantly leap into the river. He floated down the river some 60 yards, and then disappeared. leormons ROBBEILT.—At the Bradford Borough Police' Court, on Monday, an ingenious system of robbery was exposed. It appeared that a woman named Elizabeth Pickles, took a situation in a fashionable neighbourhood, ' and induced her employers to allow her husband to ' live and board on the premises, in consideration of doing odd jobs. During the last fortnight they managed *to. dispose of £lOO worth of their employer's property, chiefly plate. Detection becoming imminent, they dis- e area with the plunder, The prisoners were re._ . . A ROY'S PRII!SENT TO A PRINCESS.—A little boy in the Bute Industrial School. Rothesay, forwarded to the Princess of Wales, as Duchesi of Rothesay, a beautiful piece of mantle drapery wrought in Macroom lace and finished with gold cord and blue satin. The work occu- pied him many months. Her Royal Highness has ac- knowledged the gift, expressing "the Princess of Wales's admiration of his beautiful work, as well as her appre- ciation of the loyal feeling which made him wish to present it to her on the occasion of the silver wedding!' THE DOUBLE MURDER BY A MOTHER AT LONDON. -- At the Central Criminal Court, on Tuesday, Emma Eliza- beth Aston, 39, single woman, was placed on her trial for murdering her two illegitimate male children, at Upton Park, London. The prisoner had been deserted by the father of the children. After hearing witnesses for the prosecution, the jury, witho e hearing counsel for the defence, found that at the time of committing the alleged offences the prisoner was insane. She was therefore ordered to be detained during her Majesty's pleasure. On Sunday afternoon, a boat, containing the captain,' mate, and four other persons, left the ship Cambria, in Carmarthen Bay, to 6tcli an anchor from Rhesillv sands. The sea was calm, but from some unexplained cause the boat capsize'. and its occupants were thrown into the water. Ti' or board the ship witnesssed the occurrence, be Jere unable to render help, as their remaining boat had no 'Ars. As soon as possible, the vessel's anchor was hove up and sail was made towards the mot, but all the men had then disappeared. The catastrophe occurred only about 200 yards from the shore where many witnessed it, but could give no help. The bodies have not been recovered. TRE. RETURN OF TRE PRINCE OF WALES.—The Prince of Wales, accompanied by Prince Albert Victor, the Duke of Cambridge, Prince Christian, and the Crown Prince of Denmark, arrived at Charing Cross Station. at 515 on Wednesday morning, from Berlin, with their respective suites. General Von Loe, special envoy frem the new German Emperor 4,0 her Majesty the Queen, arrived with the Royal party, who crossea from calais in a special steamer. The Prince of Wales, attended by Major-General Ellis left Marlborough House, in the afternoon, for Windsor, on a visit to the Queen, to whom his Royal Highness is the bearer of messages from the Emperor and Empress of Germany. GRAVE CHARGE AOAINST PATlENTS.—EfenryEdward and Annie Maria Miller, man and wife, of Newton St. Cyres, near Crediton, were committed for trial at Crediton, on eaturday, charged with -the murder of the illegitimate daughter of the wife, aged 16 years, on January 25 last. The body of the girl was found in an unused mine, and at the inquest the medical evidence went to show that death had occurred before the remains were deposited in the place where they were found. The principal witness against the prisoners was a son aged eleven years, who stated that one morning the deceased fell down stairs, and was picked up by his father, who laid her on the bed, on which afterwards there was a .bag of rags. These were subsequently burned, and the theory of the prose- cution is that the girl was thrown downstairs, and killed by being beaten on the head for the sake of an insurance of £5 effected on her life. SINGHLAR CAREER OF A LEEDS 11EIRESS.—A correi spondent of a Pittsburg paper telegraphs from New York :—Detectives and friends are hunting all over the city after Julia Stanton, the heiress to property in Eng- land. Julia ‘-eas a beautiful girl, who disappeared from her' home in Leeds, England, on May 17th, 1874. Nothing was heard of her for eight or nine years. Then her parents received a letter, dated this city, saying she was married and in business on South Fifth Avenue, this city. They asked her to return home, but she refused. An emissary was sent, but to no purpose. A woman, friend of the family came over, but could not find the girl Her parents in England thought her dead. Dr. Nagle, of the Health Department here, interested hitnselfe and believes he found tee girl, who had been living with a negro, named Fender, in a basement at 202, South Fifth Avenue, now used as a junk shop. Inquiry showed that two years ago the negro husband deserted Julia. She then made the acquaintance of a poor Italian, and mar- riedhim. She felt her disgrace keenly, took to drink, and worked in saloons. All trace was lost there, and the detectives now think she was sent a prisoner for being drunk to- the House of Correction, died there, and is buried in a pauper's 'grave. Ter CLIPTON,CONVENT CASE.—Further evidence was taken on Saturdae at Bristol Assizes—before Mr. Justice Field—in the extraordinary action brought by MIMI Mason against the Clifton Wood Convent and two medical men. Dr. Shaw, one of the defendants, said he was satisfied from his examination of the plaintiff in April, 1884, that she was of unsound mind. She remained 25 minutes with her face to the wall and her fingers to her ears, and refused to answer any questions. Dr. Renville Fox, one of the proprietors of the Brislington House Asylum described the condition of the plaintiff when sent to the .1 institution. He denied haying put his arm round the • plaintiff and called her "My dear.' A letter written by the plaintiff to She Lunacy Commissioners was put in as • to the treatment at Burgess Hill. On Monday. His Lordship, in summing up, commented on the' way in which the case had 'been brought forward, and said it was specially a wicked. thing to bring against doctors allegations of conspiracy, which, hetwever, had been withdrawn. He thought the charge of malice against the' lady superior ought also to have been with- diawn.—The jury retired, and after remaining in con- sultation about an hour, returned with a verdict for the defendants.—His Lordship expressed his conctirrenee, and grsinted costs;

LIBERAL MEETING AT LYMM.

The second anniversary of Lymm Liberal Club wits held in the Congregational School-room on th°49..6l6sTria Tueeday evening, and was a great sucoess. The p eeuingi h`"• o.oramenced with a tea, after which a Wlic chair was occupied public meeting was... by Mr. James Dodds, and amoilVt . sent were Professor Swift Mac Neil, M.P. (for Donegal), Mr. NV . W. Biggs (Liverpool), Mr. I. S. Leadam (Liberal candidate for the Altrin- cham Division), Rev. W. Evans, Mr. G. L. Welford, Mr. J. E Swanwick, Mr. John Thomson, and Mr. Skilling (hon. secretary.)—The Chairman, in opening the proceedings, remarked that the club was in a most satisfactory position. The membership had been increased during the past twelve months, and those results had, he was glad to say, been brought about without recourse to any of those objectionable and questionable methods to which recourse was had by very many political clubs. He was glad also to be in a position to congratulate the members of the club upon the fact that the prospects of the Liberal cause in that division were most promising and bright. He asked those of his hearers who were electors to endeavour in that constituency to throw off the Tory yoke which for generations past had enthralled that part Of Cheshire. (Cheers.) In the course of a vigorous address, Professor Swift Mac Neil, M.P., said that the Altrincham Division was at present misrepresented in Parliament, for their member, though an excellent man, held principles different to the majority of the electors—prin- ciples which were anta„eonistic to popular rights; and, however great his excellence, or however much his een- erosity, a gentleman must represent that constituency who was in accord with the sympathies of the eleetors, and who wished to do justice to his countrymen at hu-ge. From his experience orthe present feeling of Eng;i.h constituencies, he would promise them that they would be able, if they chose, to return Mr. Leadam at the head of the poll at the next election. (Applause.) They only needed to follow, even at a considerable distance, the Northwich election. The county of Chester ought not to be behindhand in the national cause; the cause of justice. Home Rule simply meant the establishment of a statu- toryor local power in Ireland for the management of Irish affairs exclusiNely. Could anything be more reasonable than that? lithe County Government Bill, which was introduced in Parliament on Monday night, ever came into operation—he doubted very much whether it was ever meant to come into operation-(laughter, and hear.) hear)—they would be asked by that Bill to unite will their neighbours in matters of public interest, but even though that was the case they would still wish to regu- late their own households and be masters in their own homes—(hear, hear)—and that was all the Irish asked. They only wished to regulate their own house- holds and while the- would unite with the Enpli:sh, Scotch, and they- in imperial affairs, they wished to manage their own home matters. The 86 Irish members of Parliament were backed up by the people of Ireland, and by the Irish race all over the globe. So long as they were in Parliament every reform that was proposed by the English Government would be affected by their action. In justice to themselves, and in justice to some of the poor starving people who sent them to Parliament, the Irish members were bound to keep their interests in the foreground, even though popular English legislation was to aome degree retarded thereby. It was objected that the establishment of a Parliament in Dublin:would mean the destruction of capital in Ireland, but that argument was a false one, for, on the contrary, a native parliament would produce a sense of,Xsecurity which would stimulate the trade and manufactures of the country. (Cheers.) Mr. W. W. Biggs said that he believed the electors in the Altrincham division would, when their chance came, show that there was plenty of fight in them. Meanness, cruelty, and vindictiveness was the policy of the Tory party in Ireland, and they, as Liberals, were unwilling to be responsible,for the actions of such a party, and they repudiated them. (Applause.) They would have an opportunity of doing so at the next election, and of up- setting Sir William Cunliffe Brooks—(laughter)--or who- ever stood against Mr. Leadam, and sending Mr. Lead- am to Parliament to assist Mr. Gladstone in the settle- ment of that great cause Home Rule, which meant re- conciliation and peace. (Cheers.) Mr. I. S. Leadam proposed a vote of thanks to the ladies and gentlemen who had contributed to the instruction and amusement which had been furnished the audience that evening. He said he welcomed Pro- fessor Mac Neil there because he was an Irishman; and he was none the less welcome because, although an Irish- man, lie had thought fit to obtain his education in this country. (Rear, hear.) By that act he recognised that, as a citizen of Ireland, he was also a citizen of Great Britain; and it was the general desire of the Irish to re- main both citizens of Ireland and of Great Britain. (Cheers.)—Mr. Brown seconded the motion, which was carried by acclamation. Professor Mac Neil and the Chairman having acknowledged the compliment, the proceedings were brought to a close by the singing of the National Anthem .—During . the evening a musi- cal programme was carried out by Messrs. T. A. Bayley, W. H. Wallington, A. H. Charles- worth. H. D. Herring, Mrs. Lane, and the Misses Schaub, and recitations were giveh by Mr. Furness. At the tea, trays were given by the following ladies, who also presided at the tables :—Mesdames Dodds. Smith, Dutton, Swanwick, Brearley, F. 0. Moston, Brown, E. Brown, Watson, Thomson' Brocks, Evans, Murrey, Ellison. Cameron, Ross, Longshaw, Skilling, London Midgley, Robson, ;wen, and Jackson, and Misses DI; Ville, West, Brooks.

The main features of the Local Government Bill were described by Mr. Rrrcana in the House of Commons on Monday. it is ' a bold;far-reaching, and, on the whole, a democratic measure; and we are not surprised that it has startled the old- fashioned country gentlemen, who seem happy amongst the cobwebs which have been woven about them. The bill is one for brushing aside Cobwebs; and the out-and-out Tories cannot Understand how such a liberal bill has emanated an a Tory Government. They forget that Lord ...WI'S Administration exists by grace of the • Liberal Unionists; and that a measure which fell far short of that which was sanctioned, in draft, by • Lord HARTINGTON and Mr. CHAMBERLAIN, when they were in office, would have no chance whatev,er of securing the support of the Liberal Unionists as a party. Broadly speaking, it may be said of ' the bill that it extends the Municipal Corporations • A.ct to the government of counties. We are to • have County Councils as well as Town Councils; and the franchise is in each case to be the same, , which means, of course, that there swill be female suffrage just as there is at present in the . municipalities. For voting purposes, the county will be divided into electoral districts, or wards, • each district sending one representative tO the r County Council. The new machine will be called

Upon to do a large amount of work; and, with a view to prevent it being overloaded to begin with, all matters relating to education and poor-law administration will be exempt from its operations. 130ards of Guardians and School Attendance Com- mittees, as well as School Boards, will remain Untouched; but Local Boards and Commissioners, and such small fry as Highway Boards and Rural Sanitary Authorities, will be put out of exist- ence, provision being made for such duties as they are at present performing being done by the County Councils, or the subsidiary District Coun- cils. Details as to some of these matters will be found in the report of Mr. Itircitre's speech which we give in another column; and, as to others, the reader will have to wait until the new bill has issued from the hands of the printer. Broad its are the lines upon which the bill has in the main been drawn, it i! not without evidence of Tory narrowness. There are defects which will have to be removed before the measure can be re- garded as wholly acceptable to the nation. It is proposed, for instance, that the management of the police shall be in the hands of a Joint Com- mittee of the County Council and the Quarter Ses- sions. This is a sop, of course, to the country gen- tlemen who act in their magisterial capacity at Quarter Sessions. But if a Town Council, big or little, can be entrusted with the management of borough police, why should not similar trust be re- posed in a County Council ? The County Council Will be called upon to levy rates for the payment of the county police, and ought to have the full control of that body. But the distinction as to dealing with the police is carried to a ridiculous extreme in the provision that the appointment of the Chief-Constable of a County shall rest en- tirely with the magistrates sitting in Quarter Ses- sions. The County Council shall pay the salary of this tremendous personage; but it must have no voice in electing him! Taxation, however, without representation, is tyranny ; and we do not suppose this wee* section of the bill will survive the critic- ism of the House of Commons, although it is the sort of thing that would be made welcome in the }louse of Lords'. It was perhaps to be expected that the Municipal Corporations Act would be fol- lowed in providing that three-fourths only of the County Council are to be elected directly by the ratepayers, the other fourth being elected by the Councillors themselves, either from within their own. body or from without. But the aldermanic

system is a bad system, and it ought to be abol- ished rather than extended. It formed no Part of the criginal et of 1835 ; it was thrust into it as a pieci of Toryism by the Hous e of • Lords; and has, after half a century of trial, JlO-,

I thing to recommend it. Granted that aldermem are, as a rule, men who have had experience of corporate work; they ought on that account to be the more acceptable to the electors; and, whenever they were worthy of the suffrages of their fellow-bur- gesses they would obtain them. To place them beyond the reach of the bur- gesses is to render them less susceptible to public opinion, and to make them more or less indifferent to the performance of the duties which devolve upon them. The nation would not for a moment tolerate a proposal to leave it to the ;louse of Commons to elect a fourth of its own members ; and why should it be tolerated either in connection•with Town Councils or the proposed County Councils? But the chief blot on the new measure is mlde by the half-hearted way in which it is proposed to put licensing matters into the hands of the people, and by the provision for compensation for licenses that are not renewed. Every county is to be divided into Licensing Divisions, and there is to be a Licensing Committee in each division, whose duty it shall be to consider the advisability of re- newing or reducing the number of licenses. If the Licensing Committee decide, with regard to any license, that it is "one too many" for any district, the holder of the license has a power to appeal to the County Council; ancl "if the refusal- is con- firmed by the County Council on other ground than the justices' report, we enact," says Mr. "that compensation must be paid." That is to say, a non-representative body—the justices —shall alone have the power by reporting against a house to decide that the license shall not be re- newed, and that there can be no claim for compen- sation; whilst the representative body—the Licensing Committee—shall not only have no power to refuse a license without compensation; but shall give its decisions subject to an appeal to the County Council. This is an anomaly to begin with—an absurdity on the face of it. And why compensation Under any circumstances? A license is for twelve months, it is an autho- rity givea for twelve months, and no more. When the contract is at an end, there Is surely liberty on each side to say whether or no it shall be renewed. The holder of the license contracts for twelve months to provide the public with cer- , tO.ll a.ceolThiliOclOion and refl:4olllaent9 cer, stipulated conditions. If he thinks At, A the end of the term, to cease to renew the contract, he can of course do so, and the Licensing Authority have no claim upon him. And so, on the other hand, if the Licensing Authority think fit to say—" We cannot renew this license, because it is not in the public interest required," the publican or brewer cannot possibly have any just claim against the Licensing Authority. ,The law as it at present stands recognises no claim for compensation ; and the members of the House of Commons will be "led by the nose as asses are" if they walk into a trap of this kind. It is true the Government bait the trap by proposing to give power to the County Council to increase the license duty, for publicans by twenty per cent. But this extra duty would bring in thousands only, while the payment of com- pensation would swallow tens of thousands, if the licenses were reduced as they °tight to be reduced. No compensation has been given to the holders of out-licenses whose licenses have been abolished. The issue has ,been determined in the law courts; the law recognises no such claim; and the Legisla- lature must take care that a footing for the claim is not secured in the Local Government Bill. Brewers and distillers have " waxed fat and kicked" out of the gains of "the horrid traffic ; " we ought to see to it that they do not have occa- sion to laugh at us while bleeding us with claims for compensation.

Two cases were heard at the Warrington Police Court, an Monday, which curiously illustrate the difficulty of getting a conviction in the matter of offences against the licensing laws when a publican is concerned. In the first ease a woman named Dolan was summoned for having been drunk on licensed premises. Two police officers swore to visiting the Higher Angel Inn and seeing Dolan there intoxicated with a glass of beer before her. It followed, of course, that if it could be shown that the woman was being supplied with drink whilst she was tipsy, the landlord had also com- mitted a breach of the law; and he was accord- ingly summoned for permitting drunkenness on his pfemises. But Higginson, the landlord, had more at stake than the woman; so he engaged a lawyer, and prepared to defend himself, as he was entitled to do, to the uttermost. He called his wife, who said she did not notice anything to lead her to suppose that the woman was tipsy when she was served with beer, and another witness, who declared that in his opinion the woman Dolan was not drunk. There are, to be sure, people who do not think a person can be regarded as drunk who is capable of asking for snore; and others also would say that there is nothing the matter so long as the suspect can ride home in a cab. The land- lord Higginson swore that the woman was sober, but neither he nor his wife could be looked upon as a disinterested witness. It was really the evi- dence of one disinterested witness against that of two experienced police .officers; but the Bench thought there was a cbiubt in the matter, and dis- missed both cases. It would be interesting to know how many instances there are on record of cases of alleged drunkenness being dismissed in the face of the sworn evidence of two constables—cases, we mean, which did not also involve the drini--seller. They would, we are inclined to think, be found to be very few and very far between. However, it was something for the police officers to be tt ld by the chief magistrate that what they had done was "perfectly right." They must go on summoning when they seo, or believe they .Bee, that there is a breach of the law. If they do not always secure convictions, they will at least have the satisfadion of knowing that they are &Aug their duty; and that they are lessening evils doing by becoming a terror to evil-chars.

Kay l3res., Ld., Stcekpert Add, TRIAL OF Stoirnr. iiinsixErt.—On Wednesday, at the Central Criminal Court, Loudon, before Mc. Justice Hawkins, Kr. Samuel Minter was placed on his trial on charges of forgery and perjury. The trial had been remozed to London under Palmer's Act, on the usual plea that a fair trial could not be had in or near the place wherein the offences charged were committed. The result of the pro- ceedings on Wednesday was exactly what had been foreseen from the moment when the charge was stated before the county magistrates. The prisoner denied the forgery, but pktaded guilty to the indict- ments for perjury. Sir S. Russell said the Salford Town Council had already ascertained that the pri- soner had received about £22,000 while occupying a fiduciary position, and the Corporation were of course desirous, in the interest of the ratepayers, that that money should be restored to its proper owners. The Judge suggested that in lieu of the Chancery proceedings which have been instituted an arbitrator might be appointed to inquire as to the amount due to the Corporation. On the understand- ing that this would be done, the sentence wa:spcAt- ponecl until the next sessions. For all kinds of domestic sewing, iia,gley_and Wright s cotton is the best.—Advt.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH 24, 1888.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH 24, 1888.

it is worth passing for the Whole of the United Kingdom. As things go, the people are being gradually shut out of places to which their fathers have had access from time immemorial. City men acquire land in the country, and, 'in many cases, regardless of ancient rights, make it impossible to gam access to a favourite bit of scenery. The in- habitants are not strong enough to assert their rights; and what is needed is some such measure as-the one proposed to ensure a prima facie right of way.

The law does afford some protection with regard to recognised waste and common lands; but how often it is disregarded The land-grabbers are everywhere at work stealing the way-side land, and at the same time roLbing God's earth of its beauty. There is something of the kind going on just now in'Grappenhall-lane—a little beyond the borough botindary. What was up to this year one of the prettiest lengths of lane in the district is being ruthlessly despoiled. The land by the road- side, which is public property. is being taken in, and will, unless a stir be made, be lost to the pub- lic. What is the Highway Board doing to permit this piece of Vandalism? Are the members gone to sleep, or are they awake and winking at what is being done F

One of the shabbiest of the shabby things the present shabby Government have done is the fois- ting a now Irish Under-Secretary upon Parliament as if he were to be an unpaid official, and then bringing in a bill for his services to the tune of £l,OOO a year. If Mr. Balfour wants Mr. King- Harman to assist him, let him pay for his help, out of his own salary. By asking for aid, he practi- cally confesses his incapacity to do the work which other Irish Secretaries have done And who could be more objectionable than Mr. King-Harman; the red-hot Orangeman; the renegade Home- Ruler; the man who vows he will "never take office,or pension from an English Government "; and then turns his coat in order that he may brow, beat his old colleagues at the rate of £l,OOO a year?
' LOCAL NEWS.
, - CHESTER CATHEDRAL. - The preaching armngementg at Chester Cathedral from Sunday last up to the middle of April include the name of the -Rev. A. Maitland Wood, vicar of Runcorn.

POLICE INSPECTION AT Witaxas.--The Hon. Captain Legge, Her Majesty's Government Inspeetor, who was accompanied by Captain Ibbetson, on Monday inspected the members of the Widnes police force. There were present on parade Superintendent Johnston, Inspector Keighley, six sergeants, and 32 constables. The remain- der of the constables were presenton duty, not a single man being absent through sickness. The Inspiector con- gratulated the men on their smart appearance, and hav- ing examined the books, Sm., in the office, he expressed himself highly satisfied in all matters. He finally ap- pr9Yed of the alterations that had been made to the office.

. THE BEGGING NUISANCE AT RUNCORN.—Before Messrs. A. Thomas and G. L. Davies, at Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, John Leonard, a dissipated looking fellow, was charged with begging in High-street, , owthe 18th inst. P.C. Taylor proved- the case. Snerhitenflent Hollingworth said there had been frequeut complaint of the nuisance caused by beggars, and he asked the Bench to deal severely with them. On Sunday morning a gen- tleman was stopped seven times in walking from his residence to the church. The prisoner was sentenced to seven days' hard labour. Yesterday, before Mr. John Brundrit, James Maloney, of Regent-street, was sen- tenced to' 14 days' hard labour for begging in Regent. street on the previous day.

SAD END OF A DRFINKEN WOMAN AT WIDNES.-011 Thursday, at the Arch Hotel, an inquest was held by Mr. Husband, deputy coroner, touching the death of Harriett Rowe, aged 52 years, the wife of a labourer, who lives in Pear-street. The evidence showed that on the 11th February, whilst she was in a drunken condition the demised accidentally set her dress on fire, and she ran screaming into the street. A man named McNulty who was passmeat the time wrapped his coat round the woman and succeeded in extinguishing the flames. Under the care of Dr. Hutchinson the wofnan, lingered until the 20th inst, when she died from congestion of the lungs, her death being accelerated by the burns. A verdict to this effect was returned.

ALEXANDRA THEATRE, WIDNES. This new theatre. which has been erected at a cost of nearly five thousand pounds by a company of local gentlemen, was opened on Monday evening, when Messrs. Miller and Elliston's company occupied the boards with the melodrama "Alone in London." The building is estimated to seat 1,500 persons, and at the opening performance every available seat was occupied, and large numbers were standing, whilst each of the four commodious boxes were engaged. The arrangements of the theatre, both in the auditorium and upon the stage, are of the most modern and approved style, and the outlets are so fa- vourably situated that the building•pan be cleared of the largest audience in little over a minute. A. DANGEROUS MAN AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Peke Court, on Tuesday, before Mr. John Brock and Mr. H. Wade Deacon, Richard Lawrence, of 3, Marsh-street, was charged with assaulting George Jackson. It was stated that on Saturday night Jackson was returning home from the market, when the prisoner followed him down Marsh-street, and struck him on the head, knocking him against the wall and inflicting a wound on his forehead. The prisoner afterwards threw him to the ground, but he madelis escape. On three previous occasions the prrsonerhad threatened to take Jackson's life. Witnesses confirmed this statement, sad the Bench bound the prisoner over to keep the peace for six months, himself in £lo,asn4 two sureties of L 5 each, or go to gaol for days. PREE LIBRARY LECTURE LT WinxiS.—The last of the iseries of public lectures, organised by the Free Library Committee, was given in Lacey-street School-room on Tuesday evening. This lecture, like its predecessors, was very well attended. Mr.. IL H. Davies presided. The. lecturer was Mr. W. A. Watts, M.A., head master of the Farnworth Grammer School, who spoke in an interest- ing manner of the formation of 'gee and Snow," and thaw onderful part ice and snow had, played in shaping the surface of the earth. trie particularly described the glories of Switzerland. The lecture was beautifully illustrated with views thrown on a screen from an exy hydrogen lantern, manipulated by Mr. Knott. of Liver- pod. The custoinary vates of thanks concluded the proceedings. CHEMICAL LABOURERS QtrAIIIIIEL SILT WIDNES.—At the Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday-. Michael Glynn was summoned for assaulting 3Daniel Dunn. From the evi- dence, it appeared that the men are employed as cloaca- carlabourers, and that fdrsome months a feud had ex- isted between them. On Monday the two were in Cross's public-house, and the defendant commenced a cpmrrel. The landlord interfered, and Dunn left the house, but he had not walked far along the street when the defendant overtook him, struck him several times on thelace, and knocked him down. Mr. Knowles, for the defence, submitted that the assault was a trivial one, an'd suggested that the complainant had been " drown- ing-the shamrock," and on the Monday was onlylust getting over his Si: Patriek's Day ,celebration.—The Benchimposed a fine of 'los. and costs upon the .do- ferallant. ALLEGED VIOLENT ROBBBRY AT W IDEES. James Daniels, a young man, whose home is in Brynn-street,, was again brought before the Widnes Ranch on Monday charged with stealing with .vtolenca from the person of Mary Maguire tsvo shawls worth 15s. Mr. J. W. Knovvles defended. It appeared that about half-Fast eleven on Saturday night, the 10th inst., Maguire was pasamg along Lugsclale-road near the crossing, when the met-the prisoner' who placedhis arm round her neck and kissed her. lie then dragged her into the middle of doe, road, but a woman named Annie Ryan, of Warrington- road, coming up, he ran away, taking from Maguire's', shourkiers two shawls She was,wearing. (An Sunday P.C. Thompson apprehended the prisoner at his home, and he was 'identified by Maguire as the person who had assaulted her. —The prisoner, who reserved his defence. was commiteed for triaL

I A RIANGEROUS WOMAN .1.2' WIINTES.—At Widnes Police Court cri Monday, Catherine Lynch, of Margaret-street, was brought up on remand charged with hawing caused grievous bodily harm to Rose Xelly, who:also lives in Margaret-street. The evidence was repeated, and showed that on the 10th inst. Kelly., hearing the prisoner creating a 'disturbance hi the street, went from her house tofinquire the cause, The prk'soner at 4RCe seized her by the hair and at violent struggle took place between the women. 'ln the course Of the affray the prisoner bit Kelly's fore-finger severely.—Dr.,O'Keeffe informed the : Bench thatthere were five wounds upon the indet finger ' of Kelly's 'left hand, and thebe had evidently beet.,caused by a bite. 'When he first saw her she was in great pain, and-he dressed and cauterised the wounds. Thee, was still some fear of blood poisoning, and it would lab some time before the hand was well.--:-The prisoner was com- mitted to take her trial at the County Qoarter Sabrions. RUNCORN ROME. Or Cotrausstossits.--,-.A. special naset- ing was held on Thursday ,for the purpose 'of pasaing accounts to close the financial year. Mr. James Ralason presided, and there were present Messrs. W. Fisher, S.. I Taylor, P. Smith, E. Imison, W. Hankin.son, F. Wiswatl., P. Speakman; and E. Marshall (seeretrarv).--The Finance Committee recommended that cheques be drawn on the treasurer for the aggregate amount of £291 Ds. 7d., and that the irrecoverable arrears of the general district rate for the year ended 25th March,-amounting -£137 17s. 12d., be written off. It was also recommended that the sum of £4l ss. 7d. be paid to Mr. W. H. Linaker, being the balance of his costs in the matter of the liiverpool Waterworks and Improventent Bill. It was fultker re- commended that Mr. .1. Littler's assessment for house situated in Waterloo-road be reduced from £lB 6s. Bd, to £l3 13s. 4d. These minutes were adopted on the mo- tion of Mr Fisher, seconded by Mt Taylor. and the meet- ing coueluded.

WIDNES ai/lINTY COURT.—The monthly sitting of this court was held yesterday, before his Honour Judge T. P. E. Thompson. The list comprised 120 original plaints, 7 adjourned plaints, and 70 judgment sum- monses.

NELSON-STREET BAPTIST CHAPEL, WIDNEH.—III connec- tion with thts body a band of hope entertainment was given in the chapel on Thursday evening. Mr. J. Robinson presided. A miscellaneous programme of songs, recitations, and dialogues was gone through by the children, who did their part of the work in a very creditable manner. A collection was made at the close. . _

INDEPENDENT ORDER OF RECHABITES.—In connection with the Frodshant Tent of the above Order, a miscel- laneous entertainment was held in the Town Hall on Wednesday evening. Mr. William D Ringrose occupied the chair. The programme consisted of songs,. solos, recitations, and the dialogues—"The Misfortunes of Mr. Wiseacre, or All Fool's Day," and "Mrs. Maggs is caught." The proceeds were in aid of the beneficent fund of the tent. _ _

Reticoas Smoot, BoAnn.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, the following persons were summoned by Runcorn School Board for not sending their children regularly to school :—Abraham Hampson, Jackson's- lane; Thomas Lucas, Bridgwater-street; Thos. Hough- ton, Gilbert-street; John Pickering, King-street; Fanny Gandy, .Bridgewa.ter-street ; Wm. Price, Cooper-street.; Wm—Newsome, Shaw-street; Thomas Wagstaffet boat- man; Mary Burke. Brunswick-street (two cases) ;,Richd. Fish, Cooper-street. WESLEYAN QUARTERLY MEETING AT RUNCORN. The quarterly meeting in connection with Runcorn Wesleyan Circuit was held in the vestry of Brunswick Schoolroom, on Monday evening. The Rev. G. Wood, the superin- tendent minister, presided. Mr. J. R. Frith, the senior circuit steward, reported that the financial position of the clrcuit was very satisfactory, and that there was a slight increase in the number of members. The 4pchool schedules were presented by the Rev. A. P. Watson. An ' invitation was given to the Rev. R. F. Hornabrook, of Halton, to remain a third year. A FAMILY STARVED AT WIDNES.—Joseph Stanley, a labourer, was brought before the Widnes magistrates. to answer a charge of deserting his wife and four children. Mr. Treacy, the relieving officer, said that on the 10th in the prisoner's wife brought her four children to him and stated that her husband had left her, and she was destitute. • Thg whole family presented a starved ap- pearance, and he at once administerel relief and ordereil them to the Workhouse. The cost of their maintenance had been 255. The prisoner did not bear a good charac- ter. and he was sentenced to a month's hard labour.

. Sr. PATRICK'S DAY AT WIDNES.—The anniversary of the death of Ireland's patron saint was celebrated in the customary fashion at Widnes on Saturday. The Catholic , League of the Cross and the members of the local branch of the Irish National League held a united demonstra- tion, and paraded through the principal thoroughfares of the town. The brass bands of the respective orders took part. The Irish population of Widnes is very numerous, and there were few instances in which there was not dis- played amongst the personal adornments of both sterner and gentler sex a piece of green ribbon or a sprig of the "dear little 41afiirock. AN OLD HAND AT RUNCORN.—At Runcorn Police Court, on Tuesday. Thomas Brown, young man, was charged with stealing nine pairs of braces belonging to Mr William Craddock, pawnbroker, Church-street, on the previous day. The braces were suspended from a, nail at the shop door, and a woman saw the prisoner take them off and walk away. She informed Mr. Crad- dock as to his loss, and he went in pursuit and captured the prisoner with the braces Jn his possession. As the , prisoner was suSpected of being an old hand," he was , remanded for a weck so that inquiries could be made as 1, to his antecedents, RATEPAYERS' MEETING AT HALTON.--TllO annual meet- ing of the ratepayers of Halton was held at the Castle Hotel on Thursday evening. The Rev. J. Lockwood presided, and there was a good attendance. Messrs. William Stokes and William Nixon were appointed bur- 'leymen, and Mr: J. W. Haddock was re-appointed way- warden. Mr. J. S. Jeacock read the report of the Burial Board, which was adopted, and Messrs. W. Bradbury and S. Saunders were appointed to audit the accounts of that body. Messrs. J. 'Barrow and J. Looker retired from the hoard, but being eligible for re-election, they were appointed for a rariner term of three years. Mr. G. Leathwood was also appointed a member in place of Mr. R. Hughes, who had removed into Runcorn. The Chairman said his connection with 'the cemetery had brought upon himself much calumny and unpleasant- ness, but the cemetery had been a boon to the poor, and was a financial success. It was decided to submit to. the magistrates the following list of geutlemen qualified to serve as overseers :—Thos. Wright, H. Rowe. Samuel Barrow, S. Astbury-, and J. Rutter. THE WEST LANCASHIRE CUP TIE .—The final will take place to-day on the ground of Warrington club, the con- tending teams hailing from Widnes and Tyldesley. It was originally decided that the match should be played on the St. Helens ground, but it was discovered thatihis would not be available and the committee of the Union fixed upon the capital facilities that Warrington could offer. Remembering the scene that was enadtcd when Widnes entered that arena, in a cup tie competition, the Widnes committee hastily met and decided to protest against such an arrangement for the reason that it was detrimental to the success of the Wid- nes team. The players also expressed them- selves against visiting Warrington. The ' West Lancashire Committee held a hastily summoned meeting to consider the matter, and ultimately decided that the match must be played at Warrington. On Thursday , evening a Meeting of the Widnes Committee and players was held, and a resolution was adopted to play the match, notwithstanding the strong protests of several players. Should the Widnes team turn up in' their en- tirety they will render a good account of themselves, but it is possible that the committee will have several vacancies to fit. .

WIDNES FREE LIBRARY Commtpree. The monthly meeting WAS held at the Town Hall, yesterday, under the presidency of Mr. H. Wade Deacon. There were also present Messrs. S. Sadler, T. Sadler, J. Morrison, and S: Robinson, with J. T. Allen (clerk), and Miss Proctor (librarian). The librarian reported that the books har- rowed from the lending department and consulted in the reference department during the month of February numbered .5,381, being a decrease on the previous month of 130 in the lending department, and 17 in the reference department. The library had, however, been open a day lass than in January. The daily average was 214. The caSh'received for finest, dm during the month amoun- ted to £3 lie. 4d. Mr. Allen produced an esti- timate of the expenditure for the year ended March 25th, 1889. The expenditure last year was £520 ' '53 I.B,•and he estimated that next year the expenditure wotild lie £430 9s 7d. After paying salaries, and other expenses, purchasing magazines and newspapers, there would be a sum of about £lOO availalA for obtaining , books. It was unanimously resolved to increase the ; silary of the assistant libratisn, Miss Walker; from lOs pervaeek to 15s per week. The Chairman said Miss Water had been with the committee since the com- mencement, and she had carried out her duties very satisfactorily. Her hours were very long. Mr. T. Sad- ler said the salary was toe-little for the hours she had to weft. Rualcome v. Livearoon—The return match between these clubs took place at Runcorn, on Wednesday even- ing, before several thousand specters. Both teams were strong, and a fast and exciting game was played, drib- bling and passing being the order of the day. Ranoorn., however, held the upper hand throughout, the splendid, trailing of the local forward division defeating the tac- tics of the visitors. After 'a few minutes play Liverpool bad to concede a minor, and shortly afterwards Wain- wright, by a capital sprint, planted the ball over the line, and Brazenthle kieked a fine goal. At half-time the game was one goal to mil. In the second half Liver- pod on only one occasion invaded Runcorn's quarters, but strive as they would Hugh Hughes and men could net force more than miner points. lioth Wainwright -anti Broady took part in mauls over the line, but ineach instance the referee decided in favour of Liverpool The final result was Runeegn one goal, 7 minors, to one minor. Of the winners, the captain, Woods, IV Hughes.. anti P. Riley played a capital game, and for the losers , Barry at back was in magnificent form, and of the re- mainder Fernie at three-quarters did some good work.. The teams were as follows :—Runcorn: Woods, back; , Ernsendale,•W Riley, and Cawley, three-quarter backs:; H Hughes and Whitby, haff backs; Broady, W Hughes, 'Faulkner, P Riley, F Hancock, Dolan. Stubt.w, Wain- , wfight, and Ga3rter, forwards. - Goo D TEMPLARS' BI.SLAR R.T WIDNES.— Matins Tem- perance Hall, the home of the Good Templars of Wid- nes,'hs resting upon it a Mat contracted for furnishing the building with the necessary furniture, and the man- agers RTC in need of funds to-renovate and beautify the structure. With the object of wiping off the debt and obtaining the wherewithal to-necomplish the second re- quirement, a sale of work was opened on Thursday afternoon. The arrangements 'for the effort had been conceived and carried out bra committee of lady Good Templars consisting of the following sist6s : Mesdames W. iteaYi J. Reay, Harrison, T. Hughes, Corns, .7: Thompson, Wairclough, Hughcsoind W. Hill, and Misses E. Leggett, Shepherd, and Hill. These ladies also acted as Stailholders, together *kir Airs Taylor, and they had numerous articles of value to bring under the notice of the visitors. Mrs Brock, who was present with her hus- band, Mr. John Brock, J.P., gracefully performed the opening ceremony, and in a brief address she remarked that the temperasee cause was one that enlisted our kindest and warmest gympathies when w‘e realised the misery that was brought to our hearths and homes by drink. Mr. Brock, she said, joined with her in the wish for the success of the workers in the -muse now and at all times. (Applause.)—Brother J. B. Collins, D.C.T, of Liverpool, also made a speech appropriate to the oc- casion, Sister Green, of Liverpool, who has attained high honours in good templary, proposed a vote of thanks to Mrs Brock for her presence and support, and in doing so spoke 4f the good work accomplished by Good 'Am- plans, add the necessity and importance of ladies be- longing to the order and taking an active part in its operations,—The motion was carried by acclamation.

FATAL ACCIDENT ON THE RlVER.—Whilst the Rat Annie Jane was proceeding up the river towards Runcorn, she fouled the Albert Pierhead, and a man fell into the water. A man who was on the pierhead witnessed the accident, and jumped into the river to rescue the sailor, but was unable to do so. The body has not yet been re- covered. • _ _ _ _ _ _ _

CLEILICAL.—Dr. J. Bernard Sanders. 0.5.8., late icn the staff of St. Alban's, Bewsey-street, Warring- ton, has succeeded Father Francis P. Hickey, O.S B, in charge of St. Benedict's, Hindlev. Sr. HELENS AND WIGAN JUNCTION RAILWAY.— The construction of the New St. Helen's and Wigan Junction Railway was commenced on Wednesday. There was a gathering of directors and others inter- ested to celebrate the event The new line is 18 miles long, and will cost £30,000 per mile, running through a district from which 400,000,000 tons of coal are available for output, at the rate at present of 1,500,000 tons per annum. NEW SHERIFF FOR CHESTIIRE.—Baron William Henry von Schroder, of the Rookery, Nantwicb, was on Saturday appointed Sheriff of Cheshire by her aj esty in Council —On Thursday, Baron Schroder attended at the Police Court, Crewe, and took the oath of.allegiance and made•the usual declarations before Dr. Atkinson, preparatory to be sworn in. Mr. C. E. Speakman, of Crewe, was sworn in under sheriff. Mr. John Tatlock, ol Chester, will continue to bold the office of acting under sheriff.

By command, of the Queen a leye4 was held on Wednesday afternoon at St. James's Palac-, by hiS Royal Highness the Prince of Wales, at whicll the following presentations were made :--Lietitedant R. H. Codrlington, 3rd Batt. Cheshire Regiment, by C ,lonel France-Hay- hurst ; Lieutenant Edward K. Williamson, 3rd Batt. Cheshire Regiment; by Colonel France-Hayhurst; and Major C. E.
