REMARKABLE EGGS.—A few days ago a hen owned by Mr. James Barker, of Legh-street, Earlestown, laid an egg, of extraordinary dimensions. It mea- sured round the ends SI inches, round the centre 6f inches, and its weight was 4 ounces. Another hen, the property of Mr. Henry, Bent, farmer, Hall- lane farm, •Burtonwood, has recently displayed a remarkably prolific nature. Its "laying powers" on successive days have been as follows :—On Saturday list, 2 eggs; 'on Sunday, 3; on Monday, 3; and on Tuesday, 2. This "feat" is considered as something like a ".record" in the neighbourhood. How Tl:q GERMAN EMPEROR SPEAKS.—A London correspondent says :—lnformation derived from one of the German Court doctors enables me to describe the apparatus in the Emperor's throat: Over the opening of the silver tube in the larynx is a sort of I respirator, which is covered by cotton wool, and this again .by silk, over which the uniform is buttoned. Ilene() the air is almost, but not entirely, excluded. In order to speak his Imperial Majesty must com- press the wool with his hand, and then he suffers from the effort. In speaking. however, he is per- fectly intelligible to his familiars, and especially to the Empress, owing to his facility in expressing words by the mere movement of the lips. When this fails, he rapidly conveys his meaning by writ- ing, carrying tablets for tho purpose. THE LATE EMPEROR or GER.ll.lNr.—The " Wes- tern Daily Press " says that. the Rev. Thomas San- derson, formerly of Warrington, preaching at the Wesleyan Chapel, Old King-street, Bristol, on Sun- day morning, referred to the fact that one of the most distinguished figures had gone from the stage of European politics within, the last few days, and while there was much that *as good in the private character of the late Emperor, he, for one, could not speak in unqualified terms of his public career. His great achievement was the unification of the Ger- man Empire, and in that he was successful. At the same thud:. they could not forget the warlike methods by which that object was accomplished, nor yet the enormous sacrifice of lite which it en- tailed. The policy of the late Emperor was one of blood. He was one of the most powerful tsxponen:a I of the war spirit of this generation, and that spirit had little in common with the spirit of the New Testament. He expressed his sympathy —which he knew was shared by the congregation—with the present Emperor and his wife. THE "SUNLIGHT" SOAP WORKS. A number of influential residents in the neighbourhood of the new works about to be erected on the mare-in of the Bromborough Pool, by Messrs. Lever Brothers, the well-known makers of "Sunlight" soap, hay- aitg expressed some fears that, in the process of manufacture offensive odours might be given off, which wouhl materially deteriorate the value of the surrounding property for residential parpohes, it was suggested that a deputation from the Lower Bebington Local Board should visit the present works of Messrs. Lever Brothers, at Warrington, I with a, view to ascertain to what extent these fears were justified. The Messrs. Lever having been communicated with on the subject, seat a cordial invitation to the members of the board to visit and inspect their Warrington works. Accordingly a de- putation. consiging of Messrs. Wilson (chairman), Morris, Edge, M'Dowell, and Smith, with Mr. Willis Harper (law clerk), and Mr. Hopkinson (surveyor), proceeded to Warrington on Tuesday. They were met at the station by Mr. Owen (architect to Messrs. Lever), who accompanied them to the works. They were there received by Messrs. Lever Brothers, who conducted them over the establish- ment, and explained to them the various processes connected with soap manufacture. The result of their visit was that the deputation came away fully satigfied that there was nothing offensive in the processes carried on, and they assured Messrs. Lever that they would gladly welcome their "Sun- light" industry to Bebington, believing that the undertaking was one which would- confer a great benefit on the district.

UNITED METHODIST B4AAR AT WIDNES. A loataar in connection with Zion Chapel, Oak- land-street, Widnes, was held in the schoolroom on , Wednesday and Thursday. The Object it was de- sired to attain wax to reduce the debt which at preeentoxists upon the new Sunday school, which was recently erected and . opened; and the ladies of the congregation and the elder scholars had fo r • some months past been busily occupied once each week preparing goods for sale. The result was to be 'seen in the numerous useful and nrnamental articles with which the valiollS stalls were taste- fully set out. The schoolroom had been gaily de- corated for the occasion- The opening , ceremony was performed by Dr- P. Stuart, of Liverpool, on Wednesday afternoon, when there was a capital audience. Amongst those present were the Revs. E. Hall (the pastor), E. G. Hughes (congregational), IL Yeatman (Baptist), and D. Davies (Welsh Con- gregational). and Messrs. John Betney, sen., J. Whitehead, James Birkenhead, T. Perrin, H. Ather- ton, and James Waters, Mrs Stuart accompanied her husband. After the customary devotions had been performed, Mr. Hall said one of the most persistent cries that had been heard in this country for many years had been for increasing the facilities for 'giving our English children a good sound education. Ignor- ance had been seen to be inimical to the happiness and to success in every department of life. On the continent rapid strides had been made in that di- rection, and our legislature had been compelled by the example of surrounding nations to make better provision of that sort. In consequence of that pro- vision general, technical, and classical education would more than ever devolve upon day schools and col- , ' leges, but that could nerer shift from the shoulders of: parents and others the responsibility of giving children I a sound moral education. Sunday %schools were never intended to be a substitute for home effort, but as • an auxiliary to home training. When the parents had done their part it was well that the scholars should be gathered together and taught the truths that were to be found in the Sacred Sculptures, and he was sure that those who had thought of the influence and benefit of Sunday schools would thank God for those institutions. It was about 14 years ince the adjoining sanctuary was erected at a cost of about £5OO, and the whole of that debt had been wiped off. That sanctuary for many years fulfilled the double I .v.urpose of chapel and school, but the progress of the school was such (there were now 250 scholars on the rugs) that a school-room wis imperatively required, and the building in which they were now assembled was built and fitted up at a cost of £520. By various means about £220 had been raised and they were now burdened with a debt of £3OO, which they should be glad to see liquidated. (Applause.) He then introduced Dr. Stuart, who, in the course of a genial and chatty speech, expressed pleasure at beim.-b present, and, refer- ring to education, he said that not only in Widnes but in the greater towns of the United Kingdom, the best posi- tions were held by the Germans. He had nothing against the Germans as a people, but he did not see why it was necessary that they should take the best positions fram the English. The reason why they did so was that their education was more practical and more thorough, and also because, as Mr. G'oschen said, the English did not take such an interest in their work or in their masters as the Germans do. The German got accustomed to his work, and was not like our people,when the clock struck six was anxious to be off, but he was willing to stay and ' even to take his woilc home, bring it before his master on the morrow completed. He contended that English- men could not stand before the Germans under our present system. 41 conclusiop, he advised the

young men of that school to have a lofty aim, and to strive steadfastly to accomplish it. There was no reason why they should not attain the highest positions in the land. (Applause.) He then declared the bazaar open. - On the motion of the Rev. R. G. Hughes, seconded by Mr. Whitehead, Dr. and Mrs. Stuart were cordially thanked for their presence and support. Business then commenced, and the following were the fair saleswomen :—Mrs. Lock, Mrs. G. Turton, Mrs.Wll- cock, Miss Betne37, Miss Glendenning, Miss Forrest, the Misses Harrison, and Miss Whitehead The refreshment stall was in charge of Mesdames Whitehead, Hall, Houghton, Wilcock, Perrin, Scrivens, and Ogden, and the young men's stall was in care of Messrs. W. White- head, A. Smith, and W. Wilcock. On this stall was the Lord's Prayer, skilfully executed in fretwork by Mr. Halewood. There was also on view a fine model of a horizontal steam engine, made by Mr. W. Ogden, and for the delectation ef the visitors there was an amusing optical delusion on view. Mr. John Betney, junr., and Mr. J. Waters were the showmen. In the evening an,en- joyable concert was also given in the' chapel. Songs were rendered by Mrs. Lock, Miss Betney, Messrs. John Betney. and Evans. The chapel choir gave selections from" The valley of violets." • Including a donation of £l5 from Dr. Stuart, the sum of £BO was realised. On Thursday, the bazaar was opened by Mr. James Hargreaves, of Widnes, and he was supported by the Rev. G. Hargreaves, of Cardiff, and the Rev. E. Hall, the pastor. There was again a good attendance. Mr. Hargreaves, in declaring the bazaar open, said it was the duty of everyone who resided within the neigh- bourhood, and Alio had, thought of the advantages that were afforded by' schoels and chapels, to do a good share towards supporting that school in its work. They all very well knew that the people had to choose whether they would have Sunday school teachers or policemen; whether they would have schools and chapels or gaols and penitentories. If it was nothing in the world else but a pure question of profit and loss, schools and chapels were by far the cheapest institutions. (Applause.) Those persons who had come forward and done their best to help that cause of the Free Church were certainly deserving of recognition, and of the assistance and sym- pathy of every one of their neighbours. (Applause.) On the motion of Mr. Hall, seconded by Mr. Perrin, a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Har- greaves. The Rev. George Hargreaves also delivered an appro- priate address, in which he gave some interesting renuni- sences of his brother's early life. Mr. Hargreaves gave a donation of £5, and when the sale was concluded on Thursday evening the total sum of/ £Bl had been realised.

WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD. The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall on Tuesday. Mr. T. S. Timmis, J.P. presided, and there were present the very Rev. Dean Finegan, the Rev. J. Clarke, Dr. O'Keeffe, Messrs. Davies, Deacon, Imison, Reyes, Wareing And Danby (cleik).

'TEE OFFICE STAFF. _ The report of the General Purposes Committee is re- - ceived and adopted. Mr. Deacon explained that at the last meeting of the Board the question of increasing the staff in the office was raised, and the Finance Committee withdiew their motion, and had made a report to the General Purposes Committee that the salary of the junior clerk be increased from £5O to £65 a year, and that he be responsible for the . extra work entailed in the altera- tion of the duties of the Attendance Officers. The Com- mittee approved of that report, and proposed its adop- tion.—The Chairman explained that the recommenda- tion to carry out this suggestion would be made at the next meeting.

div.head: "TOUCH AND GO."
div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."
"Come, gentle Spring, etherial mildness, come ;" but not such mildness as we have had—it was killing. "Gentle Spring" came in on Tuesday with a bound—ice-bound, east wind, and in- fluenza.
A Milwaukee man made a bet that he could drink five glasses of whisky in five seconds. He won; but he was a dead man in two hours. He made a wager against time which carried him into eternity.

" Truth " says :—" I am glad to hear that the collars of the various Orders, which until now were in gold, are henceforward to be merely gilt. Sic transit. Let us hope, however, that this is only the beginning of the end, and that before long gilt collars will be relegated to the necks of poodles."

Three St. Helens men broke into a public-house at St. Helens late on Tuesday night. They were captured by the police, who found that they had secured a considerable amount of money, and a great deal of liquor. Although in the cellar, the burglars were pretty well "elevated." It is almost a pity they were disturbed; when bad men "go for" the bad drink' there is a chance of the men and the liquor consuming each other.

Please note, clergymen, deacons, political agents, publicans, and other sinners, that raffling at bazaars is illegal. On Wednesday, the secretary to the Accrington Liberal Club and the Liberal agent were summoned before the magistrates, and mulcted in costs, for permitting raffling at the recent Liberal bazaar. And serve them right; but they would be able to pay the costs—they realised nearly £5,000 at that bazaar.

The House of Lords doesn't want to be re- formed, and so Lord Rosebery has been politely bowed out. The only bishop who voted in the division on his motion for the reform was the Bishop of Chester, and he was in the majority against the proposal. Of course, and he repre- sented his clerical brethren. They know well enough that, with the first step in the path of reform, the bishops would get marching orders.

Mr. John Morley has consented to address a, political meeting at Blackburn on the 18th of April, when he comes to open tho Liberal bazaar at Darwen. Mr. Morley will have Ins foot on his native heath when he reaches Black- burn. He is a Blackburn man; and fought his first political battle in his native town in 1869. He was beaten then, but since 1869 many things have happened, and he will, next month, be a prophet honoured in lüown country,

Mr. (jhamberlain is to have the freedom of the borough of Birmingham conferred upon him, and is to be honoured with a dinner at the Devonshire Club, because of his work in connection with the Fisheries Treaty. "something too much of this." Why should there be all this fuss because a pleni- potentiary has simply done his duty P. It is a credit to the member for West Birmingham that he has refused the K.C.8., or whatever else was offered. He is not to be limed in that way.

The Liberal Unionists of Birmingham have been trying to take a rise out of Gladstonian Liberals in the matter of elections to the Four Hundred. But they have been defeated, for there are three Liberals appointed to one Liberal Unionist. Even in Mr. Chamberlain's constituency, the Gladsto- nians are found to be in the ascendant. It is not pleasant to see Liberals struggling with each other. Perhaps "it needs must be that offences come, but woe to that man by whom the offence cometh."

It is discreditable to the Germans to display, as they do, their prejudice against Sir .Morell Mac- kenzie. If report speaks truly, it is the German doctor whiz; has been at fault in the operation on the Royal patient's throat. It has been Sir Morella business to repair the bungling. Race prejudice is to be found everywhere; but the English may say this for themselves that, if a German specialist had been called in to an English Prince, there would not have been so much bad feeling in the matter on the part of the public:

The bruisers are just now having a gay time of it; Mitchell and Kilrain were received by the fraternity in Liverpool, on Monday, as conquering heroes. Brutality was encircled with a large crowd, if not with a halo. But why not go the whole hog, and do honour to such a master in the noble art as that of the thorough-paced bully who blacks his wife's eyes before she can say jack Robinson. Cheering men who fight for prize Ais but so-so; honour to whom honour is due—to the brute who fights, prize or no prize, and who always has his hand in.

There is the cock-fighter, too, should he' not be welcomed with a band of music, instead of being hunted by the police., as was the case at Abbey Hey on Saturday? It is sport-4' goad 'sport, you know" to set the game birds at each other— quite as .citing anti quite as cruel as chasing a fox or a hare with a pack of ladies and :gentle- men—and dogs. With a little more cultivation, we might get back to boar-baiting, and 'attain, who can sap? to bull-fighting? Well, well, wait till we have a King who can give his heart ~t,o this sort of Cling.

An excellent meting was held in Runcorn, on Monday evening, in favour of the Sunday closing of public houses. It was remarked that a large number of publicans were themselves in f.avour of the movement, as theybelieved it would be an ad- vantage to the trade and to the community. The principle, as the chairman remarked, has already become the law of the land in seine parts of the country; and, it is interesting to note .that pro- vision .is made:in the new Local Government Bill for County Councils having power to introduce Sunday Closing -whenever and w.bereventhey deem it desirable.

Dr. 'O'Keeffeoshowed himself considerate of the poor, .at the meeting of the Widnes School Board, on Tuesday, in .calling- attention to the fines for non-attendance of children at school. The hard- ships of parents are so great, in providing school fees when money is wanted for food, that we are not surprised to hear that the Wigan magistrates refuse to inflict a fine when they think the parents tire too poor to pay the school fees. The true remedy for this miserable and harassing state of thin wis Free Education. The State :pays t- ia- thirds Aff the cost. Why all thist,rouble about the other third'?

The other dara Warrington ." gentleman" re- ceived, by mistake, a letter acknowledging a sub- scription to a liberal Association. He noted the error in the address ; and noted, further, the contents of the communication. Like a _gentle- man, he forwarded the letter to the right quar- ter; but, unlike a gentleman, he not only ex- pressed no regret for having, in error, opened a letter which was not intended for, him; but proceeded to sneer at a subscription being given to the " separatist party." The "gentleman " in question is indebted to the Conservatire party for his "J.P."; but he is not indebted to any party for his impudence; that is entirely his .own.

A Ladies' Ambulance Class has been formed, .at Earlestown and has been remarkably -kuccessf At the distribution of certificates, on Monday evening, it transpired that out of the no ladies who joined the class,as many a 5.25 had presented them- selves for examination, and that 24 had succeeded in passing. Such a result is alike highly creditable to the students, and to Dr. Valentine their in- structo,r. It is needless to say that the information secured will make the ladies more useful members of society; they will be better wives and better mothers through knowing something of the laws of health and how to render first aid to the in- jured. The example set is well worth following.

Two or thr.3e, of the Welsh members have 'pre- pared a bill with the object of protecting the rights of the public in the matter of access to the mountains, rivers, lakes, moors and waste lands in the Principality, But if the bill is lyorth passing,

div.head: DISTRICT EDUCATION.
div.p: DISTRICT EDUCATION.

The District Education Committee reported that dur- ing February there were 87 applications for payment of fees, which were recommended to be paid in 83 cases. 179 persons appeared before the Commitbee for contra- vention of the Education Act, and fifty-two were con- victed by the magistrates. One boy was sent to an In- dustrial School.

div.head: AN ALLEGVD ILLIIDSIIIP.
div.p: AN ALLEGVD ILLIIDSIIIP.

Dr. O'Keeffe complained of the hardship inflicted upon parents who were summoned before the magistrates for two children, and had tck pa 3t a fine in respect of each.— Mr. Deacon replied that these cases were not undertaken without great consideration by the committee.—The Chairman said he had often been upon the Bench, and the magistrates never fined the parents unless there was good reason. In 80 or 90 per cent of these cases, how- ever, there was no appearance put in at all, and after hearing the evidence of the attendance officers the magi- strates had no option but to convict.—Dr. O'Keeffe said the father could not leave his work and attend court. The Wigan magistrates had refused to inflict fines where the parents were too poor to pay them.—The Chairman said the Widnes magistrates never inflicted a fine if any reasonable excuse was (ATered. The law was very clear, andthey simply carried the law out.—Mr. Deacon said it was no pleasure to the committee to send people to be fined, but Dr. O'Keeffe would see from the average attendance that there was a necessity to take action. The committee spent a considerable time every Thursday afternoon inciting parents, and when they got beyond mere words there was nothing for the committee to do but prosecute.—The Chairman: I believe the committee discharge their duty with great mercy.—Father Clarke said the committee and the magistrates simply did their duty,

div.head: MR. DAVIES.
div.p: MR. DAVIES.

The District Education Committee recommended that the resignation of Attendance Officer Davies should be accepted, and that Richard Grant be appointed atten- dance officer at a salary of £65 per annum, with uniform, rising according to the scale of the Board.—Mr. Deacon explained that Mr. Davies had been compelled to take this step owing to ill-health, and the committee had great sympathy for him in his trouble.—The Chairman said Mr. Davies had been a worthy servant of the Board eleven years; he was a very painstaking officer.—The Clerk read a letter from Mr. Davies asking for a retiring allowance.—After some conversation, the Clerk was in- structed to inform Mr. Davies that the Board regretted that they had no power to comply with his request,. and to express sympathy with him in his trouble.

div.head: 1-I.IPOR- TANT SUBJECT.
div.p: 1-I.IPOR- TANT SUBJECT.

The District Education Committoe recommended the substitution of the followit4 byelaws for those at present in force with regard to the standard of exemp- tion :—A child between ten and thirteen years of age shall not be required to attend school if such child has. received a certificate from one of Her Majesty's Inspec- tors of Schools that it has reached the Sixth Standard in the case of boys, and Fifth Standard in the case of girls, prescribed by tho Code of 1876.—A child between ten and thirteen Years of age shown to the satisfaction of the local authority to be beneficially and necessarily employed shall not be required to attend' , school for more thanfive attexdances is each 'week during. which the school is open, if such child has received a cer- tificate from one other Majesty's inspectors of schools that it has reached the fifth standard in the case of boys, and fourth standard in the case of girls, prescribed by the code of 1876.—Dean Finegan objected that the DiS- Itrict Education Committee had no rigid to deal with this subject, and the Chairman ruled, in his favour, but the discussion was allowed to proceed.—The Clerk read ex- tracts from the bye-laws showing that the standard of exemption in the neighbouring towns of Liverpool, St. Helens, Runcorn, Warrington; he, was lower than that proposed by the committee, whilst in Bradford, Leeds, Preston' Leicester, &c, the standard fixed was the same. In most cases the partial exemption was fixed at stan- dard three.—Mr. Deacon said the reason why partial exemption was so low was be,cause of half-timers. There were no half-timers in Widnes. He pointed out that there were a large number of boys in the fifth and upper standards at the age of eleven years, and would be leav- ing the school and would be rambling about the streets because they could not be legally employed.—The Chairman agreed that the standard fixed by the qpmmit- tee would be for the good of the children.—Dean Fine- gan contended that in many instances great hardship would be caused, and he suggested that a conference on the subject should take place between the District Edu- cation Committee and the Local Management Commit- tee.—This course was agreed to.

div.head: DRA-WING GRANT.
div.p: DRA-WING GRANT.

Dean Finegan moved the adoption of the following re- commendation of the Management Committee i—That 25 per cent of the drawing grant earned by the scholars and the whole of that earned by the pupil teachers in the senior boys departments for the year ending August 31st 1888, be paid to the teachers. Mr. Imison moved an amendment that 50 per cent be paid, and urgetl that the teachers were fairly entitled to half, as the teaching of drawing was not compulsory. Mr. Wareing seconded., The Clerk said the total amount of the grant for the three schools was about £l2O. Dean Finegan said the teachers had never ex- pressed a wish to have more than 25 per cent, and he did not see why they should press upon the teachers money they had never asked for. The committees recommenda- tion was passed by six votes to th ee.

SCHOOL ALTERATIONS. On the proposal of the Sites and Building Committee, the tender of Jones and Son, of Liverpool for the addi- tions and alterations required at the West Bank Board Schools, be accepted The Chairman stated three local men and three Liverpool men were invited to contract and the lowest tender had been accepted.
FINANCE.
The Finance Committee recommended for payment accounts amounting to £594 8s sd, and the sum of £294 Os id had been paid into the bank.

THE ITRE Al' SIMMS CROSS. ' Mr. Davies read a report of the Sites and Building Conunittee on the fire at Simms Cross Board School. The insurance company had paid £l5 the amoulit of the damage, and £2 2s for architects fees, and lOs for dam- age to the trowsers cif the caretaker.—The Chairman said the fire arose through a defect in the building. The workmen had se.amped a portion of their work which the Board's clerk of works ought to have been seen. The back of the fire grate had slipped down and the fire had been drawn under the floor and set fire to the joist. The defect had been remedied and there was no fear of a similar occurrence. It was quite optional on the part of the insurance company to pay the amount of the dam- age, but they had theated the roard very generously.— There was no other. business.

div.head: "A FRIEND OF MINE."
div.p: "A FRIEND OF MINE."

Travellers who have gone "far countries for to see," say that they find human _nature pretty much the same all the world over. They find wide variance in colour of skin, in physical contour, in mental characteristics, but in the essential elements that control social conduct, the human family is a brotherhood. The law, unwritten, found in no statute book, enforced by no cot:ft decrees, but having an influence circum- scribed only by the limits of earthly space, is the law of kindness. Among peoples where cruelty to human kind is almost a fixed habit, who are relentless foes, and as friends scarcely less to be dreaded, whose savage natures revel in fiendish atrocities, there yet lingers the spark of divinity which lifts man above the beasts. Sorrow melts the human heart wherever found, and sympathy mingles its tears with grief all the world over. Where pity does not dwell, there lives no thing of human kind. It is "the touch of nature that makes the whole world kin."

What a terrible world this would be to live in were it not for the sympathy and loving-kindness shown us when sorrow comes, for it is decreed that in all lives "some days must be dark and dreary." The thousands of voluntary testimonials which the proprietor's of Warner's SAFE Cure have received in re- gard to the efficacy of that remedy, reveal this "touch -of nature" in a peculiar manner. The great majority of them acknowledge that it was through some kind friend who, in pity for their sufferings, had make known to them the wonderful merits of this great remedy. The testimonial of Mr. William H. Pearce, of 45, St. Anne-street, Liverpool, is a fair sample. For months he was greatly troubled with terrible pains in the small of his back, and was constantly obliged to rest from his duties. He had no appetite, food being obnoxious to him, and his mouth in the morning tasted greasy, and his tongue was thickly coated. He consulted his medical man, who informed him that he was suffering from kidney disease. He made use of the doctor's prescrip- tions, but did not improve. "At last," he says, "a friend advised me to try narner's SAFE Cure, which I 'did, and continued taking it regularly, according to 43irections, for some three months, with the result &at to-day lam a perfectly cured man, and have none of the distressing symptoms from which I previously suf- fered." How many men there are to-day in the world, round- ing out lives of usefulness, making the word happier and better, who would have long since passed to the other shore, had it not been for the loving-kindness of friends shown in the practical way mentioned by Mr. • Pearce. div.head: FOOTBALL.
div.p: FOOTBALL.

Soeretaries of Football Clubs are requested to note that reports M matches played on Saturday must be sent to the head officio. Bois sey-street, Warrington, not later than ten o'clock on Wednesday morning

RUGBY RULES JOCKEY STAR V. WARRINGTON HORNETS JUNIORS.—This match was played on the ground of the former on Satur- day, and resulted in a victory for the Stars by 1 goal, 1 try, and 5 minors, to 2 tries. J. Gleave and M. Bran- non played best for the winners, the latter scoring both tries. S. Gleave kicked a grand goal from the place. J. Sankey and W. Makin scored tries for the Juniors. Neither team was fully represented. WARRINGTON V. MANCHESTER RANGERS "A " TEAMS. —The above teams met on the Wilderspool ground on Saturday, in fine weather. Owing to the semi-final for the West Lancashire Cup being played at Warrington, the • match was not commenced until 5-30, in consequence of which two 25's only had to be played. The visitors won the toss, and the home captain kicked off from the pavilion end, Graham returning to Bibby, who was held by McDougall. Vickers and Phelan took play to centre, where Antrobus passed to Bibby, who kicked well, but Ellison returned to Jolley, the latter player sending the ball into touch. A kick by Sanson transferred play to the Rangers' 25, and the home forwards breaking away with a dribble, J. Bate grounded the ball over the line. Isherwood took the place kick, but failed to augment the point. After the drop-out, passing between Antrobus, Whittle, and Appletdn was witnessed, the last-named player being pushed into touch hy Ellison. From the line-out, the home forwards worked the ball up the field, Ellison returning into touch, but Jolley, bouncing the ball into play, kicked to Galley, who made his mark, nothing being gained by the free kick. The grand passing of the home backs again forced play into the Rangers' 25, Bibby taking a drop at Goal, and Hill touch- ing down. McDougall dropped out, Jolley making a good return. A grand dribble by the Rangers' forwards now placed the Warrington line in danger, but after ex- kicks between Bibby, Graham and Jolley, play rested near centre. With the aid of a free kick, the visitors again forced the home team on the defensive, Sanson eventually relieving the pressure by an opportune kick, and, following up, regained possession and passed to Isherwood and Adamson, who dribbled to centre. On call of half-time the score stood :—Warrington 1 try and 1 minor, to Rangers nothing. On change of ends Urwin restarted for the Rangers, Jolley returning into touch. Ellison put in a dashing run, and looked likely to score, but he was stopped by Appleton; Bate running the ball back to centre. Scowby, McDougall, and Boucher got in a good dribble, but Jolley responded with a tremen- dous punt into touch. Davies now got possession and made a grand run, being pulled down near the line, the visitors saving by touching down. After the drop-out the Rangers' front rank took operations to the Warring- ton half, Bibby saving well. Whittle passed to Bibby, who made a short run and kick, and Sanson secured the ball and ran in behind the posts, Appleton failing at the place kick. On call of time the score stood—Warrington two tries and three minors, Manchester Rangers nothing. Teams :—Warrington: Full back, Jolley; three-quarter backs, Sanson, Appleton, and Bibby; half backs, Whittle (captain) and Antrobus; forwards, Molyneaux, Davies, Jones, Thornley, Adamson J. Bate, Isherwood, G. Beard, and Acton. Manchester Rangers : Full back, D. Hill; three-quarter backs, Ellison, Graham, and Phelan; half backs, Vickers and Parlane; forwards, Mc Dougall, Boucher, Frost, Urwin, Unsworth. Kinder, Scowby, Dehn, and Galley. WARRINGTON V. MANCHESTER RANGERS. The first-named club journeyed to Rusholme on Satur- day with an indifferent team, being without Barnes, Fair Turner, W. Dillon, and T. Davies. The Rangers had their full strength up, and a capitally-contested game was witnessed. The weather was lsrilliantly fine, but Cold. At 3-15 Herbert Haselham started operations, the ball going in touch at the' Warrington quarter-flag. After some play of a loose character, Jolley' was the first to break the monotony by a smart run and kick to the Rangers' line. A Hamlett retaliated, and Donaldson supplemented his efforts by a good run to half way. The home forwards now compelled Nevins to save. Frank Turner dropped out, Randles showing up with a smart dribble to the Rangers' quarters. Wilson spoiled his career, placing the oval in neutral ground. Jolley from a neat pass by Warren made tracks for the opposing line, but was checked close to the line by Wilson. The Rangers were forced to kick dead, and from Haselham's udrop-out Warren placed them again on the defensive. Hmart tactics by the Manchester team again forced Nevins to save. Frank Turner dropped out, landing the ball in Rangers' territory. Speakman essayed to get away, and a pass from the latter toEvans gained ground. Wilson relieved the pressure slightly, and from a pack at midfield Warren ran round only to find an obstacle in Parlane, Warren passed smartly to Jolley, who made off at top speed, being brought down on the line. The Rangers now showed up better, but Nevins by a huge punt again placed Warrington on the aggressive. Grand play by Massey, Evans, and Jolley almost ended in the latter getting in, and Povey and Ashton now threatened the Rangers' goal, but relief came about by a good. dribble by Mee and Harry Haselham. Massey, Evans, and Speakman indulged in some neat Passing, placing the game at the Rangers' quarter flag. Here A. Hamnett relieved, but Massey responded in brilliant style, trans- ferring operations from the Warrington line to that of the home team. The Warringtonians strove hard to ob-- taM a major point, and the much-coveted try was al- most notched after a grand run by Jolley. Success, how.- ever, attended their efforts, for, shortly after, Evans getting possession at half way gave Massey a chance, and the latter, seizing the favourable opportunity, drop- ped a splendid goal. This was a brilliant feat, and cer- tainly is his finest effort this season. Half time was . called, the score reading Warrington one goal and two zninors,to Manchesterßangerstwelminoni. Frank Turner re-started, the home team replying to half way. H. Haselham showed prominence with a good dribble, peak- man saving. Evans put in a neat run and pass to Jolley, the latter punting to half way. Sabin put in a sterling run, but the smart tacking of Massey prevented him becoming dangerous. The game now raged at the quarter-flag of the Rangers, and smart play, in which Frank Turner, played a prominent part, trans- ferred the game to the Rangers' 25. Donaldson ran the leather back, Nevins replying with interest. From a _pack here Haninett threatened theWarrington goal, but _Evans baulked the movement by intercepting the pass- ing of the Manchester backs. Nevins and Massey indi- viauany put in some neat work, but a fine effort of Wil- son nearly resulted in a score. FrOm a scrimmage near the arrington goal Parlane passed to Donaldson, but W Massey brought him to grass before he could gain a yard, and soon after Speakman brought relief to his side k the quarter-flag The play was of a give-and-take nature, by a neat kick to -each side ariving to add to the • score, and quick work in the Warrington 25 ended in A. Hammett equalising. Frank Turner recommenced hos- tilities, and smart dribbling by Povey and sure tackling by Littlewood almost ended in the visiting team being again _ again in the majority. However, Wilsonsav;ldarran ,endtao pack was formed on the line. A pass from Evans found the latter struggling to get over, but Mc- Dougall stopped him. A miss now let in the

home teant, who relieved the pressure, but all their efforts could not prevent the Warringtonians visitin,,c, their territory. The home team began to show signs of lack of stamina, whilst the Warringtonians ap- peared quite fresh. Nevins placed the game near the line, and again the home team had luck to get away, Henry Haselham nearly scoring, and a minor resulted from the latter's good play. Warren held A. Hamnett before he could,get away, and after a pretty exhibition between Massey, Evans, Warren, and Speakman, Jolley put in a good kick to the Rangers' line. Again the home team scored another minor through a long kick from half-way, and it was after this that the Warringtonians made their final effort. Warren struggled hard to score, and took the game tothe line, Wilson saying. Handles replied to the drop-out, and smart following up by Ash- ton and Donohue prevented a return. Littlewood got over from the succeeding pack, but he failed to gain the referee's verdict, and although Povey and Jolley each made determined efforts to cross the line it was without avail, and after seventy minutes of an interesting game both teams had scored exactly alike, namely—one goal and four minors.

...... The play all round was of a very even nature, both teams being equally matched. It must be taken into account that Warrington were shorthanded, whereas the home team had their full strength. Nevins played bril- liantly at full back, and of the three-quarters both Jolley an Massey played well. Jolley had extremely hard lines, as he got to within an ace of scoring frequently, and some of his runs were greatly admired. Evans, a recruit from the " A " team, played a cool game, tack- ling, running, and passing Ivith judgment which stamps him as a player of no mean order. Warren played a de- termined game, whilst Speakman was to the fore when required. In the front division Frank Turner, Povey, Littlewood, and Ashton claim attention. On behalf of the Rangers Wilson, A. Hamnett, Parlane, and Harry Haselham deserve mention. The following were the teams :—Warrington : Full back, Nevins; three- quarter backs, Massey, Evans, and Jolley; half-backs, Warren and Speakman; forwards, Ashton, Frank Tur- ner, Hayes, Povey, Littlewood, Handles, Donohue, Holmes, and ,E. Dillon. Manchester Rangers: Full back, Wilson: three-quarter backs, Sabin, A. Hamnett, and Donaldson; half-backs, Parlane and H. Hammitt ; forwards, Harry Haselham, Herbert Haselham, lace, Pollard, F. Hamnett, Barrow, Jonas, Cownian, and Mc- Dougall. Referee, Mr. Allen, Salford.

div.head: WEST LANCASHIRE CUP: SEMI-FINAL. WIGAN V. TYLDESLET.
div.p: WEST LANCASHIRE CUP: SEMI-FINAL. WIGAN V. TYLDESLET.

The penultimate between these teams was decided at the ground of the Warrington Club, Wilderspool-cause- way, on Saturday, and so great was the interest aroused by the event that special trains were run from the res- pective districts, so that at the best part of the after- noon the attendance could not have numbered much less than 10,000 persons. The proceedings were most orderly throughout, and nothing whatever occured to mar the pleasure of the game. Shortly after the adver- tised time the teams entered the field, the Wiganers being especially well received, while the "dark horse" (as Tyldesley had previously been termed) came in for a large amount of popular applause. Tyldesley kicked off, and for a lengthy time the play was of a fairly even character, the first point scored being a dead ball from a long kick by Tyldesley. At length a free kick fell to the latter, which was improved by a drop into touch. Soon afterwards, however, the Wiganers were on the ball, which during a subsequent melee, was rushed over the line to the boundary. Some capital punting by Shaw, the Tyldesley captain, now took the ball within the Wigan half, where scrimmages for a length of time were indulged in. On the final break up of the pack Shaw was slightly at fault, but quickly recovering, saved splendidly. Some fine passing by the three- quarters gave Wigan a decided advantage, from which, on lining out, Slevin had a splendid chance, which was marred by the knocking on of the ball. A moment later, however, Hatton ran in on the left for Wigan, amidst tumultuous cheering, but on Samuels being called up the attempt to "place," although a good one, resulted in failure. For a length of time succeeding the drop out, play was located within the Tyldesley half. For a moment the pressure was eased, and when half-time arrived the Wiganers were leading by a try to nil. Atkinson having reNstarted on behalf of Wigan. Slevin made an effort, but failedin his endeavourtoget through, following which a free kick fell to Tyldesley. Shaw made a dash right into the arms of the " Philistines " instead of Darting with the ball. At this time the Tyl- desley forwards were doing some grand work, the weak spot in the team being the right wing three-quarter. Again the Tyldesley forwards broke away in perfect unison and only Slevin's presence of mind and decision prevented an imminent try. Ramsden noSt made ample amends for previous shortcomings, Hampson also showing to advantage after the ball had oscillated back ,th mid-field. Twenty minutes had elapsed from the change of ends when Hampson, from a grand kick by the Tyldesley back, Woodward, crossed the Wigan line. A wild scene of exultation ensued, which, however, toned down materially when Shalk signally failed from the place. Following the drop-out extreme pressure was brought to bear upon the Wigan line, which Shaw eight minutes later again crossed, Woodward failing at goal. No sooner had the ball been re-started than by the aid of Sutcliffe Tyldesley again scored, but still the major point could not be secured. Soon afterwards Wigan touched down, and to all appearances the match was over. Berry made a grand left-foot drop at goal, the ball going barely half-a-yard outside the posts. Wigan rarely got over the half-way line, although later on, Samuels made a grand run on the right, only, however, to be precipated into touch at the Tyldesley quarter-flag. ,Again the ball was taken back to the centre. Slevin be- came conscious of the gravity of the situation, and made a strenuous effort to tgeak through on the left, but without avail, the quick and decisive action of the Tyl- desley men completely frustrating all attempts to reach their line. Le Peton made a last resolute dash, but clung to the ball too long, and a seeming chance was thrown away. Ever afterwards Tyldesley had the best of the play, and although the game was prolonged for nearly five minutes beyond the stipulated time (a slight delay of half a minute or so having occurred owing to a mishap to Le Peton) the issue was in favour of Tyldesley by three tries and a minor to one try and a minor point. Wigan had undoubtedly the best of the first period of the play, but from the moment Tyldesley scored, their opponents seemed to lose heart, and played with the con- sciousness of a beaten team. The teams were as follows —Wigan: Baldwin, back; Slevin (cantain), Hunter, and Samuels, three-quarter backs; Mitchenson and Le Peton, half-backs; Hall, Hatton, Swift, Dempsey, Car- rington, Halton, Wardle, Robinson, and Atkinson, for- wards. Tyldesley H. Pearson, back; 3. Fearnley, F. Shaw (captain), and W. H. Ramsden, three-quarter backs; J. Berry and C. Hardman, half-backs; G. Wood- ward, Smith, J. Hampson, T. Hilton, W. Sutcliffe, Ram- ble, W. Healey, P. Eckersley, and J. Hodgkinson, for- wards.

div.head: NOTES BY THE WAY.
div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY.

The only interesting Rugby mateh in St.. Helens, on Saturday, was the meeting of Widnes and Litherland in the semi-final tie of the West Lancashire and Border Towns Challenge Cup. There was a good attendance of spectators, the majority of whom were supporters of the Widnesians, and had accompanied their team in three special trains, which arrived from Widnes. During the first half the Litherland men worked hard and welt, and several times completely carried the scrimmages, but their backs were no match for their sturdier opponents. Towards the close the Widnes team showed their supe- riority, and their better staying powers compared with their opponents enabled them to severely press the lat- ter. The result was a win for Widnes by two goals, two tries, and six minors (28 points) to one minor (one point.) The weak spot in the Litherland team was the back divigion, but Quio-g played grandly all through. The winners were seen to good advantage, especiallyin the second portion of the game.

The attendance and excitement on the Wilderspool ground, on Saturday-reminded one of the time when Warrington were bidding, as events proved, success- fully, for the West Lancashire trophy. Both the compe- ting toams—Tyldesley and Wigan—were warmly sup- ported by crowds of admirers who had followed them from their respective localities, and it was hard to say whether the cheers were louder when Wigan scored or whea Tyldesley equalised. With regard to the play, Wigan as usual played hard in the first part of the game, but there seems to be a want of staying power in the team, at least there was on Saturday, and Tyldesley, a tough lot of fellows, carried the day somewhat easily. The strength of the winners lay in their forwards and half-backs—as fine a sample as could be desired—and their weakness at three-quarters and full back. On not a few occasions the ball was decidedly mulled by the Tyldesley backs, and it showed a want of smartness on the part of Wigan that they clid not take better advan- tage of these opportunities. In addition to the semi-final the. Warringtonians are to-day to be favoured with a view on their own ground of the final encounter for the trophy between Widnes and TyldeMey. This should turn out to be a capital contest. Without venturing too far on the slippery ground of prophecy, we should be inclined to say that unless Tyldesley backs smarten, up there is a consider- able presumption in favour of the cup finding its way to the chemical town. The forwards, it may be expected, will be pretty equal in strength and staying capacity, and it will probably depend on the backs as to who is to preserve the trophy for the next twelve months. MEETINGS OF THE WEST LANCASHIRE COMMITTEE. The committee met at the Goat Hotel, Livempuol, on Saturday everting, Mr. J. P. Mearns, vice-president, in the chair. There were also present representatives from St. Helens; Tyldesley, Wigan Rovers, Illundellsands, Widnes, Liverpool Hornets, Warrington, Aspull, Wigan, Litherland, 4th L.A.V. and Messrs. W. R. Thompson, H. Varley, and W. S. Rlwcliffe (vice-presidents), R. Wil- cock (hon. treasurer), and F. T. Parry (hon. sec) The chief business of the meeting was to consider a protest lodged by Wigan against Tyldesley for playing Berry' (late of Kendal Hornets), who, it was alleged, had not played in five matches, in accordance with the rules of the competition. After a careful consideration of the matter, the committee decided in Tyldesley's favour. Berry, it may be said, had only played in four matches, but was down to take part in a game which had to be abandoned owing to frost. A special meeting was held by the executive committee on Monday evening to con-

sider whether the final tie of the West Lancashire Cup should be played at St. Melens, as fist decided, there being a grand polo match in aid of the local charitable institutions on the day of the final to-day (Saturday). At the request of Mr. Pilkington, it was unanimously deci- ded that the tie between Tyldesley and Widnes be played at Warrington.

div.head: WARRINGTON COUNTY PETTY SESSIONS.
div.p: WARRINGTON COUNTY PETTY SESSIONS.

WEDNESDAY.—Before Messrs. P. Stdbs and J. Tinsley. I Does AT LARGE.—WiMam Partington Skelton ap- peared to answer a charge of having allowed his two dogs to be at large, and not under proper control, at Great Sankey, on the 19th inst. Sergeant Devlin stated that on the day in question he saw the two dogs, bne of I which was a rough-haired terrier, and the other a large' mastiff, on the Liverpool-road, Great Sankey. About 200 yards behind them was a little girl, wheeling a perambulator. Some cattle were passing, and the large dog twice attempted to bite them. He asked tht girl to whom the dogs belonged, and she told him to Mr. Skel- ton. He told her to call them, and she did so, but they would not come. He then went to Mr. Skelton's house, and informed Mrs. Skelton that he would have to report the case. Mr. Percy Davies, who appeardd for the de- fendant, said that he should have to deny the statement of the police officer. Instead of being 200 yards. away from the girl, the dogs were only about two yards. away, and were near the policeman's heels while he talked to her. Wheia she called them they came to her imme- diately, and. as to the cattle, the men in charge of them ' asked the girl to send the dog to prevent them getting into ‘a stone-yard they were passing, and she did so. The dogs, especially the large one, were constant companions of the little girl, and were perfectly under her control. I In support of this he called Martha Hughes, the girl in question. Mr. Skelton gave evidence as to the peaceable nature of the dogs. The Chairman said that the question was not as to whether the dogs were quiet or not, but as to whether the girl had sufficient physical control over them, and he was satisfied that she had not. They would fine Mr. Skelton 2s ad and costs.

THE SHIP CANAL WORKS, AND HOW THEY WILL AFFECT WARRINGTON AND THE DISTRICT.
No 10. —THE CANAL AT LATCHFORD.

In the sketch which we gave last week of a pros- pective ramble around Latchford, after the Ship Canal has been made, we brought ourselves by the new routes which will take the place of the old ones from Chi* Church to a spot on the southern side of the psesent level-crossing at Latchford Station and sear to the house of Mr. S. Gaskell. We mentioned two or three matters that would naturally strikt an observer standing at this point—such as that Mr. Gaskell's house still stands on the brink of the canal, that the surface of the canal is thirty feet below the level of the road, and that the apparatus for working the swing bridge is on the northerly side of the canal. But what will perhaps be still more obvious is that the roadway' leading to Knutsford-road passes under the great embankment of the Warrington and Altrincham railway by means of a bridge with an arch of thirty-five feet span and a height of sixteen feet. It will also be noticed that off to the left the new Latchford Station lies at a high level, at what height may with tolerable accuracy be inferred from the fact that the new railway at this point will be thirty-six or thirty-seven feet above the level of the roadway.

div.head: ANOTHER NEW ROAD.
div.p: ANOTHER NEW ROAD.

To our right as we stand on the south side of the canal a new road will branch off Grappenhall-lane and will run in a pretty straight line in the direc- tion of Morris Brook Farm, which is situate on the Warrington and Thelwall-road. Turning into this road we may notice that it skirts the south bank of the canal throughout its length, and that it is not less than thirty feet in width, for it is laid down for the benefit of Daresbury Highway Board, within whose jurisdiction this road will be, that all the new roads to be made in their district "shall be constructed by the company of a width (unless otherwise provided) of thirty feet at the least, and shall be made, metalled and channelled to the rea- sonable satisfaction of the Highway Board." For a distance along this road we shall have, still further to the left than the canal, the railway embankment full in view and indeed for the most part obstruct- ing all other view in that direction. A wall of two or three hundred yards will bring us into Knuts- ford-road, which will be intersected at right angles by the new road. Here it may be noticed from the swing bridge, which is to preserve the continuity of Knustford-road, that the waters of the canal are still some thirty feet below the leuel of the ground. Crossing Knutsford-road and continuing our walk in the direction of Thelwall-lane, we shall find that the new road carries us close past the back of the residence formerly occupied by Major Cartwright, some of the outbuildings of which, ,indeed, will in all probability have been swept away to make room for the thoroughfare. Passing on, however, a very few minutes walk will bring us to Cross-lane, or rather to what remains of this means of communication between Thelwall-lane and Knutsford-road. for at the time of which we are speaking it will have been closed for the greater part, and a portion of it cut away to alloW of the passage of the Ship Canal, and another portion covered with the railway embankment. ' ------- - • -

div.head: RAILWAY CROSSES THE CANAL
div.p: THE RAILWAY CROSSES THE CANAL

At this point in our ramble it will be noticed that the embankment and the canal come very near to each other, and indeed that a little to the Thelwall side of Cross-lane the railway passes from the north to the south side of the canal, the medium of crossing being a great viaduct fifty-one feet above the level of the ground, seventy-two feet above high water level at ordinary spring tides, and between seventy-eight and seventy-nine feet above the intended water level of the canal The new road- way on which we suppose ourselves to be will, of course, as it skirts the south bank of the canal, pass through the railway embankment or under the via- duct at thiwaint, so that on its more easterly part, while we still have the canal on our left, we shall have the embankment on on our right gradually diverging more and more to the south as it descends from its highest point over the canal. Afterpassing through the embankment,and continu- ing about a hundred yards farther on into what at present are the grounds of Alderman Pickmere, we shall find that the canal is rapidly opening out into Latchford Locks. These locks, or rather the wider part of the canal which will contain the locks, will stretch from a point near Alderman Pickmere's house to the furt'her side of Morris Brook farm, and will include the whole of the present Warrington and Thelwall road between those two points. The new road will still .continue alongside the canal, and, as the widening process referred to will take place entirely on the north side of the canal, the hitherto straight line of the road will not be broken.

div.head: FOOTWAY OVER THE LOCKS..
div.p: FOOTWAY OVER THE LOCKS..

At. present there is a roadway running from Knfitifford-road a few hundred yards on the War- rington side of the Dog and Dart Inn,. Grappenhall,. and terminating in Thelwall-lane a short distance• on the Warrington side of Morris Brook farm house.. The end of this road terminating in Thelwall-lane will be swept away by the canal, but it is interesting to note that from the end of the road verging on the canal the Canal Company are to provide and "for ever niaintain a foatway protected by suitable and stifficient handrails for the use of the public free of charge across th&canal at or near the Latchford Locks." This footway will enable us to pass at this point from the new road on the south bank of the canal to another road which is marked on the plan and alluded -to in the Act of Parliament as on the north side of the canal. A GOOD AND SUFFICIENT CART ROAD.

This road in its turn, it would seem from a provi- sion in the Act "for the protection of Arthur Hugh Smith Barry," is to be connected with the present Thelwall-road on the Warrington side of the locks. The provision reads as follows :—"The company shall construct contemporaneously with the canal, and for ever afterwards maintain on the north side of the canal, a gbod and sufficient cart road to con- nect the road numbered on the said plan 78, and on the deposited plans 106 (road referred to) in the township of Cirappenhall in a westerly direction with the Latchford and Thelwall road in the same township, such road to be constructed within the limits of deviation shown on the deposited plws or upon land sold by the owner (Mr. Barry) to the company for the purposes of such road and the owner and his tenants and all others on his or their behalf, with his or their permission shall be entitled to the free user thereof in connection with the said estate for all purposes." _

div.head: LOCKS,
div.p: THE LOCKS,

Before passing away from Latchford Locksit may be noted that they form the first break in the canal from Bastin= tidal locks. In other words, from Easthara to these locks the canalruns at one level, and in order to enable it to do so it is fortified with erafiankments at some parts of its course, and, as we have already seen, towards-the close of the length it runs through deep,cuttings. At Latchford Locks. the level of the canal will be raised some fifteen feet, and all the apparatus requisite to enable vessels to reach the higher from the lower level or vies versa will be worked by hydraulic power. (To be continued.)

div.head: FEATURES OF THE MOORE SECTION.
div.p: FEATURES OF THE MOORE SECTION.

The works at Moore, in their present stage of develop- ment, are scarcely as interesting as those in some of the other districts, nor is it likely that there will be any- thing more serious or uncommon than the excavation of a trench and the necessary embanking. The largest amount of interest will naturally be concentrated where the most skill will be brought into requisition, as at Barton, Irlam, Latchford, and Eastham, where the locks will be made; upon the sites of the docks at Salford, Partington, and other places; upon the railway diver- sions, and upon the swing aqueduct at the crossing of the Bridgewater Canal. Such as these will be landmarks along the course, though the canal proper, as an inordin- ately big cutting, will by no means be out of touch with the important events likely to occur during the process of construction. One very noticeable feature that is somewhat prominently displayed along the whole of the canal site upon which entry has already been made, is the elevated water - tank. The various sec- tions can no more dispense with this contri-

vance than railway stations can with their cisterns for replenishing the eiagine's boiler. Wherever a locomotive engine is stationed on the works, there will also be the inevitable water-tank; arranged so that the engine can be fed In the orthodox manner. The water is pumped into the elevated tank from such sources as may be readily available ; in many cases out of that subterranean reservoir, the earth itself. In this neighbourhood nb fault can be found with the dry- ness of the material now in process of excavation, for the fault is rather the other way ; and at one spot, by the shed akthe extreme end of the first cutting, there is a "yulsometer " pump hard at work, which, besides lifting out of the trench a copious supply of water, brings also a fair amount of sand which the water has charitably su§pended. Water is an element that always more or less presents itself when the earth is opened, and in many cases its treatment is an item that adds considerably to cost. Colliers know what underground water is, and the ship canal navvies will also have ample acquaintance with it before their labours are com- pleted ; and it may seem strange that so much trouble should be taken tc, get rid of a volume of water during the construction of a channel designed to hold as much water as can be economically serviceable. The discovery of a peat-bed in this, neighbourhood as a result of exploring the earth brings us within theregionof physical science, a regionby no means familiarly known to nine-tenths of the genus homo ; nor is it likely that their aspirations will induce them to trespass beyond the threshold, even though the "Golden Calf "be found in its purest form, entombed in the sanctuary of Mother Earth. This one branch of physical science—geology, is generally accredited with a particular amount of dryness, although it endeavours to translate a history that is neither written nor traditional but which is inscribed in nature's hieroglyphics on the rock pages composing the crust of the earth. Every cutting that is made, and every mine that is sunk, open these pages, bringing to light some fresh food for theo- rists, and some additional substance for commerce. The richness and fulness of the earth in every form and variety represent, with human labour, the whole capital of inan, and until brought into circulation are as- un- productive as the miser's hoard. A cutting of such depth and length of the Ship Canal, though traversing a Country well known to the economic scientist, will natur- ally expose some of that hidden treasure, and increase our knowledge of the terra cognita. Already on the section at Moore has a fine bed of peat been uncovered : a substance—call it mineral If you will—that has some commercial value, especially in a country like Ireland, where indigenous coal is scarce, and imported coal burdened with freight charges ;,and.as it is a fuel, will probably not be despised in the locality where it has been found. It is a substance that occupies the borderland between the vegetable and mineral king- doms, being coal in a chrysalis state. The etymology of the word Moore, or More, is almost an antiquarian joke. To quote the expression of an old chronicler, the name signifies "a more barren ground than marshes be ; a miry and moorish soil, yet serveth not to get turf thereon." There is little doubt but that Martinscroft, cilatebrook Moss, Risley Moss, and Rixton Moss were united ongi- nally to the parent stock now represented by Chat Moss. Whether within range of history or not the miry and moorish soil at Moore was analogous to the existing mosses record does not say, but it is quite 'evident that there was such a conditimi, or the peat would not be there..

div.head: BARTON.
div.p: BARTON.

The meadows at Salt Eye, Barton, have been made the scene of active industry, the operations in connec- tion with the construction of the Barton section of the canal being commenced there. The number of navvies employed continues to be augmented. A large quantity of material and implements has arrived during the week, including a barge load of sleepers (about 18 tons), and one locomotive engine named "Dungeness." Two other locomotives, named respectively "The Barton" and "The Irwell," and one powerful steam navvy will also be removed from the Pdtricroft Goods Yard to the meadows. Messrs, Walter ,Carter and Co., Manchester have obtained the contract for the removal of imple- ments, and hundreds of people witnessed the drawing of the " Dungeness " by a road engine through the streets to Salt Eye. The navvies are principally engaged mak- ing an embankment, as there the course of the river Ir- wellis greatly deviated.

div.head: SALFORD.
div.p: SALFORD.

On the Salford seC-ETn; OT-tile canal works, which extends to the aqueduct at Barton, the activity that has been displayed since the commencement of the oper- ations is still continued, and the face of the country is now rapidly assuming an aspect much different to that which the inhabitants have been accustomed to. At Lane End, Eccles, and in the vicinity of Barton Corn Mills, on Sir Humphrey F. de Trafford's estate, work goes on with unabated vigour, upwards of 100 men being now engaged. At the latter place rock has been touched, but blasting operations will not be commenced uatil the whole of the top soil has been removed. The corn mills referred to and also the Roman Catholic. Schools will now shortly be pulled down. The work, too, on the Barton section of the undertaking has been commenced in earnest, upwards•-of 50 men now being engaged in the construction of the ballast line and making preparations for one or more steam navvies to be got to work:.

div.head: LANDOWNERS' CLAIMS.
div.p: LANDOWNERS' CLAIMS.

The action of Park Yates v. Walker relating to the works now in progress in Cheshire for the construction of the Manchester Ship Canal came on on Saturday be- fore Mr. Justice Kekewich, sitting in the Chancery Divi- sion. The plaintiff in the action is the ground landlord of certain land at Ince, in Cheshire, and he seeks to restrain the defendant (the contractor) from committing waste and permanent injury to his property. The defence is that there is no intention of causing perma- nent injury, and that the defendant has obtained the consent of the plaintiff's tenant to bring locomotives, &c, on the land. On the motion being mentioned on Satur- day Mr. Farwell, for the plaintiff, said that some of the defendant's affidavits had been filed too late for him to answer, and after a discussion between the learned coun- sel and Mr. Moulton, Q.C. (for the defendant), he motion was ordered to stand over for a week, the under- takings given on the previous Saturday being continued. • At Chester County Petty Sessions on Saturday, Messrs. Thompson and L. Dawson, farmers, Stanlow Point, Cheshire, and cattle dealers, Liverpool, brought a claim for £3,000 against the Manchester Ship Canal Company. Mr. Pickford appeared for the claimants and Mr. J. H. Bradbury for the Company.—Mr. Pickford said the case arose under section 121 of the Land Clabses Act, which provided that if any of the lands required by the Com- pany were in possession of any, person having any greater interest in it than a tenant from year to year, and if such person was required to give up possession before the expiration of his term or interest, he was en- titled to compensation for the value of his unexpired term or interest and for any just allowance made.by the incoming tenant, and for loss or injury to the land: This, he said, was a claim by Messrs. Thompson and Dawson against the Ship Canal Company to recover com- pensation for the value of their interest in certain lands that had been taken by the Company, and for damage done to the land left by severance. The claimants held a farm of 243 acres, near Ellesrnere Port, from the Dean and Chapter of Chester, and it was peculiarly situated for their purpose, being bounded by the Mersey, by the river Gowie, by the Hooton and Helsby Railway em- bankment, and by a wide ditch. The tenancy was from year to year and terminable upon six months' notice, and it would expire in February, 1889, but fee' the fact that the custom existed on the property of the. Dean and Chapter never to enforce the six months' notice except for some good reason. This was a consideration which materially enhanced the value of the tenancy. The chief- purpose the claimants used the farm for was to pasture ' cattle that they kept for the Liverpool market, and as they had large flocks of Iceland and Canadian sheep , which were too wild to be restrained by ordinary fences the fine natural boundaries of this farm were of especial value to the tenants. Its proximity to the Mersey and to Liverpool was an additional element of value in the eyes of the claimants. The Canal Company had, takep 102 acres of this farm, and the remaining 140 acreswas cut off from access, and left without farm buildings. Messrs. Thompson and Dawson claimed £2,000 for the loss of the value in the land, and £l,OOO for the injury they would sustain in their cattle dealing business through the curtailment of a farm. Messrs. Thompson and Dawson had annthei farm at Knotty Ash, but it was the land at Stanlow Point they used for grazing purposes chiefly.—Mr. Thomas Thompson, one of the claimants, said he was a wholesale butcher in Liverpool, and was in partnership with Mr. Dawson, the other claimant. They took the farm in question in 1882, and had ex- pended £l,BOO in corn, cake, and turnips, besides pay- ing £507 to the outgoing tenant for straw. The- rent was £448. Last year they sold about 400 cattle and 6,000 sheep, 4,000 of the latter being Icelanders. He would not be able to carry on the Iceland sheep trade when this farm was cut up.—ln cross-examination wit- ness admitted first lodging a claim, for £5,000 for two years' tenancy and afterwards claiming £43000 for one year's tenancy of this very farm, The profits of tha firm were £1,500 a year after deducting the personal living expenses of himself and his partner.—Mr. Thomas Rigby, secretary to the Cheshire Chamber of Agricultdre and the Royal Manchester, Liverpool, and North Lanca- shire Agricultural Society, in his evidence described the farm as tinique for the convenience and safety of stock. Apart from the loss the claimants would have by the effect of this on their Liverpool business, witness estim- ated the compensation for the 102 acres at £1,164, this ; being calculated as if the claimants were outgoing ten- , ants and bent on making the best of it. He estimated the depreciation on the remaining 140 acres at 10s. an acre.—Cross-examined. This was on the understanding I that the claimants had a year's notice.—Mr. John White, , estate agent, Warrington, assessed the compensation at . £2,038, exclusive of general injury to the Liverpool busi- ness.—Mr. Henry Hulme, farmer, Little Woolton, de- posed that the farm was now quite £1 an acre better I than when the claimants took it in 1882.—Mr. Thomas Borthvrick, farmer and wholesale butcher, Liverpool, , said he had to pay £7 an acre for similar land near Liver- pool—Mr. Bradbury, for the defence, characterised the ' claim as extortionate and exorbitant, and submitted that the claimants had no right to get compensation for ; the Liverpool cattle dealing business. The Canal Com- pany's liability ceased when the cattle were delivered in Liverpool. He complained that the claimant had not ' produced books, and argued that the evidence he ad- duced was based on a twelve months' notice, whereas

ATTEMPTED MURDER:--A, very deliberate attempt to murder was made at Barnsley on Wednesday. James William Richardson, a young married man, employed at Messrs. Chamberlain's brickmaking works, was sum- marily discharged by his foreman, William Bourridge. about seven o' i clock n the morning. Ifn the course of the forenoon he presented himself in the office and de- manded the wages due to hint-. Bourridge was at that time in consultation in aminner room with a member of the firm, and on his passing out into the grounds Richardson fired a revolver- at- him several times, shoot- ing him in the head and abdomen. The desperate fellow then volunteered to give himself up to justice, and he walked with Mr. Frank Chamberlain ' to the Police Court, and was there remanded for a week. No hope whatever is entertained of the recovery of Bourridge. WIRRAL HIGHWAY BOARD AND THE CONTRACTOR. At a special meeting of the Wirral Highway Board, held at Hooton on Monday, the Clerk reported that the available balance in hand was £B3l Os. Bd., but that cheques were to be signed that morning amounting to £7OO 12s. Bd., leaving the actual balance at Sl3O Bs. only. But in addition to this there was a sum et £6OO due to the Board by Mr. Walker, the Ship Canal contrac- tor, and the Board was in a very fortunate position with reference to that matter. The magistrates had decided against Mr. Walker, who had given notice of appeal'. The i notice of appeal was given n time, but there was a further statutory provision which compelled the con- tractor to enter into a recognisance three days after giv- ing notice of appeal. The solicitors connected with the contractorwent for their holidays; and the recognisance was not entered into. (Laughter.) He therefore immediately wrote for the money, and he got a letter from the solicitors asking him to fore- go the Board's rights. He replied that as clerk to the Highway Board he was not in a posi- tion to forego anything in order to put the ratepayers to expense. A further letter was received, making an , appointment for March 20, and stating, "You can rely upon our finally settling this business then, either by paying under protest, or, upon your hearing the circum- stances, by allowing the appeal to proceed. The course he should take now would be to treat the notice as waste paper.--Mr. Eddowes: That is a sound legal position?— The Clerk: Of course it is. lam strongly of opinion that they are bound to pay the money, and I don't think this Board would be justified in giving them ,an oppor- tunity to put theratepayers to expense. I 'shall insist on payment beingmade to-morrow, and then we shall have a balance of ROA which will take us nicely over. —The Chairman (Mr. Charmley) : And what if we don't get it P—The Clerk (Mr. Churton) I shall tell them I shall go to Birkenhead and issue a distress warrant, and take one or two of those engines; that's all .—(Laugh- ter.)—The Chairman r You'll want a driver. (Laugh- ter.)--Mr. T. Davies:. I hope you will not take them along our roads to cut them up again.—The Clerk : It is clear that they intend to pay under protest. We'll take as many protests as they like; but it is the money we want.—The subject then dropped.
