div.p: Ittars to Mt Odor.

THE HEALTH OF MANCHESTER. Sir,—l have read, with very much astonishment, an extract from your publication stating that there are one hundred patients suffering from small pox in the hos- pital, and probably another hundred under treatment in their own homes. As this statement is absolutely with- out foundation, I shall esteem it a favour if you will con- tradict it in your next issue so as to avoid creating un- necessary alarm. I may add that not more than 80 cases have occurred in this city during the last four months. All of these patients have gone into hospital, and Ido not believe there is one at the present time under private treatment. We find that all these cases have arisen from visits to neighbouring towns, or from contact with persons coming tUerefrom.—Yours truly,
HENRY WHILE, Health Department, Town Hall, Manchester,

March 20th, 1888. [lt is absurd to say that our statement as to 100 cases was "absolutely without foundation," while at the same time admitting there have been 60 cases. And why does Mr. Whiley confine himself to "the city of Man- chester " ? There is a " greater Manchester" which goes beyond the city, whose patients are admitted to the Manchester Hospital for infectious diseases. Our statement was—" at Manchester there are at least 100 cases of small-pox in hospital." We have reason to believe that statement was., correct ; and ask our correspondent to settle the matter by g iv- Ing the exact number of" cases of small-pox in hospital" at the time the statement was made. We are glad to hear that our estimate as to the probable number under private treatment is probably incorrect; but it should be understood that it had reference to greater Manchester—including the twenty authorities within a radius of four miles of the City Hall, not the city alone.—En. Er.]

MRS. PARKER'S EMIGRATION SCHEME. Sir,—Witk regard to Mrs. Parker's scheme for the emigratiny of young Englishwomen to California, it must be admitted that its best friends are its enemies. One of the first to sound a hostile note was the British Consul, or vice-consul, or sub-vice-consul— I forget which—at Los Angeles. Some people seemed to attribute a great amount of importance to the utterances of this gentleman. They evidently thought he was a very little less personage than a Lord High Ambassador or a' Plenipotentiary Extraordinary, but, of course, some slight reflection went to show that even the representa- tive of Her Majesty's Government in an obscure Cali- fornian town is not such a very weighty individual as might at first be supposed, and when Mrs. Parker published an unmistakeably satisfactory account from one of her protegees as a refutation it was seen that she had scored heavily. Then Mr. Whitham' writing with all the intimate local knowledge which a few weeks' residence at a distance of five hundred miles from Los Angeles would, of course, give him alluded in ominous but rather vague and not altogether apposite terms to Mrs. Parker's project. In his letter last week in your columns, he includes a cutting from a San Francisco paper, which he says "contains a remarkable verifica- tion of his statements respecting Mrs. Parker's ill-judged mission." Looking through this cutting, I find that two of the most striking statements are that at Los Angeles female servants receive from 25 to 45 dollars a month, and that one of the young women sent out by Mrs. , Parker had refused an offer of 35 dollars a month. That is to say, nearly £2 a week and keep—four or five times more than could be got in England—had been offered to and refused by one of these poor deluded damsels. Really, sir, I cannot see where Mr. Whitham's veri- fication" comes in. Mrs. Parker tells young women that in California they will be much better off—pecu- niarily and otherwise—than in England, and Mr. Whitharn's " cutting " proves that so far as earnings are concerned they will be four or five times better off. To my mind the verification" is all on the side of Mrs. Parker's promises.—l am, sir, ' ONE WHO LIKES FAIR-PLAY.

div.head: FEW THOUGHTS ON VACCINATION.
div.p: A FEW THOUGHTS ON VACCINATION.

_ notice that the Warrington Board of Guardians are again troubling themselves with the thorny subject of compulsory vaccination. It appears that the anti- vaccinators are not without representatives on the Board 'to speak a good word for them, but here, as elsewhere, • their spokesmen rarely take up what it seems to me is the best "line of defence." .To totally deny the efficacy `0( YaCCivation is a hopeless plea in face of unimpugned ind unirnpugnable statistics. One cannot help think- ing that deniers of the prophylactic value of vaccination only need to study statistics in order to be converted as three eminent Germans—Drs. Boeing, of Nerdingen ; Weber, of Cologne; and Betz, of Heilbronn—were by a like process. Let us consider for a moment what sort of evidence it was through which these three doctors found salvation. In Germany from 1816 to 1872 small-pox mortality averaged as a rule between 15 and 25 per 100,000, except when epidemics broke out, in the course of one of which the mortality rose as high as about 250Wr 100.000. In 1874, re-vaccination at the ag,e of twelbe years was made compulsory in Germany, and from 1875 to 1882 the mortality from small-pox never rose higher than 36 per 100,000, and went so low as 0.3 and 0.7. This is pretty suggestive as to cause and effect, and other figures with regard to re-vaccination in the German and other armies are still more convincing. In fact, reliable statistics leave those who dispute the efficacy of vaccina- tion not a leg to stand on. Yet, paradoxical as it may seem, I am disposed to think that the future is on the side of the anti-vaccina- tors—not because vaccination is not useful, but because it will be unnecessary. It is a curious fact, vouched for by Dr. B. W. Richardson—no mean authority—in his interesting pamphlet entitled •" Hygeia" that "no malady, once originated, has ever actually died out." That is to say, we still have amongst us the germs and possibilities of the Black Death, the plague, which des- troyed 7,165 people in London in a single week, and the dancing manias and sweating sicknesses which used t 3 devastate Europe. Yet, how is it we so rarely hear of anyone suffering from these dire diseases? The answer isthat they are repelled by the advances of sanitary science. Erasmus, who visited London in the reign of Henry VIII, ascribes the sweating sickness and the plague, from which England was hardly ever free at that time, to the incommodious houses, the nastiness of the streets, and the "inconceivable sluttishnals" that prevailed within doors. And there can be no doubt that.were England to relapse into its former in sanitary conditions, it would be afflicted with all the old diseases. It is, then, a fair argument for the anti-vaccinator to use that, if so many of these other virulent diseases have been got rid ef by sanitation alone, smallpox may be banished by the swim Means. No one will deny that vaccination is an evil ; its itification is found in the fact that it is a lesser evil which wards off and protects from a greater. To my mind therefore the strongest and only hopeful argu- ment of the anti-vaconator is that sanitation—which is rip evil at all either lesser or greater, but an unqualified good—is the best preventive of smallpox. A a ssupport or this argument they .have the fact that it ii improved • sanitation alone which xeeps down other diseases that at one tithe were, perhaps, even moredestructive than small- pox.—l am, sir, Warrington. March 20th, 1888

div.head: LOCAL FOOTBALL MATCHES.
div.p: LOCAL FOOTBALL MATCHES.

RUNCORN v. SWIN?ON." A" TEAMS.—The return match was played on the ground of the former on Saturday. Swinton having started the ball, the home team soon be- gan to press. After a drop by Lunt, quickly followed up by the home forwards, enabled Ford to score, Booth failing to add the major point. Shortly afterwards Evans passed to Crompton, and the latter, after a mag- nificent dodgy run, got in between the posts, the kick at goal again failing. The second half was all in favour of the home team, the ball being rarely out of the visitors' quarters. After a good dribble by Gatley, Hampson got over, Crompton kicking a line goal. Later on a mull by Booth enabled Manion to score an unimproved try for Swinton. After some desultory play, Evans got another try. The kick again failed. Smart play by Ford resulted in Abrams again getting over, the game eventually end- ing in a win for Runcorn by one goal, four tries, and eight minors, to one try and one minor. SWINTON V.* RIINCOUN.—The return match between these champion teams was decided at Swinton on Satur- day, but owing to the counteracting influences of the county match at Whalley Range, the event did not at- tract so large an amount of attention as it otherwise would have done. Neither of the clubs was fully repre- sented, but the game, nevertheless, was a good one, and although a draw was the result, Runcorn in the end had the advantage of minor points. W. Hughes put the ball in motion in behalf of the visitors, and Roberts returned into touch at his own 25. The throw out was followed by H. Hughes trying to drop a goal, but only a dead ball was recorded in favoiar of the Runcorn men. After the kick out Cawley punted in good style, and play oncemore raged in the Swinton territory, where Woods got into possession, and essayed to bring about the downfall of his opponents' goal, but his attempt failed, and a dead only was scored. The visitors renewed the invasion, and Woods again got in his drop, a minor point being his re- ward. Roberts brought the leather out, and with a fine kick transferred hostilities into the Cheshire stronghold, after which some smart passing was witnessed between Wainwright and Broady, but the advantage gained was more than neutralised by the excellent efforts of Sharpies and Buxton. Some exciting and hard play ensued, which culminated in Roberts kicking over the Runcorn line, and forcing Brazendale to kick dead to prevent fur- ther disaster. The home forwards, by dint of hard work, were instrumental in operations being conducted for a time in front of the visitors' goal posts, but the strenuous exertions of the Lancashire men to register some tangible point were of no avail, Roberts eventually qending the ball dead with a rather strong kick. At this point Sharpies went full back, and Mills occupied the position of centre. Some nice passing between G. Buxton, Mills, and Roberts resulted in the latter punting into tcruch at the Runcorn quarter flag. The line out was followed by sterling play by the visitors, who worked the game to centre, the score at half time being Runcorn three minor points to Swinton two minor points. Upon resuming the home team played up manfully, and Mills went to threequarters and Sharpies full back. This change seemed to work, and Mills was kept very busby some really well-judged passing by Walsh of the second team, who was playing a thoroughly sound half-back game. Notwithstanding Mills, Robert?, and Winterbottom's efforts to score, the Runcorn's defence was too good,and time was called with the score standing—Runcorn 5 minors, Swinton 4 minors. Teams ;—Buncorn : J. Brazendale, full back; M, Cawley, T. Woods, and W. A. Rilq, three- quarters ; H. Hughes (captain) and G. Whitley, half backs ;W. Hughes, W. H. Broady, J. Clarke, G. 'Wain- wright, W. Dolan, F. Hancock, J. Gayter, W. Stubbs. and R. Riley, forwards. Swinton: Tr Mills, full back; F. Sharpies, S. Roberts, and W. Winterbottom, three- quarter backs; G. Buxton and S. Walsh, half backs; T. Kenyon, T. Clayton, T. Bothwell, N. Hotchkiss, S. Pollitt, J. Birch, J. Kenyon, T. Hallam, and S. Hall, for- wards.

WEST LANCASHIRE CUP : SEMI-FINAL. WIDNES v. LITHERLAND. This match, which was fixed to be played on the St. Helens club ground, was got through on Saturday last in a most satisfactory manner. The weather was most favourable for football, but a light cold wind kept the spectators hi mind that it was not summer time. The turf was in very good condition, and there would be about 5,000 present. At about half-past three Captain Smith led his men on to the field, and they looked a fine and smart lot. Shortly afterwards the Litherland team made their appearance, and, although there were one or two stalwart looking fellows among them, they certainly appeared to much the weaker team mcompanson. Smith havingwon the toss, elected to play down, having, if anything, the advantage of the wind and slope, but the sun directly opposite. Litherland kicked off, and Hughes, failing to return, was collared at about the twenty-five yards flag, where a scrimmage was formed. Farrell having obtained the leather, ran to centre and kicked across to Bingham, who made a poor kick into touch. From the line out Kiddie passed the ball into a Lither- land man's hand, and the ball being further transferred. Pennington, who was well in front, picked up, and dropped, the ball going dead. After thedrop out, Hard- man dribbled back in pretty fashion, being attended closely by Farrell, their career being stopped near the Litherland line by a good save. Plumpton next looked dangerous, having the ball directly opposite his oppo- nents' goal, but was tackled. The same player, from a pass, punted, but only a dead ball ensued. From the kick out Harding obtained, and ran round, but, being tackled, passed to Farrell, who kicked into touch. Wil- kinson getting a free kick from a knock on, Plimpton took the place kick, and the ball was well followed up, but, for some infringement, the ball was ruled back. From a scrimmage Smith passed to Farrell, who got well off and then transferred, but Litherland foiled the at- tack. The Litherland forwards were now working hard and seemed to carry one or two scrimmages, but the Widnes fellows, after this, rallied, and played up better. Barker here passed well to Harding, who missed a splen- did opportunity. Litherland gained ground from a free kick, but a combined rush/ in which Pennington and Smith showed prominently, carried the ball back again to near the Litherland goal line. The ball was then well kicked by a Litherland three-quarter back, and Bingham took a long drop towards goal, but it was very nicely returned, and Farrell appealed for a fair catch, but it was not allowed. Plumpton and I3arker then gairifel ground, and Pennington showed up well with another fine dribble. Litherland had new the advantage in con- sequence of Plumpton being out of his position, but he afterwards made amends by picking up, after a miss, and kicked right across, Kiddie catching the ball, and after a short run passed to Smith, who dashed aheaci'and planted the ball over the Litherland line; but the- re- feree, for some reason or other, did not grant the try, the ball being brought out to be scrimmaged, from which Barker dropped on the ball and obtained posses- sion from a maul. , Plumpton took the place and made a capital bid for goal,the ball dropping about a foot short of the cross-bar. First try for Widnes. From the laCk out Farrell tackled, and Pennington again used his toes with success, Plimpton kicking a dead ball. Bingham returned the ball from the drop out over the line, but it was kicked back into touch.. Plumpton' from a free kick for off-side tackling, kicked another dead ball,when half time was called. After the interval Smith kicked off from centre, the ball going into touch. Farrell picked"l up and passed to H(rdman, the latter upon beingtackted to Hughes, and through Kiddie Wilkinson obtained and' ran over, but still again the point was disallowed. Hard'- lug kicked and dribbledacross to touch in goal, a minor being the result. Litherland from the drop out earned' the ball to the Widnes territory, and through Bingham mulling it necessitated' Plumpton kicking dead and thus. yielding the only point that Litherland scored throne-- out the game. Plimpton and FaaTell next gained ground'. Plumpton had now gone to centre, and Barker to wing three-quarter, Farrell going totralf. Farrell took a kid& from a fair catch by Plumpton, and, following up, way collared close to Lithellandli line. Bingham, exchanging kicks, Farrell, Pennington, and Wilkinson put in some work, Litherland having a free kick allowed for off-side tackling. Plumpton making a fair catch, took his kitt. the ball landing in touch. Bingham here put in a good run, and kicked well into touch. From a rush Gandy got over, but again no point was granted. Bingham, returning, Wilkinson kicked the ball over Litherland line, the ball going dead. Hardman, when being taeldied. I passed, theba,ll changing hands rapidly. From a scrim:- mage the ball was passed to Plimpton, who ran round and scored a try, his kick at goal failing. From the kick out Plumpton and Farrell carried the ball back• into touch, but the referee had the ball returnedabouttwenty yards through some informality. Farrell passed spten- didly to Plimpton, who ran and transferred to Harding, the latter being brought down. Following weif up, Smith pushed a Litherland man off, and Farrell 'pounced on the ball over the line, securing a good try, upon which Plumpton put the finishing touch. From thekick out Hardman returned. Kiddie passed to Farrell, who punted nicely, and Barker following up, comple&Kl the try, from which Plumpton landed a nice goal. Lither- land seemed to be completely non-plussed about this stage, Widnes doing just what they liked with them. The ball being passed to Plumpton, he sent it across to Bingham, who mulled it, Wilkinson just saving in neat style. Farrell, taking a drop, the ball travelled along the floor to Litherland goaLthe full back touching down. From a pass by Farrell Barker got over the line, but another objection stood in the way, and the ball was ordered into play. After this Plumpton kicked another, minor, the whistle then sounding time, leaving Widnes- the easy victors by 2 goals, 2 tries, and 4 minors to 2 minor; Although Widnes were much superior to their opponents, yet the Litherland men made a plucky fight of it, and at times showed sdine very good play. It should be mentioned that Parkinson was unable to take his position at three-quarter, Harding filling the vacancy, but it is hoped he will be fit to play in the final on Shtur- day next. The following were the teams: Widnes—S. Bingham, full back ; Plumpton, Farrell, and Harding, three-guar- ter backs; Wilkinson and Barker, halfbacks; Kiddie, Hughes, Pennington, Gandy, Smith icaptain), Hard- man, Woods, J. Bingham, and Barber, forwards. Lither- land—lves, full back; J. Houghton, J. Webster, and li, Quigg, three-quarter backs; T. Larkin and M. Larkin, half backs- Blundello C. Wood, Moss, Pyles, Wilson, Bar- low, Richardson, Singleton, and Hohne, forwards,

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH 24, 1888.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH 24, 1888.

SUNDAY CLOSING MEETING AT RUNCORN. The campaign in the cause of temperance was brought to a conclusion on Monday evening, when a public meeting was held in the National Schools in support of the Sunday closing of public-houses. There was a good attendance. The Rev. A. Mait- land Wood, M.A., vicar, presided, and there were on the platform the Revs. W. H. Cogswell, MA., W. Preston, M.A.. G. A. Tindall, 8.A., 8.5. C., J. D. Ozanne, and Mr. T. Miller, of Chester, who has been conducting the campaign. Letters of apology for non-attendance were read from gthe Revs. G. Ward, A. P. Watson, and J. D. Thomas. The Chairman, in opening the meeting,mentioned three methods by which it was possible to check the sin of intemperance. Firstly. Christian workers could endeavour to reclaim drunkards; secondly, they might through the pulpit and the Press en- deavour to promote a healthy and sound public opinion on the subject; and thirdly, it could be done by means of the legislative action of the State. (Applause.) Although they could not rea- sonably suppose that the State could do anything to compel all the subjects of the State to be tem- perate, yet they might hope that the Stat 3 might be able to do something that would tend to remove excessive drinking, and the temptations for such from the way of all loyal subjects of the country. (Applause.) As to Sunday closing they were all agreed that the Lord's Day should be free from ordinary labour as far as it possibly could be, and certainly it should be free from the labour which was involved by keeping open somany houses of public entertainment. They knew thatlehere was not a single thing in the world that interfered with spiritual influence more than the sale of strong drink on that day. An- other reason why Sunday closing should be brought about was that there were a great many respectable peo- ple engaged in keeping licensed houses, numbers of them having been servants in gentlemen's families and who had saved up money which they had invested in trade, and who had respectable wives and nice children; and 1 it must be to them a terrible thing to be obliged Sunday after Sunday to keep their houses open and for them to hear the language which they ought not to hear on that day. These were substantial reasons why public-houses should be closed on Sundays. (Applause.) The Rev. W. H. Cogswell moved "that this meeting con- siders that the sale of intoxicating liquors on the Lord's Day is unfair and injurious and ought pot to be sanc- tioned by the law of this country.' (Applause.) Mr. J. D. Jones seconded the motion, and said it was high time that this christian country of ours abolished the present system of carrying on the worst of trades on the best of days. (Applause.) This was a political question; but it was free from party polities and was a sort of politics they could all agree upon. From the bottom of his heart he wished that instead of party poli- tics they might have social politics, for whilst people were fighting against each other, several questions, which were eating out the life of this country, were being left untouched. It was his opinion that social questions should be firmly grappled with by the State and the country should be made more fit for honest and good people to live in. (Applause.) It was evident that 4' we did not destroy the liquor traffic it would_ dest;

Lroy in the estimation -of other nations. If we did not reform in this direction we should have to play second fiddle to other nations; and that he did not desire to live to see. He wished to see this country setting a good example to all the nations of the world. (Applause.) The resolution was carried unanimously. Mr. T. Miller then proposed that a memorial in favour of Sunday closing should be signed by the Chairman and forwarded to the Prime Minister, the Home Secretary. and the member of Parliament ior the Division. Mr. Miller remarked that from what he had seen of Runcorn men and women during the past week he believed there was a feeling of intense earnestness prevailing such a feeling that had not previously existed in Runcorn on that subject. They appeared to have realised their in- dividual responsibilities and that there were dutieswhich they owed to themselves, to their families, and 'to the community, and to the King of Kings and Lord of Lords. (Applause.) The Rev. W. Preston seconded the motion, and said they had been singing about freedom; but when drink and Satan reigned there could be no freedom. He ap- pealed to those present to assist in putting down the curse, and in making the slaves of Satan and slaves of drink what they ought to be—free men, true and proper Englishmen. (Applause.) One great step towards the accomplishment of that would be Sunday closing. (Ap- plause.) This had been found 'successful in some parts of the country, and why should it not be a universal , success. (Applause.) Some years ago he made a canvas of ' the publicans of the town and he found that two-thirds of them admitted that Sunday closing would be a blessing to the community; but some of them would not consent to close unless-the others undertook to do so, and a num- ber of them held out against the suggestion. It would be a blessing to the inhabitants of the town, and to tha publicans themselves, if the houses were closed on Sun- days, and he did not believe that it would in the least injure the publicans. (Applause.) The Chairman remarked that ttle principle of the thing was already part of the legislation of this country, and they only desired it to be extendedr which was a very reasonable request. The motion was carried, and the customary votes of thanks concluded the meeting.

TERRIBLE ACCIIYENT AT WIDNES. IMPORTANT VERDICT. At the WidnevAccident Hospital ons Tuesday, Mr S. Brighonee, the coroner, held an inqoest on the body of a labourer named William Cank, aged 56 years, who had lived at 31, Bank-street.. Mr. Y. J. Poole, solicitor, watched the proceedings-on behalf of the relatives of the deceased, and Mn Tay- lor represented the Arm of Messrs. Hutchinson and Co. Mr. Kyle and Mr. Rawcliffe were- also present from the works. /t appeared that Calni . had been employed at the works of Messrs. Hutchinson and Co. for many years, and at half an hourrpast mid- night on the ICth February he ascended to the top of a condenser in folfilment of one of his duties. The night was dark and stormy, and according to the deceased's-own version of the accident as related to Miss Downie. the matron at the hospirts4 his foot slipped on theice•Costed boards, and he-fell on to the narrow platform upon which he had been pre- viously standing, The lamp which he was-carrying went out, and' he stretched forth his left handy to try and discover wheretho hand rail was, bin he failed_ He then put forth his right hand, and in ciNag. so, MI through an open space to, the ground below; a.digance of about fifty- feet.. Some workmen near heard his feeble cries fer• assistance, and he' was conveyed to- the Atcident Hospital, where it was discovered that he had received serious in- jury to the spine and other parts of the bodjyand that his right leg-was fractured. Every attention- was paid to the unfortunate man-by Drs. Cooper and Hutchinson, but he succumbed to shock to the system. on Monday morning. Before the inquiry on Tuesday,. the • jury., of which Mr. 'P.' Athertonwas foreman, visitedthe scene- of the accident; and foundi that the open space-of four feet through whieh the deceased had fallen was boarded ever. A number cf iWitnesses-were called, and were °questioned by Mr. Poole to show that the place was of a very dare gerouls character, and that it was not sufficiently-pro- ; tected. Mn Kyle stated that the condensers had been ' erected for 12 or 14 yaars and there had never been an accident bifore. He said object of having the-open space was to facilitatuthe repairs necessrlry to the-con- densers. John McEcoachy, the foreman, in reply 10-Mr. Poole, saiderepairs were-needed once every two or-three years.—Mr.. Poole: Drat you think the man would have been alive now if that open space had been covered —The Coroner They have admitted i'z-by boarding it themselves. He afterwards added that it was. quite clear that if the plazeiltad been in the same condition at the time of the accident as it was that day this sad'affair could nonhave happened..--The jury after a lengtyy de- liberation in private, returned a verdict of Accidental death, t-Ind added a.tpresestment that ix,. their opinion the 'place where the deceased fell through ves not sufficiently protected, that the- rail placed over the same-was not sufficiett, and that the place ought to to ;tame been boarded as it appeared at present.

RATEPAYERS' MEETING AT RUNCORN. Th 9 annual meeting of the ratepayers of Runcorn was neld in _Bethesda School-room oh, Thursday evening. Mr. .E. liaison, an overseer, presided, and the attendance was up to the average,. The first business was to elect two gentlemen to audit the acccunts of the Burial Board, and on the proposi- tion of Mr. Toone, seconded bze Mr. T. Cock, Messrs. C. Cooke and :T. Cooke (insurance agents), were ap- puinted t otttlfil that duty. It was resolve that the accountaahould be produced to the auditors on the fourth Apriii. and that the meeting to received theirsre- port should-be held on the nth April.—ln consonance with custure, the Chairman gave some details of the :financial operations of the overseers-. They had, he said, commenced the year with £666 4s in hand, and in- cluding this the total receipts had been £5,307 4s 10d, the April rate having prodececl £2,532 is sd, and the October sate £2,106 7s 2d. On the other side there hod been paid to the Board of Guardian,st £3,183, an increase of £414 on the previous year: to the School Board £950, a decrease of £2OO, and to the Burial Beard £2BO, an increase of £6O on, the previous year; The cost of the registration of voters was £46 is 4d, but half of this expense would be received from the Govern- ment. The other expenses, including the assistant over- seer's (Mr. Sutton's) salary, printing, and items, amounted to £263 14s. The balance in hand at the present time was £584 9s 6d. The rateable value of the township in April was £52,371, and in October was £59,989 14s 2d, but of the latter amount £7,618 14s 2d was the subject of appeal by the Manchester Ship Canal Co.—Mr. Sutton having stated that Mr. Whittaker desired that he should not again be put in office as an overseer, as he was "get- ting into years," and had been in office long enough, it was resolved to submit to the magistrates the following list of names of gentlemen qualified to serve asoverSeers: —Messrs. W. Headley, E. Imison, S. Taylor, W. Haukin.

son, H. J. Grice, J. Pritchard, W. Mellor, J. R. Frith, G. MOSS, and G. Bellamy.—The Chairman observed that Mr. Whittaker was one of those unselfish sileat men, who were worth a world of talkers, and he had invariably given unremitting attention to the duties of his office, and had carried out whatever work had been entrusted to him in a most efficient and capable mart- ner. He was sure that meeting would desire to show theit appreciation of the good work which he had per- formed for such a long period of time.—Mr. Hankinson moved in felicitous terms a vote of thanks to Mr. Whit- taker for his past servicekand the motion having been seconded by Mr. Heesom, was carried by acclamation. A vote ot thanks concluded the proceedings.

div.p: OUR FINANCIAL LETTER.

[FRolt OR OWN 001 RESPONDENT...I 17, Union Court. Old Broad-street, E.C. Mr. Goschen's conversion scheme and its influences upon the market is still the leaning subject of interest en the Stock Exchange. The full effect of this conversion will not be realized for some time to come, but already there are indica- tions of a return to very hazardous speculative business for which perhaps the most fittest term, would be pure gambling. Investors in the 3 per cent, cannot be expected to accept such a loss as Mr. Goschen would force upon them. Consequently many of them are looking abroad for investments, which, if not so sound, will yield them something, better than n per cent. An active demand is thus created for every class of in- vestment that yields something better them what is offered them by New Consols, and as a consequenve prices in every department have steadily advanced. Home Rails have become an active 'field for investors, as have also Egyptian and one or two Colonial Stocks. The rise' in the former amounts in some instances to over 4, and swill stocks as North Western and Great Eastern, which hardly varied per cent, in a month, have suddenly jumped up from 2t04 in a week. Even such speculative stocks as Mexican Rails have caught the impetus given to general investments, and quite a brisk businessillas been done in them at from 2 to 3 per cent, higher than a fortnight previously, although towards the close of the week there is a tendency in the more speculative class of Home Rails to lower prices, as aaresult of some large selling on behalf of the speculators to realise. The gamble still continues fa diamond mining shares, the chief attention still being concentrated upon Be Beers. Dur- ing the past week some heavy speculative dealings have taken place, and as a consequence the prices of Be Beers has dbOpped from 49, at which it stood last Thursday, to under 45. Fortu- nately everything indicates that this craze is confined to,a few leading financial houses, and Hatton Garden and the public have Rept aloof. There is no doubt that legitimately large profits are to be made in Kimberley Diamond Mines, but at the same time the present price of the shares is no guide as to the intrinsic value. There has been quite a lull in the speculation for copper since the diamond craze began, and copper shares havebecome comparatively neglected. Tiutos, around which so much excitement was concentrated a short time since, are steady' at a fraction under 19, while Mason and Barry has scarcely varied since last week. Gold mining shares have been comparatively neglected re- cently, owing to the attention that has been given to the in- vestment business, and, as a consequence, prices in nearly all mining shares have become weaker. In this class Indian gold mines are certainly deserving attention,. and Mysore gold, which is the leading Indian mine, will probably very shortly ,be quite £2 higher than they can be bought at at present. Don Pedros have also become quiet, but during, the past day or two there has been considerable demand for these shares, with the result that prices have stiffened. In other mining shares there are a 'few which if bought at present price should prove a very profitable investment. Among these New California's at 7s 6d should.be worth double their present price in a month or two. Consolidated Esmer- alda should also improve in value. A special feature of the past week has been the remarkable rise that has occurred in the shares of the Nitrate Railway Company; Our readers will remember that we mentioned this company in January as being likely soon to come to the front. The company promoter evidently realizes that there is a chance for him while the conversion scheme • fil in progress, and all sorts of ventures from bread companies to sewing machine companies are being offered the public: After the repeated failures of the various sewing machine companies that have been offered the public we cannot db otherwise teen express astonishment that any promoterrshould offer another. With a share capital of £150,000 and £6ol`oo'3 per cent. debenture stock, the Springwell Brewery Company, Limited, has been formed for taking over and carrying use the well- known brewery at Heckmondwike. Dewsbury, neseLeeds, and known as the Springwell Brewery. It was established in the year 1867, and has been successfully carried on ever since. As the business is very large, and with a view Jo future exten- sions, it is considered desirable to continue ita development by means of a joint stock company, with its stockieand shares Issued to the general public.

;ALLEGATIONS,A.GATNST A PARNWORTH CLERGYMAN. thi F2iday, at thf•Law Association-rooms,. Liver- pool, a court appointed by the Bishop of Linerpool sat to consider certain charges of drunkenness which had been, brought against the Rev. George Bond, Vicar of Farnworth, in the diocese of; Liver- pool. The • Win.. Archdeacon Lefloy presided over the court, which otherwise consisted of the, Rector of Liverpool (Canon A. Stewart), , canon Warr, Mr. John Brancker,, and Mr. R. Gladatmne. Mr.. Gamon was a:resent, as registrar to the lAshop. Mn. Arthur Lowndes, proctor, appeared i* support of the charges amd M William Mackenzie, solicitor, represented the defendant, who, was present dur- ing the inquiry. The investigation took place in consequence of a petition. which as pre- sented tc. the Bishop signed •by Mr. Peter Longton and. 14r. Thomas Baker. "2h,e court basing assembled, Mr. Mackenzie,. on be- half of the defendant, asked elle court to exercise the right and powers they had under- the Act of Parliament, and to direct that the inquiry be held ia privarfeinstead of in publior.—Archdeonon Lefroy: This inqpiry will accordingly be held itt private.— lffpon,thas.intiniation beinglmade the reporters who , were in attendance retired—At the close of the 'evidence, and after tile curt had &aerated, the Teporters4weee admitted, when Archdeacon Lefroy • 'delivered the decision of the court as:follows :—The `comraissionnrs, having heard all the depositions of • the various witnesses, tvad having carefully con- ' sidened these depositions, have come unanimously to the conclusion that there is sufficient prima facie evidence for instituting proceedings against the party accused. THE DEFECTS OW THE LOCA.TrAiOVERNMENT BILL. "Truth " says There are two criticisms of many others which might be made that occur tamewithregard to Mr. Ritchie's 111. (1) It fails to base county govern- ment upon the government of; the village by.tho village. (2) It creates a vested interest in the liquor licenses that does not exist at present. Micense is now for one yew At the end of the year it is renewed for a further year or it is refused, If refused, etmn without cause assigned, the holder has no claim to compensation. By\the bill no holder of a license, unless he has misconducted himself or his house, can be deprityed of it without compensation. Now, supposing that there are 20 public-houses in a town, and,it being deemed that there are 10 too many, these 10 are suppressedwith compensation to their owners The value of the remaining 10 would be doubled. Put- ting aside, therefore, the question whether compensation ought to be granted, it is obvious that with compensation every reduction of the number of public-houses in a place would increase the amount of compensation that would have to be granted to those remaining if they too were suhressed.

div.head: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD ELECTION.
div.p: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD ELECTION.

Thursday was the last day for nominating gentle- men to serve on Widnes Local Board in place of the five members who retire by rotation. The nomina- tions are as follows:--,-Messrs. B. Brown, Francis Heyes, John Taylor, David Wright, F. C. Liddell (chemical manufacturer), and John Horrabin (tool- maker, Halton-view.) The first-named fiver gentle- men are the nominees of the Owners' and Occupiers' Association, and Mr. Horrabin is nominated by Mrsrs. Wm. Gerrard, Thomas Minton, James r Randle, John Smith, and John Williams. Messrs. Brown, Heyes, Taylor, and Wright have served the ratepayers on the Botird for many years past, and Mr. Liddell is selected in the place of Mr. W. T. Husband, who resigned a few months ago. An effort will be made to avoid the cost and trouble of a contest by inducing Mr. Horrabin to withdraw.
BLOCKING WIDNES DOCKS: HEAVY FINE.

Before Mr. G. Pilkington and Mr. T. S. Timmis, at Widnes Police Court, on Thursday, William Deacon, master of the flat Buckley, was summoned for ob- structing the traffic in the Widnes Dock, the pro- perty of the London and North-Western Railway Company, and refusing to obey the orders of the pier master.—Mr. Preston, junr., prosecuted on be- half of the company, and Mr. J. W. Knowles defew- ded.—Mr. Przston statedthat on the 18th February, the flat "Belgium," laden with salt, was making for the Widnes locks, and in order that the flat could pass through in its proper turn a rope was made fast to the "island." At this time the defendant came up with his flat "Buckley," and fastened a rope in front of the mast of the "Belgium," and when asked by Fox, the pier master, to slacken his rope, be used violent and abusive language. In conse- quence of his refusal to obey orders, the complain- ant lost fifteen minutes, and as time and tide waited for no man, this was of considerable importance. The practice of disobeying orders was grow- ing, and .he asked that a heavy penalty should be inflicted.—Witnesses were called who con- firmed this statement.—Mr. Knowles contended that the defendant only sought to go through the lock in his turn as he was before the Belgium. He had no desire to break the law, and he denied that be was ever asked to slack the rope.—ln answer to questions by the magistrates, Fox, the piermaster, said it was the rule to allow the laden fiats go into the lock first, because they could get the " light " flats in after. On this occasion it was ebb tide, and there were seven or eight flats waiting to enter. The Belgium was drawing six feet of water, and the Buckley only three feet six inches.—The Bench said it was of the greatest importance that the rules for regulating the traffic should be obeyed, and the defendant would be fined 40s and costs making alto- gether £3BB.

div.head: ALKALI WASTE.
div.p: ALKALI WASTE.

_ Mr. S. G. Rawson, B.Sc., demonstrator of chemis- tryl in Liverpool Unive *ty College, on Tuesday de- livered a lecture in the c oal theatre on the re- covery of sulphur from alkali waster There was a large attendance, including several of the leading alkali manufacturers from Widnes and St. Helens, The lecturer explained by diagrams the new pro- cess of Mr. Chance, of Birmingham, by means of which carbon-dioxide gas was passed into the al- kali waste which had been made info a thin cream. The reaction took place in iron vessels, calcium carbonate being formed, and sulphuretted hydrocen evolved at the sametime. Then the sulphereted Ey- drogen was passed main the series of cast-iron vessels, termed carbonators, until the gas produced contain- ed about 30 per cent. a sulphuretted hydrogen. This woo then passed on into a gasholder. The calcium carbonate produced wtas removed from the carbona- tors Mil used afresh either in the manufacture of soda mah or of cement,.for both of which purposew it seemed to be well fitmd. The surphuretted hy- drogen + was either burnt to form sulphurous acid gas and' used in the lead; chambers in the ordinary way, orpassed through a, clans kiln; by means of which brimstone can be used, The lecturer said it seemed probable that the. process would pay even if the present prices for pyrites remained station- ary, adv6nced, or fell, because in the two formerin- stancee it would be profitable to.inanufacture either sulphuric acid or sulphur, and in the latter case the production of sulphur would be the more advanta- geous, as there was a large market throughout the world for Sicilian sulphur; and sulphur obtained by the newprocess would Vs able to take its place. At the close.a cordial vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Rawson.

Womax.—On Friday morn- ing. a man named Henry Pass was murdered by a woman named-Jemima Cobbley, a marine Wore dealer, of Cheapside, Birmingham, under extraordinary circunaa. stances. Pass was keeping', company with Cobbley's sida- ter. A quarrel had taken place between them, which caused the woman to break the engagement off. Early on Friday morning; Pass went to Cobbley's house, an& was refused admittance: He rushed round to the back and forced an entrance. Mrs Cobbley, thinking he had come to do some violence;. armed herself with a hammer,. and dealt him several blows on the head with it, ,mash- ing his skull. The.mamdied shortly afterwards at the hospital, and hie murderer-was at once arrested by the police, the accused being brought before the magistrates ' on Friday morning and remanded.

TERRIBLE EXPLOSION. AT A POWDER MILL. A disastrous explosion took', place, on Friday, at Fernilee Gunpowder Mill,. near Buxton, Derbyshire. The works are a miscellaneous collection of sheds and mills, isolated in a valley near the source of the river Gorft. Two sisters', named Martha and Maria Turner, eighteen and sixteen years of age respectively, and a mechanic named John Whitfield, who was working in the cartridge room, were so . severely injured that they were at once removed to the 'Stockport Infirmary. The building was blown to atoms.

THE FLOODSHSK HUNGARY.

PESTH, FRIDAY.—Most distressing reports continue to be received of the floods in the TheissTalley. Yesterday, the water at several points burst the.dlykes, whereby the towns of Csaba and Bakes -escaped destruction, but enormous tracts of cultivated ion& were laid waste. Over 80,000 acres are now submerged, and for miles the eye meets nothing but water._ Railwa,y, communication is almost entirely interrupted.. THE FIRE AT THE :OPORTO. THEATRE.

The remains of, the victims of the disaster at the Baguet Theatre were on Thsarsday exposed for identifi- cation at the cemetery, the number of bodies amounting to sixty-six. Besides these,, there are also fifty-three heaps of unrecognizable human, remains. The identifi- cation was accompanied by many heartrending scenes. In some cases whole families perished together. Several 1 works of charity have been organised for the benefit of the families of the poorer victims.
